#5576. Spain’s Housing Crisis Sparks a Revolt Against Tourism. Could America Feel the Fallout?

Millions of workers walked off the job across Spain on Wednesday, demanding relief from soaring rents, evictions, and housing speculation. It was the the country's first general strike in 14 years.

In Barcelona, protesters rattled house keys and chanted, “O baixen els lloguers, o cremen els carrers," which translates to “Either rents fall, or the streets burn.”

Over the past decade, rents in the City of Counts have climbed more than 50%, with tourism adding pressure on an already strained housing market.

In the coastal city of Málaga, Mónica Reino, 56, has watched that transformation unfold in her own apartment building.

“Every year it gets worse,” she told AFP, estimating that half of its 20 apartments are now tourist accommodations.

Tourism is far from the only force driving Spain's housing crisis. In popular vacation destinations, property owners can earn more from short-term visitors than year-round tenants, creating a financial incentive to convert residential housing into tourist accommodations.

A day after the strike, lawmakers narrowly approved a package of housing measures, including a new 10% tax on qualifying vacation rentals.

The conflict mirrors one already playing out in vacation destinations across the United States, where booming tourism has helped sustain local economies while putting housing increasingly out of reach for residents.

But as restrictions on vacation rentals make accommodations scarcer and more expensive abroad, could more travelers turn to U.S. destinations, intensifying the housing pressures those communities are already struggling to contain?

Spain's efforts to restrict short-term rentals were already changing the market well before this week's protests and housing vote.

Available short-term rental listings fell 5.9% in October compared with a year earlier, while average nightly rates jumped 12.5%, according to a new analysis from AirDNA, which tracks vacation rentals across platforms such as Airbnb and Vrbo.

Part of the price increase reflects a shift toward more expensive properties as licensing restrictions remove rentals from the market. But even rates for comparable existing properties rose 8.2% over the past year.

Spain had an estimated 355,000 tourist dwellings in 2025, according to the Bank of Spain. Although they represented just 1.5% of the country's housing stock, they accounted for roughly 10% of its rental market, with much higher concentrations in tourist neighborhoods.

Research suggests those concentrations can have substantial consequences for local rents.

Airbnb's expansion pushed residential rents up 7% in Barcelona neighborhoods with the highest levels of activity between 2012 and 2016, according to a 2020 study published in the Journal of Urban Economics. Across the city, the estimated increase was 1.9%.

"Short-term rental activity can crowd locals out of homes that might otherwise serve as conventional rental homes, reducing the number of options available for those living in the area permanently and raising prices," Joel Berner, senior economist at Realtor.com®, says.

But he cautions: "This effect is probably not the main factor affecting affordability."

Even so, Barcelona plans to let all 10,101 existing tourist-apartment licenses expire in 2028, while Málaga has suspended new licenses for three years.

The restrictions could return some tourist accommodations to residential use. Whether enough properties will become available to ease housing costs remains uncertain.

Spain welcomed more than 80.5 million international tourists during the first nine months of 2026—a 5.2% increase over the same period last year. Americans accounted for nearly 3.9 million of those visitors, with arrivals growing more than twice as fast as overall international tourism.

On its face, it's a counterintuitive trend: Higher accommodation costs have hardly deterred American travelers. But part of the explanation may lie in who can afford to keep traveling.

Higher-income households, supported by record household wealth, are driving a disproportionate share of U.S. travel spending, according to the U.S. Travel Association. While rising costs are forcing some households to adjust their plans, wealthier travelers are better positioned to absorb higher prices.

And generational wealth could add to the advantage, too. Visa estimates that $36 trillion will pass from baby boomers to younger generations over the next two decades, with housing and travel among the sectors expected to benefit.

If that pattern sounds familiar, it's because inherited wealth is also helping determine who can afford to own a home at all. In Spain, parents gifted their children more than 30,000 homes last year, while in the U.S., a record 10% of first-time homebuyers relied on an inheritance for their down payment, according to a November report from the National Association of Realtors®.

And if rising accommodation costs abroad encourage more travelers to vacation closer to home, those pressures could intensify.

There's no evidence yet that the restrictions sweeping across Europe are redirecting tourists to U.S. destinations, but domestic demand is already growing fastest in smaller, relatively affordable markets.

Nights booked in small-city and rural U.S. markets increased 8.4% in October from a year earlier, compared with just 1.1% growth in urban markets, according to AirDNA.

"The closest parallels are American tourism hubs where housing is limited and the conversion of homes into STRs force tourism industry workers to live far away," says Berner. "Think Hawaii, Mountain West ski towns, or New Orleans.

"In the more urban locations (like New Orleans), the upward pressure on rent is more concentrated in tourist-heavy neighborhoods than in the metro area at large. But in the more remote destinations without suburbia to absorb displaced locals, the effect is stronger," Berner says.

Nantucket, MA, offers a particularly telling example. The tiny island of just 48 square miles hosts nearly 2 million visitors annually.

More than half of the housing stock (55%) is reserved for seasonal or occasional use, according to a Realtor.com analysis. That scarcity set against high demand has helped push the median home listing price to $4,925,000 in June—more than 11 times the national median of $430,000.

And it's not just lower-income workers being priced out, either.

Roughly 1,080 renter households, including those earning well above the local median income, were effectively shut out of homeownership without significant financial assistance, according to a 2025 housing assessment.

The shortage is so severe that it’s threatening the island's ability to sustain its workforce. A 2026 workforce housing study found that 64% of surveyed employers had lost or declined to hire workers because of housing challenges.

Nantucket Cottage Hospital has identified housing as the leading reason candidates turn down jobs or employees leave.

"Workers get displaced, but communities get hollowed out, too," Berner says. "Schools get weaker, tax bases become more fragile as they are more exposed to tourism downturns, and entry into the community through homeownership becomes more difficult."

For communities that depend on tourism, restricting vacation rentals presents another dilemma: How much visitor spending can they afford to lose in the effort to preserve housing?

On Long Island's North Fork, officials are considering restrictions that would cap short-term rental permits in Southold Town at just 119 properties, compared with approximately 640 active listings in October.

Those rentals generate an estimated $27.5 million in annual revenue for property owners, according to town figures reported by Newsday.

But reducing that business doesn't guarantee more housing for residents. Nearly 37% of the town's housing units were seasonal residences in 2020, and many owners purchased their properties primarily as second homes.

As Realtor.com previously reported, those owners may simply stop offering short-term stays rather than sell their properties or convert them into annual rentals.

Diane Mollica, a local real estate agent with the Gambino Group, says many owners primarily use their properties for their own enjoyment, making a widespread shift to year-round housing unlikely.

Yet the housing shortage is already threatening the businesses that depend on tourism.

"We cannot build a sustainable tourism economy on the backs of a workforce that can no longer afford to live here," Amanda Giuliano, a Southold business owner and co-chair of the town's Economic Development Committee, told Newsday. "If we don't have people working, there will be no tourism."

Spain faces the same conflict on a much larger scale.

Tourism contributed €200.7 billion (about $221 billion) to the Spanish economy in 2024, accounting for 12.6% of GDP, according to the country's National Statistics Institute. The industry supported more than 2.7 million jobs, representing 12.3% of employment nationwide.

That economic dependence helps explain why then, even against a backdrop of a nationwide general strike, the 10% tax on vacation rentals passed only in a 35 to 34 vote.

The new levy is scheduled to take effect on Dec. 1. But even so, the measure could be short-lived. Spain faces a snap election on Nov. 29, triggered by parliament's earlier rejection of the government's housing decrees, and the opposition Popular Party has pledged to repeal the measures if it takes power.

And even if the restrictions survive, reducing tourist accommodations could still come at a cost to the businesses and property owners who depend on them, without producing enough homes for local workers.

Berner argues that increasing housing supply offers a way to accommodate both.

"Encouraging more homebuilding is the only long-term solution to a housing shortage and has the ability to expand tourism capacity as well," he says.

Allaire Conte is a senior advice writer covering real estate and personal finance trends. She previously served as deputy editor of home services at CNN Underscored Money and was a lead writer at Orchard, where she simplified complex real estate topics for everyday readers. She holds an MFA in Nonfiction Writing from Columbia University and a BFA in Writing, Literature, and Publishing from Emerson College. When she’s not writing about homeownership hurdles and housing market shifts, she’s biking around Brooklyn or baking cakes for her friends.

#5575. How Kyle Whissel built eXp’s top real estate team

The San Diego-based CEO recruits up to 15 agents a month, has a dress code and gives his trainer authority to cut newcomers.

Kyle Whissel has a standing instruction for his “60-day” bootcamp trainers: they should be willing to cut people.

His team brings in 10 to 15 new agents a month, puts them through approximately 60 hours of training over two weeks, and gives the trainer a goal of removing two people from each class.

It’s a striking approach from the leader of eXp Realty’s highest-volume U.S. team in San Diego, California. Whissel is CEO of the Whissel Beer Group, formed in 2025 when his Whissel Realty Group merged with Daniel Beer’s Beer Home Team.

According to Whissel, the team made $875 million in sales volume across 1,042 transaction sides last year (it was the first team in San Diego to break 1,000). The median price in San Diego — which is where he likes to focus his attention  (“we love that median price,” he said) — is around $1 million, he told Inman.

They’ve done that by hiring — and retaining — the right people. “We’ll give people an opportunity to prove themselves … but we’ve grown far more by cutting people than simply by hiring more people,” Whissel told Inman‘s Taylor Anderson during an interview at eXpcon in Salt Lake City earlier this month.

The company’s saying: “Expectations without enforcement are simply suggestions.”

Whissel’s recruiting process starts with a conventional, short interview, but he views the company’s two-week training period as a far better measure of whether someone belongs on the team.

Spending 60 hours in training gives leadership a chance to observe how that person behaves, learns and responds to expectations. Role-playing and scripting exercises also reveal whether new agents have the communication skills needed to work with clients.

The process continues after training, too. New agents are assigned mentors, and Whissel said those mentors are empowered to recommend removing someone who fails to meet team standards.

“If you’re going to be disrespectful to our team, I’ll be damned if I’m going to give you a client because you’re probably going to be disrespectful to them too,” he said.

Whissel also has activity and production expectations for agents already on the team. They include participating in role-playing sessions and attending meetings, along with meeting production targets.

Whissel’s hiring philosophy reaches back to his own first job, scooping popcorn at a movie theater, where he would compete with others to see who could serve the most customers. He looks for that same competitiveness in prospective agents, even if their previous accomplishments have little to do with real estate.

An applicant who participated in a college sorority, for example, might be asked whether they held a leadership position. Whissel said he wants to understand whether someone has a history of taking initiative.

In August 2025, Inman reported the merger of Whissel Realty Group and Beer Home Team, two of eXp’s highest-producing organizations. The combined company launched with approximately 160 agents and more than 60 staff members across five offices.

He said the first six months involved understanding the two organizations’ systems and getting them aligned. Whissel now believes it could take 18 months to fully integrate the companies.

“We’re going to be almost flat year-over-year,” he said, referring to the team’s expected 2026 performance, “but we’re setting up for a really, really big 2027,” he said. “You’ve gotta take a step back to take two steps forward.”

He remains optimistic about 2027, when he expects the operational investments to begin contributing to stronger growth.

Agents need to understand assumable mortgages, he said. “If you are working with a seller … and you’re not asking questions to figure out ‘does this seller have an assumable mortgage?’ (If it’s FHA, VA or USDA, those are assumable), I’m gonna beat you, because I am asking those questions.”

To find out whether a mortgage is assumable, agents simply need to get the closing disclosure from the seller. “It’s simple,” he said.

#5574. Thanksgiving Is the Worst Day of the Year for Cooking Fires—Is Your Kitchen Prepared?

If you’re hosting loved ones this Thanksgiving, now is the time to get your kitchen ready. Otherwise, a nice holiday meal could turn into a costly and dangerous ordeal.

According to the latest data from the National Fire Protection Association (NFPA), about 1,139 home cooking fires were reported to U.S. fire departments on Thanksgiving Day 2024.

That’s a 321% increase over the daily average, making Turkey Day the leading day of the year for home cooking fires.

“People don’t ever set out to leave the kitchen unattended, but a minute is all it takes for a grease and oil fire to take over, and there’s a greater risk of that happening on Thanksgiving when every burner is going,” says Payton Kashani, personal injury attorney, president, and managing partner of Sunset West Legal Group PC in Los Angeles.

By preparing your kitchen ahead of time, you can reduce the risk of fires and enjoy a delicious and safe celebration with family.

The NFPA says that unattended cooking is the leading cause of home cooking fires. And that’s quite common on Thanksgiving Day.

Many dishes are usually being cooked at once on the stove, oven, and various countertop appliances. Add in a house full of guests that bring constant interruptions and you’re left with a risky situation.

“Thanksgiving fires aren’t usually about cooking appliances going wrong. They tend to happen in those few minutes when someone steps away to greet a guest at the door. Distractions like this can wind up causing serious burns with long, painful recoveries that shake up a family’s normal life,” explains Amanda Demanda, founder of Amanda Demanda Injury Lawyers in Miami.

Grease and oil fires are particularly concerning because there are so many dishes cooking at the same time.

Additionally, despite the fact that the NFPA strongly discourages the use of oil-based turkey fryers due to fire and burn risk, many people put a frozen or wet turkey into hot oil and cause a fire.

“Fires can also stem from flammable items that get left near the stove, like kitchen towels or food packaging. Loose sleeves may get caught up in the mix, and when things catch on fire, many of the injuries that arise happen from people trying to fight the fire themselves,” adds Demanda.

Before Thanksgiving cooking gets underway, prepare your kitchen and anyone who’s going to be in it or near it.

When you’re frying, boiling, or broiling, stay in the kitchen and set timers so you’ll know when dishes are ready. Once they’re done, check that all burners and your oven are off before you leave the room.

Keep everything that can catch fire well away from the burners, oven, or any other appliance that generates heat. These include towels, paper and plastic bags, oven mitts, wooden utensils, and food wrappers.

“If you’re going to wear long sleeves, make sure they’re close-fitting rather than loose,” says Demanda.

Demanda recommends keeping a lid on standby.

Your fire extinguisher should be within reach as well. Just make sure it’s always near the stove and everyone in your home knows how to use it.

In addition, skip the task of oil-frying your turkey if possible. If you like the taste, buy it already fried or use an oil-less fryer instead.

“In the event you do use a traditional fryer, keep it away from your house, place it on a flat, even surface, and ensure [the turkey] is fully thawed,” says Stephanie Fox, national spokesperson at American Red Cross.

Lastly, direct kids and pets out of the cooking area.

“Kids and pets running around your kitchen are a burn injury waiting to happen, so make sure you have a spot for guests to gather away from your cooking zone,” adds Demanda.

Rich Repich, home services expert at Cinch Home Services in Boca Raton, FL, recommends setting up appetizers and drinks in a different room so guests don't crowd the cook and giving them a separate table to leave any used dishes.

#5573. 12 housing bills that could shape affordability after the midterms

Concerns over housing supply and affordability have reached a fever pitch and become a major issue for voters in this year’s midterms.

With the midterm elections just days away, housing affordability remains a pressing issue for voters — and a growing legislative priority for lawmakers in Washington.

Congress has spent much of the past two years considering proposals aimed at lowering housing costs, helping first-time buyers, unlocking existing inventory and encouraging new construction. But despite growing bipartisan interest in housing policy, many of those proposals remain stalled in committee as voters prepare to decide which party will control Congress.

Lawmakers scored a significant bipartisan victory in July with the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, a sweeping package aimed at boosting housing supply and addressing barriers to development. Yet much of the broader housing agenda remains unfinished, including proposals to expand homebuyer assistance, increase affordable housing investment and raise the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Some bills have continued attracting additional congressional support in recent weeks, but none of the proposals highlighted in September has advanced since. With both chambers largely out of session until after Election Day on Nov. 3, further legislative action will likely have to wait until lawmakers return to Washington.

Inman revisited the most consequential housing bills that could help shape the federal government’s approach to supply, affordability and homeownership in the next Congress.

What it does: The bipartisan legislation would double the capital gains exclusion on the sale of a primary residence, from $250,000 to $500,000 for individuals and from $500,000 to $1 million for married couples, and automatically adjust those limits over time to account for inflation. Why it matters: Supporters argue that the limits, which have remained unchanged since 1997, discourage longtime owners with substantial equity from selling and effectively lock inventory off the market. NAR has made the proposal a major 2026 priority and is currently framing it as one of the fastest ways to increase existing-home supply. Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means and the Senate bill before Finance, and neither has advanced beyond referral. Support has continued growing, however, with 159 House cosponsors and 25 Senate cosponsors as of late October, including lawmakers from both parties. With Congress largely out of session until after the election, inclusion in a broader tax package during the lame-duck session or next Congress remains one possible path forward.

What it does: This legislation would establish a refundable federal tax credit equal to 10 percent of a first home’s purchase price, capped at $15,000. Eligibility and the size of the credit would be subject to income and local home-price limits.

Why it matters: Unlike proposals intended to increase supply over time, the bill would directly reduce the cost of purchasing a first home for qualifying households. The tradeoff is that giving buyers more purchasing power does not add more homes to the market, and in a supply-constrained market, it can also put upward pressure on prices.

Status: Both versions were introduced in July 2025 and remain before the House Ways and Means and Senate Finance committees, respectively. Neither chamber has taken action beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Maxine Waters, D-Calif., the bill would increase the mandatory share of Federal Home Loan Bank earnings devoted to the system’s Affordable Housing Program. The Consumer Federation of America estimates the change would generate roughly $300 million in additional annual funding for affordable housing development, down payment assistance and home repair programs, without requiring additional taxpayer funding.

Why it matters: The 11 Federal Home Loan Banks provide liquidity to more than 6,500 member institutions, including banks, credit unions and community development financial institutions. Housing advocates have argued that the system should devote more of its earnings to its public mission. In a broader reform proposal, the Coalition for Federal Home Loan Bank Reform has called for doubling the mandatory Affordable Housing Program contribution from 10 percent to 20 percent, which it estimates would add about $600 million annually for affordable housing.

Status: The House Financial Services Committee considered H.R. 10325 on Sept. 16, but a motion to report the amended bill favorably failed 21–28. That leaves the measure facing a significant setback in the House, even as housing and consumer groups continue pushing for broader FHLBank reform.

What it does: Designed to make it easier to pull together a down payment, this bill would raise the amount first-time buyers can withdraw from an IRA without paying the usual 10 percent early-withdrawal penalty from $10,000 to $50,000.

Why it matters: The proposal targets a major barrier for many prospective first-time buyers: saving enough cash for a home’s down payment and covering closing costs. It would expand access to buyers’ existing retirement savings rather than create a new federal subsidy. NAR lists the bill among its current legislative priorities.

Status: The House version remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate companion, introduced by Sens. Ruben Gallego, D-Ariz., and Todd Young, R-Ind., is before Finance. Neither has advanced beyond committee, though the Senate bill’s bipartisan sponsorship distinguishes it from some other first-time buyer proposals.

What it does: Seeking to make homebuilding and rehabilitation more feasible in distressed neighborhoods, this legislation would create a federal tax credit to support the construction and rehabilitation of owner-occupied homes where development costs exceed what finished properties can command on the market. The credit is designed to help close that gap and make projects financially viable.

Why it matters: The credit is intended to make starter-home projects possible in communities where builders currently cannot make the numbers work, with a particular focus on for-sale housing rather than rental development.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance. In May, the bipartisan sponsors released planned revisions, including more flexibility for state housing finance agencies and a shorter four-year authorization, that they intend to carry into the next version of the bill, whether in a year-end package or the next Congress.

What it does: This proposal would establish a federal investment tax credit covering 20 percent of qualifying costs to convert nonresidential buildings into housing, increasing to 30 percent in certain areas where development is particularly challenging. At least 20 percent of the resulting units would need to remain affordable to households earning no more than 80 percent of area median income for 30 years.

Why it matters: The bill targets two persistent real estate problems at once — underutilized commercial buildings and the shortage of housing. Office-to-residential conversions have attracted substantial interest, but challenging layouts, financing hurdles and construction costs can make projects difficult to pencil out. A tax credit is intended to help close that feasibility gap. NAR also lists this bill among its 2026 legislative priorities.

Status: Introduced in March 2025, the bipartisan bill has attracted 57 cosponsors, including lawmakers from both parties, but remains before the House Ways and Means Committee without advancing beyond referral.

What it does: Focused on expanding and modernizing the Low-Income Housing Tax Credit, the proposal includes a broad series of changes involving tenant eligibility, project financing and credit administration.

Why it matters: LIHTC is a central federal financing tool that helps drive the construction of affordable rental housing across the country. Congress already adopted two pieces of the broader proposal in 2025, permanently increasing annual Housing Credit authority by 12 percent and lowering the bond-financing threshold from 50 percent to 25 percent. According to the National Council of State Housing Agencies, roughly two dozen other provisions remain unenacted.

Status: The House bill remains before Ways and Means and the Senate version before Finance, with both measures drawing broad bipartisan support. Advocates continue pushing the remaining provisions either through the standalone bills or as part of future tax legislation.

What it does: The bill would update federal rules for mortgage revenue bonds and mortgage credit certificates used by state housing finance agencies, including increasing limits on certain home improvement loans and changing refinancing and recapture provisions.

Why it matters: Those programs can help lower- and moderate-income households access lower-cost mortgage financing, giving this technical tax legislation a direct connection to homeownership affordability.

Status: The House version, introduced in February 2026, remains before Ways and Means, while the Senate bill remains before Finance. The Senate measure was discussed during an Oct. 21, 2025, Senate Banking housing subcommittee hearing, but neither version has advanced beyond committee.

What it does: Seeking to open underused land owned by churches and other religious organizations to new housing development, this bill would preempt certain state and local laws that block affordable housing on those properties.

Why it matters: Religious institutions collectively control substantial amounts of land, including parcels in expensive housing markets where zoning can constrain redevelopment. The bill is notable because it tackles supply by asserting federal authority over certain local land-use restrictions, rather than relying primarily on grants or tax incentives.

Status: Introduced by Reps. Scott Peters, D-Calif., and Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., in September 2025, the bipartisan legislation remains before the House Financial Services Committee. Rep. Emilia Strong Sykes, D-Ohio, joined as a cosponsor in October, but the bill has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: This measure would amend the Fair Housing Act to prohibit discrimination based on a person’s source of income, veteran status or military status.

Why it matters: The change would expand federal fair-housing protections for veterans, service members and renters who rely on housing vouchers or other lawful sources of income. It could also create new federal compliance obligations for landlords, property managers and real estate professionals.

Status: Both versions remain in committee, with the House bill before Judiciary and the Senate measure before Banking, Housing and Urban Affairs. The House proposal has continued attracting support, reaching 23 cosponsors following the addition of Rep. Joaquin Castro, D-Texas, on Oct. 22. Neither chamber has advanced the legislation beyond referral.

What it does: Rather than establishing a tax credit or housing-production program, the Saving the American Dream Act would require HUD, Treasury, Agriculture, Veterans Affairs and the Federal Housing Finance Agency to coordinate housing research and market data and submit a joint report to Congress identifying opportunities to improve housing affordability.

Why it matters: Federal housing policy is currently divided among HUD, Treasury and other agencies. Supporters of the effort argue that greater coordination could reduce conflicting policies and give Washington a more coherent strategy for addressing affordability.

Status: Introduced in September 2025, the bipartisan bill remains before the House Financial Services Committee and the Veterans’ Affairs Subcommittee on Economic Opportunity. It has attracted 40 cosponsors, including two who joined on Oct. 1, but has not advanced beyond committee referral.

What it does: Introduced by Rep. Norma Torres, D-Calif., on Oct. 22, the legislation would establish a new HUD grant program to help states streamline financing and administrative processes for affordable housing development. The proposal would authorize $90 million annually from fiscal 2027 through 2029, including funding to consolidate state financing programs, simplify applications for builders and improve access to development assistance.

Why it matters: Affordable housing developers often navigate multiple state agencies, financing programs and administrative requirements to move projects forward. By simplifying those processes, the proposal aims to reduce administrative barriers that can delay projects and increase development costs. States that meet the bill’s initial requirements could also use funding to streamline zoning, permitting and Low-Income Housing Tax Credit administration.

Status: Torres introduced the bill without cosponsors on Oct. 22, and it was referred to the House Financial Services Committee. It has not advanced beyond committee referral.

NAR’s current legislative agenda is centered heavily on housing supply, with the trade group estimating the country is short 4.7 million homes. Following the passage of the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July, NAR has continued pressing lawmakers on housing supply, with its latest advocacy materials putting particular emphasis on unlocking existing inventory through the More Homes on the Market Act and proposed changes to the capital gains exclusion for longtime homeowners.

The organization is also pushing lawmakers to fully fund several HUD programs, including fair housing enforcement and housing counseling services, while calling for long-term reauthorization of the National Flood Insurance Program. NAR says the flood program supports roughly 500,000 home sales each year and argues that lapses or uncertainty around coverage can disrupt transactions in flood-prone communities.

The flood insurance program’s current authorization expires Dec. 11, the same day a temporary spending measure funding federal agencies, including HUD, is set to expire. The deadlines leave Congress facing another round of funding and insurance negotiations during its post-election lame-duck session.

Passage of ROAD has not ended NAR’s work on the legislation itself. Many of the law’s new grants and housing programs still depend on future congressional appropriations and HUD rulemaking, including incentives for local housing production, zoning and permitting reforms, commercial-to-residential conversions and home-repair programs. NAR is now encouraging states and local governments to prepare for those programs, while pressing Congress to provide the funding needed to put them into effect.

Implementation of the law is also underway. On Oct. 22, the Treasury Department proposed regulations clarifying restrictions on large institutional investors purchasing single-family homes. Under the law, beginning Jan. 7, 2027, investors controlling at least 350 single-family homes will generally be prohibited from purchasing additional properties, subject to exceptions for activities including build-to-rent and renovate-to-rent programs.

For qualifying programs designed to help renters become homeowners, the proposal also establishes a framework for a 30-day first-look period and a right of first refusal before investors sell the properties to other buyers.

Reporter’s note: This story was originally published on Sept. 24, 2026, and has been updated to reflect the latest available information.

Additional note: AI tools were utilized in reviewing and verifying current federal housing bills, legislative priorities and related reporting for this story. All substantive details were checked against congressional records, primary-source materials and prior reporting before publication.

#5572. Homeowner’s Massive 60,000-Light Christmas Display Dubbed a Safety Hazard by HOA

'Tis almost the season for goodwill toward all—unless you’re Neil Heuer and his neighbors.

Heuer, a semi-retired tech entrepreneur, lives in Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in community in Waxhaw, NC, with his wife and their children. Over the past several months, he’s been locked in a battle with Aero Plantation's HOA over his annual Halloween and Christmas displays, which his neighbors say disrupt the neighborhood and make them feel unsafe.

Heuer has been putting on the light shows, which include more than 60,000 lights, choreographed animatronic displays, and coordinated music programming, for the past five years. He estimates he's spent more than $70,000 on the exhibitions.

But after last year’s shows, his neighbors began complaining. Those complaints led to a hearing, a lawsuit, and proposed potential changes to the HOA’s bylaws that would prohibit Heuer’s Christmas and Halloween spectaculars in the future.

For his part, Heuer believes the drama has little to do with the lights and more to do with a golf course dispute and a once-anonymous newsletter he penned to bring HOA issues to light.

"I realize that this is a little unorthodox, but, you know, everybody celebrates things differently," Heuer says of his light display. "I have friends that celebrate their birthday for the entire month and I might be lucky to have a slice of cake on my birthday, but it doesn't matter. This is this is my hobby. I love to share it with people. I sit outside and record it myself, and I smile. I'm I'm just so giddy with it.""It's it makes me happy, which is good," he continues. "Especially right now because I do feel like it's draining. It's been a very draining experience."

Neil and Stephanie Heuer moved to Aero Plantation, an exclusive fly-in neighborhood that includes a private airstrip, tennis courts, an equestrian center, and other luxury amenities, six years ago.

The Heuer's five-bedroom, 8,000 sq. ft. home sits on 2.36 acres and includes a pool and a four-car garage. Property listing photos show a home hidden in a copse of woods on the edge of a pond.

Heuer told Realtor.com he initially got into the holiday displays because of his interest in tech and because his children enjoyed the shows.

“The kids got a kick out of it, and I thought it was cute,” he says.

His neighbors enjoyed the shows, too, he says.“There's a time I can tell you that our neighbors came over and danced in our driveway. We sat and just talked and sat on the front porch and just... It was really nice," he adds.

Two years ago, though, things took a turn.

Heuer alleges the inciting incident was a disagreement with the HOA board’s vice president over a proposal to “rejuvenate” the community’s golf course. Heuer objected to using reserve funds on the golf course. The vice president offered to pay for the upgrades personally, promising that annual maintenance on the course would be around $8,000, Heuer said.

“After that, I started an anonymous newsletter,” says Heuer, meant to “ask questions”

The newsletter "was critical of the HOA, but there was nobody asking these questions. I was anonymous because I really didn't want to receive backlash for asking questions. I didn't want to be on the receiving side of what I'm experiencing now, basically, if that makes sense.”

When it was uncovered that Heuer was behind the HOA-critical newsletter, “they basically weaponized the HOA against me,” Heuer says.

At this year’s annual community meeting, when it was revealed that the golf course’s upkeep would run closer to $16,000, he brought up the discrepancy.

“Everybody looked around at me and said, ‘Sit down and shut up,” he says.

Heuer contends that those factors—not the light show itself—have upset his neighbors and led to a hearing earlier this year over alleged HOA violations.

In a letter sent to Heuer this past August, the HOA’s legal counsel, Benjamin Karb, wrote that “Inviting unknown members of the public into the subdivision is the type of offensive activity that is a nuisance or annoyance to the neighborhood” and accused Heuer of violating the HOA’s Declaration.

"They believe the roads are private and that nobody belongs here who doesn't live here, I guess," Heuer says. "Let me tell you, 90% of the cars that go by my home I don't recognize. There are people driving by every day who aren't neighbors. And somehow, when they're here to watch my show, they suddenly have a problem. And the people watching my show are families with kids in the backseat."

In September 2026, the HOA held a hearing on the holiday display, alleging it violated the community’s declarations on exterior lighting, signage size, traffic and guest limits, and architectural alterations.

Of major concern was the flow of traffic through the neighborhood by locals looking to see the light show. Aero Plantation is not gated, but it is a private residential community, and the HOA owns and maintains the roads.

In a September 15 letter following the hearing, Karb wrote that when it came to the visitors, the board "did not find a violation exists at this time.”

However, Heuer was found in violation on lighting and signage sizes. The board was unable to make a determination on parking and whether the Heuers had architecturally altered their home’s exterior.

Ironically, the sign that violated the community’s signage limits was one Heuer erected to let visitors know that the off-duty sheriff’s deputies patrolling the neighborhood had been hired by the HOA, not him.

In early October, Heuer filed a lawsuit in North Carolina’s Union Superior Court alleging the HOA overstepped its authority, failed to provide proper notice and hearing procedures, and that the restrictions being enforced had never been formally adopted in the bylaws.

That case is ongoing, but in the meantime, the HOA board sent out a notice that it was adopting new parking rules in the community.

"While normal visits from family, friends, and personal guests are always welcome, the Rules explicitly address situations where activities conducted, sponsored, or permitted by an Owner attract non-resident traffic—even if the Owner did not personally invite or know each visitor. Owners are held directly responsible for any traffic, stopping, or parking resulting from these activities on our private roads," the notice reads.

Around the same time, a notice was sent to homeowners about two proposed amendments to the bylaws, one of which would establish “standards for public attractions and activities that generate substantial or recurring nonresident traffic within the community,” and another that would create “standards for flashing, strobing, pulsating, and high-intensity exterior lighting and authorize the Board to adopt implementing rules consistent with the Declaration.”

The vote on amending the bylaws is scheduled for the end of January, so Heuer plans on going big once more with his holiday display this year.

"Whatever these cockamamie rules that they're trying to change will not apply to this year,” says Heuer.

Realtor.com reached out to the HOA board to inquire about the dispute. In an emailed response, Aero Plantation HOA President David Arno wrote: “Mr. Heuer filed a lawsuit against the Association, to which the Association will respond through the appropriate legal process. The North Carolina Planned Community Act authorizes an HOA’s members to implement additional changes to a Declaration, which is what members are being asked to decide. The Board does not intend to comment further other than to remind members to voice their opinions by deciding if they want to approve the proposed changes or not.”

After a notice about the proposed amendments were sent out, Heuer emailed his neighbors, imploring them to think twice about adding more amendments to the bylaws.

“Look, you may not like our light show, you may like it. But I don't think we need more rules,” he says.

Regardless of the vote's outcome, Heuer and his wife have decided they’re moving out of Aero Plantation as soon as their youngest daughter, currently a sophomore, graduates from high school.

"There's two things I can assure you," he says. "One is that I will not live here after my daughter graduates. And my next neighborhood will not have an HOA."

Julie Gerstein is a writer and editor based in Philadelphia. She previously worked at Business Insider as an executive editor covering news, entertainment, and digital culture, and was the company's founding Singapore bureau chief. She was also a senior editor at BuzzFeed, covering lifestyle, fashion, and beauty. She earned a B.A. in women's studies from the University of Pennsylvania and an M.A. in media and cultural studies from the University of Sussex.

#5571. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5570. Savannah Guthrie Extends NBC News Contract as Search Continues for Her Mother, Nancy Guthrie

To see our latest updates on the Nancy Guthrie case, please click here.

Savannah Guthrie has extended her contract with NBC News, solidifying her spot as a co-anchor on “Today.”

The decision comes months after it was previously reported that the host was expected to “never return” to her on-air role, as she waited for answers regarding the Feb. 1 kidnapping of her mother, Nancy Guthrie.

Guthrie, 54, returned to the show—and her home in New York City—after a six-week hiatus.

“Savannah is the best in the business,” a Page Six source said on Nov. 12. “We want her to stay for as long as she wants to stay.”

In 2024, the outlet previously reported that the journalist—who joined “Today” in June 2011 as chief legal correspondent and a co-host of the show’s third hour—earns between $7 and $8 million annually.

A People magazine source described Guthrie as “not only so unbelievably strong,” but as “the glue that keeps the show together.”

Authorities are still investigating her 84-year-old mother’s abduction from her Tucson, AZ home—and Guthrie continues to feel the weight of the tragedy each day.

“It’s always with me,” she shared during a June episode of the morning news show. “I cry every morning on the way to work, and I cry every morning on the way home.”

The most recent update in the case comes with a former FBI agent’s revelation that she had received four disturbing ransom messages concerning Nancy’s disappearance. The former agent, Jennifer Coffindaffer, shared she had been targeted by individuals claiming to have information about the disappearance, and demanding cryptocurrency in exchange for her return.

Coffindaffer could not confirm the authenticity of the communications, and believed the messages may have been sent by individuals hoping to capitalize on the high-profile investigation.

The former agent passed the communications to the FBI. The bureau was able to confirm that the cryptocurrency wallet address provided did not correspond with those associated with previous ransom notes investigators considered to be potentially authentic.

Anyone with any information about Nancy Guthrie's case should call 1-800-CALL-FBI, 520-351-4900, or 88-CRIME, or visit tips.fbi.gov.

Coffindaffer had initially chosen not to share the emails publicly, but had a change of heart after Lauren Serpa, a woman who lives near Nancy’s home, had received and shared similar communications—which included unsettling photos of Nancy and religious references that appeared to be tailored to the family’s Catholic faith.

Coffindaffer had become concerned that others following the investigation could become targets for individuals seeking money.

Guthrie has made a series of public pleas, in hopes of sharing a “very specific message” with the individuals who could have information about her mother’s disappearance.

“It has been months since our mom was taken from us. Our family is in agony. We are in a nightmare that will not end. Nothing about our situation has changed. We have done our part. But we will never stop looking for her,” she said in a July statement shared to Instagram.

“We will always ache for her and feel that hole in our hearts,” she continued. “The world can be a cruel and unforgiving place, and I know that you have tried to do things the right way, so I am asking you, begging you to do the right thing now.”

Guthrie closed the statement with an ask for help, and a promise that it’s “never too late to do the right thing.”

“I always believe there is a way home,” she said. “Please make the right choice.”

Nancy was first reported missing at around 12 p.m. local time on Feb. 1, around 14 hours after she was dropped off at the property following a family dinner. When she failed to turn up at her usual church gathering on Sunday, her friends alerted her family, who found her home was empty.

Officials have noted during a Feb. 5 media briefing that, while times are approximate, the team pieced together several pieces of evidence to indicate Nancy's movements—and the timeline of her apparent abduction.

5:32 p.m. Nancy travels to Annie's house in an Uber for "dinner and playing games with the family."

9:48 p.m. A garage door at Nancy's house opens when she was dropped off at the property by her daughter.

9:50 p.m. The garage door closes, indicating that Nancy was inside the home.

1:47 a.m. Nancy's doorbell security camera is disconnected.

2:12 a.m. Movement is detected on a security camera at the home. No footage of this is currently available.

2:28 a.m. Nancy's pacemaker app indicates that the device has been disconnected from her phone.

11:00 a.m. Nancy fails to arrive at the home of a friend, where she had been due to watch a church service livestream.

11:56 a.m. Nancy's family travels to her home to check on her and finds the property empty.

12:03 p.m. The family calls 911 to report Nancy missing.

12:14 p.m. Police officers arrive at Nancy's home.

Police uncovered evidence inside the property suggesting the 84-year-old was "taken" from her home against her will, and "harmed" during the alleged "abduction."

Law enforcement still had no suspects, but were investigating multiple ransom notes and tips providing potentially helpful information.

Savannah Guthrie releases her first public plea, asking for help in finding her missing mother.

Authorities detained a man for questioning after reviewing footage of a masked, armed intruder tampering with a security camera outside of Nancy's home. It was unclear if the person who was questioned was the same individual from the footage.

The FBI announced it was conducting a new "extensive" search for Nancy in the area surrounding her Arizona home. The Pima County Sheriff's Department noted it had received nearly 18,000 calls about the case, and that "several hundred detectives and agents" were assigned to the ongoing investigation.

The Guthrie family was officially cleared as suspects.

Law enforcement officials revealed the kidnapper had a "target."

"I think this was an individual who had a target for whatever reason, and he has made it tough, but I've got some pretty tough investigators, too," Pima County Sheriff Chris Nanos shared.

Guthrie broke down in tears as she offered a reward of up to $1 million for anyone who was able to provide information leading to the recovery of her mother.

It was reported that the FBI decided to pull nearly all of the agents assigned to the case out of Tucson and return them to the agency's Phoenix headquarters.

A man was arrested outside of Nancy's home on DUI charges after he was seen driving past the property "50 to 100 times" while looking at a photo of the missing woman on his phone. A spokesperson confirmed the arrest, but noted it had no connection to Nancy's case.

Additional evidence was identified—ranging from DNA found on various objects and thumbnail images from motion-activated cameras in Nancy's backyard—but the search continues.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5569. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5568. Five thoughts from Cisco’s first quarter of fiscal 2027

GUEST COLUMN by Zeus Kerravala

Cisco Systems Inc. opened fiscal 2027 with a quarter that should put any question about whether artificial intelligence will act as a massive tailwind for it to rest. Revenue and earnings hit records, growth rates were the best Cisco has posted in more than 15 years, and management raised its full-year outlook and AI infrastructure revenue target.

While Cisco has delivered a string of solid quarters, some investors are concerned about the durability of the growth. After listening to the analyst call, I maintain that accelerated growth is what Cisco watchers should expect, as AI will act as a catalyst for several years. Here are my five thoughts, plus the one metric I think investors should care about most:

Asked why this isn’t simply the top of a hyperscaler spending cycle, Chief Executive Chuck Robbins (pictured) cited five growth drivers: hyperscale AI, the campus refresh, the “post-Mythos” security upgrade cycle, sovereign infrastructure and enterprise hybrid data centers. “All five of these are multiyear, multibillion,” he said. “And they’re all in relatively early stages.” In particular, the enterprise opportunity is in its infancy. Using the baseball analogy for “what inning” we’re in, the pitchers are still warming up, and enterprise is what Cisco does best.

Though hyperscalers have been driving AI growth across the industry, only one of the five trends Robbins highlighted was related to that group of companies. Chief Financial Officer Mark Patterson reinforced the point by breaking down the guidance raise, noting that a large share came from Cisco’s core, non-hyperscale business. “It’s not just campus,” he said. “It’s broad-based, and the core continues to do quite well.”

The market still views the enterprise as a slow-refresh business. The call made a strong case that it’s about to become the bigger part of Cisco’s AI story.

During the investor Q&A, a data point was worth highlighting. Robbins said that of the campus switching Cisco sold this quarter, “only 9% was really coming from the new portfolio.” Despite multiple quarters of strong campus growth, the installed base has barely moved to the next generation.

Two forces will push this base to accelerate an upgrade. One is agentic AI, which Robbins said is driving “modernization for bandwidth reasons” because agents generate traffic that campus networks were never designed to handle. The other is the security fallout from frontier models such as Anthropic’s Claude Mythos — the Mythos moment. “We’re beginning to hear from customers who are attributing orders to early Mythos implications,” Robbins said, noting that European service providers are upgrading managed customer premises equipment.

Robbins added that customers “got to get the architecture exactly right.” That suggests a long, deliberate redesign rather than a buying spree, which is characteristic of a multiyear cycle.

Cisco has long been criticized for building its own silicon as the industry shifted to merchant silicon. Robbins said that outside of optics, the hyperscale AI business is “100% Silicon One-based platforms.” The P200 continues to win scale-across deals, and the G300 is now in customer labs.

Asked why Cisco keeps winning those deals, Robbins kept it simple: “It’s really about performance and power. And there’s just this whole focus on diversity of silicon in the space.” The second point is the more strategic one. No hyperscaler wants a single supplier for any critical layer of its AI fabric, and Cisco is the credible second source.

The bigger long-term play is the enterprise. Silicon One is already shipping across parts of the enterprise portfolio, and Robbins said the target to convert all of it by fiscal 2029 “is still on track.” That gives Cisco a single silicon architecture from the hyperscale data center to the branch, with cost and roadmap control competitors can’t match.

The reality is that at Cisco’s volumes, it makes no sense to buy merchant silicon. Not only can it build it cheaper, but it can also optimize it specifically for its own features and capabilities.

A theme running through the call is that AI is decentralizing. “Our enterprise customers will be running AI applications in the cloud, but they’re also investing heavily in private data centers,” Robbins said. “They want to run open-weight and open-source models in their own data centers. They want to train on their own data in their own data centers.”

Sovereignty is driving in the same direction, with Cisco extending its Sovereign Critical Infrastructure portfolio from Europe to Canada and preannouncing India. Robbins noted that Cisco is “one of the few companies that has maintained a robust on-premises portfolio.” For years, analysts treated that on-premises focus as a liability. In a world where countries and regulated industries want operational control, it has become an advantage.

Equally important is what Cisco isn’t chasing. Robbins called neocloud exposure “relatively immaterial,” adding that “we’ve been very conservative relative to the credit situations.” That’s a disciplined choice. Cisco is growing into the safest parts of the AI build-out rather than financing its riskiest buyers.

Given the number of neoclouds, one could look at them as a massive pot of gold, but they often required vendor financing. If the neocloud isn’t successful, it’s the financing organization left holding the bag. This was the case with CLECs in the Internet days. Cisco was conservative then and will continue to be.

Security has been the weak spot in Cisco’s story, so this quarter’s progress matters. Robbins said core security orders, excluding Splunk, were “the best it’s been in three years,” with firewalls, Zero Trust secure access, and AI Defense all gaining customers. Patterson said Cisco is “a little bit above the expectations that we set out” and feels “good about turning the corner.”

The refresh cycle drives near-term numbers, but the strategic prize is trust for AI agents. Robbins said enterprise conversations now center on “agentic security, agentic identity, agentic observability, as well as the new security architecture needed for the AI era.” The network is where agent traffic flows, making it the natural enforcement point. Cisco owns more of that network than anyone.

Investor concerns received clear answers. On margins, Patterson said, “gross margins are pretty much right on target,” and on supply, “we’re seeing not a lot of issues at all.” Robbins added that Cisco is growing revenue “with less headcount than we had at the beginning” two years ago.

The number I’d watch most closely isn’t AI revenue, campus orders, or gross margin. It’s the growth of Cisco Cloud Control. Robbins mentioned it almost in passing, noting thousands of sign-ups and integrations with AI Canvas, Cisco IQ and Cisco Model Foundry. Most people will think of Cloud Control as a network management tool, but that badly understates its potential.

Cloud Control is now Cisco’s core product. The best analogy is VMware vCenter, the data center’s control point that turned a collection of products into a sticky platform. Cheaper, sometimes free hypervisors never made a dent in VMware’s share because the operational control gained from vCenter far outweighed the few bucks saved on hypervisor licenses. Cloud Control is broader and potentially more impactful because Cisco is positioning it as the control point for enterprise AI, not just the network through the following capabilities.

Cisco’s numerous network and security competitors have their own agentic operations platforms, and many beat Cisco to market. However, Cisco played the long game. In my conversations with Chief Product Officer Jeetu Patel, he has been emphatic about how important Cloud Control is to Cisco’s vision of shifting to a platform company. It enables customers to manage the underlying infrastructure, including third parties, through a single dashboard.

If Cloud Control becomes the enterprise IT console for managing AI-era infrastructure, Cisco stops competing on boxes and starts competing on control. Hardware cycles always ebb and flow, so always being best of breed is impossible. Whether this one becomes a transformation for Cisco depends on whether customers run their environments on Cloud Control. My advice to Cisco is to start disclosing active usage, partner integrations, and attach rates for the platform.

My advice to investors is to start asking for them. That number will tell you what Cisco is worth five years from now.

Zeus Kerravala is a principal analyst at ZK Research, a division of Kerravala Consulting. He wrote this article for SiliconANGLE.

#5567. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.
