#5566. Hit Songs to High-End Homes: Inside Taylor Swift’s Real Estate Portfolio

Taylor Swift has once again found herself at the center of the cultural conversation, as she's set to return to her country music roots and take the stage at the 2026 CMA Awards—her first performance at the event in 13 years.

The pop star's last sang an acoustic rendition of her hit song "Red" at the awards show in 2013. While it's anyone's guess what Swift, 36, will do this year, she's among the nominees for Single of the Year, thanks to "I Knew It, I Knew You" from "Toy Story 5."

The ceremony is also set to hold a special tribute for country music legend, Dolly Parton, who passed away at the age of 80 on Aug. 25. It's unclear if Swift will be part of the memorial.

Of course, the "Patient Zero" singer is no stranger to speculation, especially after the busy year she's had both professionally and personally. Over the summer, Swift tied the knot with Kansas City Chiefs tight end, Travis Kelce in a star-studded ceremony at Madison Square Garden.

The newlyweds also seemingly have their hands full with a new $5.35. million sprawling lakefront estate in Ohio, not far from Kelce's childhood home. But it's not the only impressive dwelling in the singer's headline-worthy real estate empire.

Over the years, the 14-time Grammy winner has assembled a multimillion-dollar property portfolio that includes eight homes.

The collection spans across New York, Rhode Island, Tennessee, California, Rhode Island, and Ohio, with each home reflecting a different chapter of her life and career.

The singer, who reached superstardom after the release of her 2006 self-titled debut album, has homebuying down to an art.

Let's take a look at some of the properties the Grammy winner has scooped up over the years—from a glamorous landmarked Beverly Hills abode to a downtown Manhattan compound, and more.

Swift grew up on a picturesque Christmas tree farm near Reading, PA, and she honored her childhood home in her 2019 song “Christmas Tree Farm.”

Swift's father, Scott, purchased the 11-acre farm from a client and spent time tending to the grounds when not working his full-time job at Merrill Lynch, according to Refinery29.

A few years later, Swift moved with her family to a nearby house in Wyomissing, PA.

When the property hit the market in 2022, fans got a rare look inside the Georgian-style estate.

Standout features of the five-bedroom house include a sun-drenched breakfast nook, a glossy brick fireplace, and plenty of wainscoting.

The stately residence was listed for $1,099,000 in February and sold for $800,000 in June—a 27% reduction. Is this potential proof that not everything Swift-related turns to gold?

The family moved out of Pennsylvania when Swift was a teen.

In 2003, the family relocated to Hendersonville, TN, so that Swift could pursue a music career. Here, her parents paid $790,000 for a 6,758-square-foot home that sits 30 minutes by car from downtown Nashville.

The waterfront home with "fantastic views" of the Cumberland River features four bedrooms, five bathrooms, and well over an acre. The family still owns the property.

Swift purchased a $2 million luxury condo in Nashville's vibrant Music Row neighborhood for herself just four years after signing a record deal with Big Machine Records.

The three-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom penthouse boasts over 3,500 square feet of living space.

According to reports, she also scooped up the smaller one-bedroom apartment below hers that same year for $387,000. She's still the owner of both units.

Swift added another Tennessee property to her real estate portfolio when she snagged a Greek Revival mansion in the gated Northumberland Estate neighborhood of Nashville.

The singer purchased the four-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom mansion in 2011 for $2.5 million. The classic mansion from 1934, which sits on 5 acres, is now estimated to be at least double what she paid.

The glamorous home features a striking curved staircase, vaulted beam ceilings, floor-to-ceiling windows, and marble fireplaces. Swift purchased the property for her parents.

Swift shook things up in 2012 when she headed West and picked up a $1,775,000 midcentury modern home in Los Angeles.

The four-bedroom abode featured floor-to-ceiling windows, a private courtyard, a lagoon-style pool, and a 1,000-bottle wine cellar.

She sold the property six years later for $2.65 million, clearing nearly a million in profit.

You might have missed this quick flip. In late 2012, Swift bought a seven-bedroom waterfront home in Hyannis Port, MA, for $4.1 million.

The singer sold the property just a few months later for $5.67 million.

If you’re well-versed in Swift’s discography, you're likely familiar with her Watch Hill, RI, retreat. Dubbed “Holiday House,” the historic abode was purchased by Swift for $17.75 million in 2013.

Built in 1930, the extravagant seaside estate once belonged to composer and socialite Rebekah Harkness, who was married to William Hale "Bill" Harkness, “heir to the Standard Oil name and money,” as Swift sings. (Bonus points if you can name the song.)

The mansion features eight bedrooms, a 36-foot-long parlor, and an octagon-shaped dining room.

In 2014, the “Love Story” songstress purchased not one—but two—penthouses in New York City’s ritzy Tribeca neighborhood.

The transaction included a 5,869-square-foot apartment for $14.85 million and a neighboring three-bedroom unit for $5.1 million.

Swift combined the two spaces, creating a massive nine-bedroom, nine-bathroom mega-apartment with wood-beamed ceilings, a dramatic curved staircase, and oversized windows.

She purchased a third unit in the building a few years later for $9.75 million, increasing her New York City home’s layout by over 3,500 square feet.

Swift added a second West Coast abode to her portfolio when she purchased a historic Beverly Hills mansion for $25 million in 2015.

The lovely landmarked estate was once the home of movie producer Samuel Goldwyn, co-founder of Goldwyn Pictures.

Nestled on 2 acres in a cul-de-sac, the nearly 100-year-old home features a championship tennis court, a pool house, and a rose garden.

Despite her dalliances with the West Coast, Swift couldn’t get enough of Tribeca.

In 2017, the musician purchased yet another Tribeca property: the townhome adjacent to her massive penthouse.

The 5,000-square-foot townhouse was transformed into her private penthouse entrance, adding 3,660 square feet to her sprawling city residence. She paid a whopping $18 million for the three-story pad.

Swift famously lived in a sweet Cornelia Street carriage house for part of 2016 and 2017 while her gigantic Tribeca compound underwent renovations.

She rented the circa-1800s four-bedroom, five-bathroom West Village home, complete with blond parquet floors and antique brickwork, for $36,000 a month.

Swift famously immortalized the address in her song "Cornelia Street." It went back up for rent after Swift's departure and is currently off-market.

In 2018, Swift’s father purchased a St. Petersburg, FL, penthouse for $4 million.

Residents of the luxe high-rise have access to 24/7 security, a top-notch fitness center, two heated swimming pools, and a billiards room. Even with the enhanced security, the home was burglarized in 2020.

Although Kelce is the one who snapped up the property, the newlyweds have a gorgeous new place to call home: a palatial eight-bedroom, 8.5-bathroom property the athlete purchased for $5.35 million in March.

The historic residence was built in 1895, and spans an impressive 21,140 square feet. The home was initially listed for $6.99 million in 2024, before the asking price was reduced to $5.99 million the following May.

Kelce secured the estate at a further discount, $1.64 million below its original asking price.

The Bratenahl, OH abode is close to Cleveland Heights, where Kelce grew up alongside his older brother, Jason Kelce.

The proposal had some trouble gaining approval, with a local regulation stating that solid fences and walls—as well as fences with less than 75% openness—cannot exceed 30 inches in height.

However, it seems they've gained quite a bit of support form neighbors, with one speaking anonymously to Page Six to push back on previous reports that the proposal had angered residents.

"I think they're excited," the neighbor told the outlet. "I think it's great. I don't think people are angry."

#5565. How Daylight Saving Time Changes the Real Estate Showing Playbook

With Daylight Saving Time already ended, showings that previously took place in daylight may now happen entirely after sunset. For agents, this creates challenges, including scheduling, affecting buyer engagement and property presentation. Here are some key challenges:

Daylight Saving Time changes showing logistics for agents managing multiple buyers and listings. The clock change hurts most in the after-work window. For example, in Austin, the sun now sets around 5:30 p.m., so the 5:30 p.m. to 7:00 p.m. slot that used to cover two or three homes in daylight now covers maybe one. Agents with several active buyers have to stop routing by geography and start sorting by need. One buyer has to see a yard, a view or the street before they can decide, and another is fine walking a condo at 7 p.m. That means moving showings to weekends and lunch hours, and having that talk with buyers at the start of the week rather than in the car at 5:45 p.m.

Traditional open house strategies may or may not remain effective during shorter fall and winter days. The traditional open house was never great at selling homes. It’s great at finding buyers for the agent sitting it. Shorter days don’t change much on their own, since most open houses already run on weekend afternoons. What changes is the margin. Fewer buyers are out in November and December, so a three-hour Sunday open with no promotion behind it will be quiet. We’d rather see agents run shorter, promoted windows and invite the buyer agents who have already shown interest. The open house should be one tool in the showing plan, not the whole marketing strategy.

Agents can protect a property’s curb appeal and first impression when buyers arrive after sunset. Our honest answer is to avoid showings after dark when you can. On the buy side, we tell clients not to tour homes at night. You can’t judge the yard, the street, the drainage or the neighbors’ houses, so it’s a poor experience and usually means a second trip anyway.

On the sell side, we discourage evening showings, and that’s easier than people expect: it’s close to dinner, buyers are tired, and walking through a stranger’s house after dark just feels odd. If a buyer insists, we take the showing, because we want as many showings as we can get. When we do, every exterior light is on, including porch, landscape and garage lights, and every interior light is on too, so the house reads as warm and lived in from the curb. We also make sure the path to the lockbox is well lit, and we include daytime photos in the listing so the buyer already knows what the dark is hiding. Then we offer a daylight second look, because a buyer who liked it at night is almost always worth bringing back during the day.

Showing schedules should be designed around individual property characteristics rather than convenience alone. Scheduling for convenience treats every house the same, and they aren’t the same. A west Austin home with a Hill Country view or a big lot has to be shown in daylight, because that’s what the buyer is paying for. The rare exception is a property whose selling point is the night, like a downtown condo with a lit skyline. The listing agent should set the best showing windows at the pricing conversation and get the seller to agree to them upfront. A buyer who sees a property in the dark and walks away rarely comes back for a second look.

Brokerages can use showing data and buyer feedback to identify seasonal obstacles to buyer engagement. Most brokerages collect showing feedback and do nothing with it. Single comments don’t tell you much; the patterns do. Look at what time of day each showing happened, whether evening showings turn into second showings or offers at the same rate as daylight ones, and whether the same complaints keep coming back: couldn’t see the yard, dark street, hard to find the house.

If a listing gets plenty of evening traffic and no second looks, the problem is presentation, not price, and better lighting, better photos or a daylight window can fix it. Sellers will cut the price long before they ask why showings aren’t turning into offers, so the brokerage has to look first.

Eric Bramlett is the broker/owner of Bramlett Partners, an independent brokerage in Central Texas.

#5563. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5562. Fisher Island Penthouse Sells After $12.2 Million Price Cut—Becoming the Private Island’s Second-Priciest Sale Ever

A stunning seven-bedroom penthouse at Palazzo Della Luna on Fisher Island, which originally hit the market in Miami Beach for $50 million in June 2025, sold on Oct. 28, 2026, for $37.8 million.

Even with a discount of $12.2 million, or about 24%, off its original asking price, the sale is the ultra-exclusive island’s second-highest residential sale ever. The island's top record-breaking sale was a five-bedroom condo that sold for $40 million in 2021.

The seller was represented by Sam Gaita of The Corcoran Group, and the buyer was represented by Andrew Holtz of Compass.

According to The South Florida Business Journal, the seller was “ALJ Properties USA LLC, managed by Alicia L. Jarrett and Camilo Miguel Jr. with the same address in Miami as Mast Capital, where Miguel is founder and CEO.” The penthouse last changed hands for $23.75 million in 2021.

Built in 2019, the sophisticated 9,852-square-foot home has luxurious finishes, including gallery-style walls, wide-oak flooring, and a Boffi kitchen with double Miele and Sub-Zero appliances. The sale works out to $3,837 per square foot.

Floor-to-ceiling windows surround the unit, and retractable glass walls open to 4,500 square feet of outdoor terraces with panoramic views of the Atlantic Ocean, Biscayne Bay, and the Miami skyline.

The lavish primary suite has a fireplace, lounge area, dual walk-in closets, and a fluted marble bath with sweeping 180-degree views.

The condo also has a 2,500-square-foot rooftop terrace for entertaining, with an outdoor kitchen and its own private pool.

“Without question, the private rooftop terrace with a swimming pool is the most impressive feature,” Gaita said. “This is the only ‘lower’ penthouse on Fisher Island offering a private rooftop with a pool, which is an extremely rare feature throughout all of Miami.”

There are also separate staff quarters and garage parking for two cars.

“Fisher Island is an ultra-exclusive, private country club island accessible only by boat or helicopter,” he noted. “This 216-acre private island offers a private beach club, yacht club, multiple dining venues, tennis, pickleball, padel, spa and more, reserved for members and their guests only.”

Gaita said what ultimately drove the record sale was “attracting the buyer who best aligned with and appreciated the one-of-a-kind features the property has to offer.”

He also noted that its exclusive location “on a private island comparable to a country club, isn’t something that can be easily replicated and serious buyers understand that value."

#5561. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5560. Bill Cosby Knocks $2 Million Off Original Listing Price of Manhattan Townhouse in Latest Attempt To Sell

Bill Cosby has been looking to offload his longtime New York City townhouse since early 2025, and he's slashed the price once again.

The six-bedroom, 4.5-bathroom dwelling now boasts an asking price of $4,999,000, with the listing touting it as a "rare Treadwell Farm townhouse opportunity under $5 million."

The disgraced star first listed the home in April 2025, shortly after news broke that he was facing foreclosure on this property and a much pricier Manhattan townhome he owned at the time.

The more expensive abode was sold for $28 million, while this particular home had a complicated journey.

In July 2025, the asking price was dropped to $6.75 million. Then in December, the listing was removed.

At the time, listing agent Adam Schneider of Corcoran Westside Columbus told Realtor.com® that Cosby and his wife, Camille, chose to delist the home to carry out a series of updates after they resolved the financial issues clouding the property.

"All issues with the lender have been resolved," Schneider said in a December 2025 email. "The property is now being renovated and we plan to list it in the New Year."

The home returned to the market in January 2026 for $6.75 million. At the end of April, the price dipped to $5.99 million.

The townhouse would go on to be listed and removed twice more in 2026—reappearing in August at the same $5.99 million asking, and again in September at a reduced $5.49 million.

The listing directly speaks to the price reduction: "At this reduced price point, the opportunity is clear: there is very little in the 20-foot Upper East Side townhouse market that is this substantial, this flexible, and this well-positioned."

While the listing does not explicitly mention the aforementioned renovation, it does suggest there is still room for change.

"The next owner can preserve what works, improve what matters, and invest directly into a home that reflects their own taste, lifestyle, and long-term vision," it reads.

Spanning 5,000 square feet across a basement and four levels, the property has an open floor plan and includes elevator access and private outdoor space.

"Its flexible floor plan allows for bedroom and bathroom realignment, giving the next owner the option to refresh for the 2020s, personalize, or more fully reimagine the home over time," the listing reads.

The home has a handful of original features, including the red oak banisters, exposed brick, and mahogany and mosaic hardwood flooring.

Crown moldings, high ceilings, and period fireplaces also add character throughout.

A large eat-in kitchen anchors the garden level, and it has been equipped with stainless-steel appliances, including a restaurant-grade Montague Grizzly stove.

A formal dining room includes a wood-burning fireplace, as well as French doors that lead to an enclosed sunroom and a landscaped backyard.

Two generously sized living rooms round out the second level, while the third foor has two large bedrooms and a shared sitting or dressing area.

The primary suite is located on the fourth level and includes a fireplace and two additional spaces that could be used as bedrooms, offices, or other purposes.

The basement includes laundry facilities and storage space, while the rooftop has "meaningful potential for future customization and expansion."

Previous reports indicated that the property had primarily been used by Cosby's son, Ennis, who was murdered in Los Angeles in 1997. It is not clear whether the actor continued to use it regularly, as it is understood that Cosby and his wife—who remained by his side throughout his sexual assault scandal—have been living primarily at their home in a suburb of Philadelphia.

The couple purchased the townhouse in 1980 for $1.19 million.

Hannah Chambers is a senior celebrity and lifestyle reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2026. She has been writing entertainment and lifestyle content since 2016, with her work appearing in Cosmopolitan, BravoTV, NYLON, Bustle, Elite Daily, and The Zoe Report, among other publications. Hannah received a bachelor’s degree in journalism from The University of Maine. In her spare time, she loves to chat about pop culture and is a major fan of reality TV.

#5559. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5558. Inflation, Supply Policies to Have Most Impact on Housing Affordability Post-Elections: Economists

American voters made it clear that affordability was one of the main drivers that tipped them in favor of putting Democrats in control of Congress in the 2026 midterm elections.

Democratic candidates flipped both the House of Representatives and Senate blue, buoyed by voters who have seen their everyday living costs skyrocket under the second Trump administration—and made it clear they wanted change.

But now the real work of making those campaign promises a reality begins—with housing affordability a top concern. Any solutions Congress might come up with to combat rising housing costs will take time to put into motion and generally inspire bipartisan cooperation, three top economists tell RISMedia.

Before any policies come into play, economists say inflation is a critical risk to mortgage rate stability and, in turn, the health of the housing market.

Inflation, economic headwinds top issues to watch

Getting inflation under control and expanding housing supply without creating outpaced demand could help shape housing affordability, economists say.

October’s hotter-than-expected inflation reading, up 0.4% instead of the 0.3% forecasted month-over-month, makes it highly likely the Federal Reserve will hike rates when it meets in December. In fact, 90% of analysts polled by CME Group anticipate the Fed will hike its target rate by 0.25 percentage points to 4.00% to 4.25%.

“What matters most for buyers and sellers is whether inflation eases and mortgage rates become more affordable and the labor market stays healthy,” says Odeta Kushi, deputy chief economist with First American Financial.

Have an opinion on this topic? Please submit a Letter to the Editor.

Another inflationary metric to watch is the U.S. national debt, Kushi notes, which now stands at more than $40 trillion. This will become even more urgent when the current debt limit of $41.1 trillion is reached by May or mid-2027. If there’s a congressional standoff over increasing the debt limit, that could drive inflation—and borrowing costs—higher while creating more financial market volatility, she explained.

But getting inflation under control depends on a lot of moving parts, according to Jake Krimmel, senior economist with Realtor.com®. Under the Trump administration, it’s impossible to pinpoint those moving parts amid a trade war (and tariffs), geopolitical tensions and mixed economic readings.

Krimmel stressed that inflation also erodes purchasing power. “Inflation eats away at paychecks and makes it harder for people to save.”

“The big wild card heading into 2027 is the same one that we’ve been talking about probably since February, which is the effect of the (Iran) War on the longer end of the curve, the Fed’s rate path and the economy more broadly, especially with respect to inflation, consumer confidence and consumer spending,” Krimmel says. “We don’t know what 2027 will bring, but uncertainty is a feature in this market.”

Mischa Fisher, Zillow’s chief economist, points to a simple formula that will bring mortgage rates down to more palatable levels for homebuyers to act.

“We know, generally speaking, that the best way out of this is higher incomes, lower mortgage rates and more supply,” Fisher says.

According to Zillow’s October housing report, the monthly mortgage payment on the typical U.S. home reached $2,004, up 12.8% from a year ago. That means a median-income household would need to spend 34.7% of its income on total housing costs—up from 32.7% a year ago and far beyond the typical 30% benchmark, Zillow reported.

Fisher noted that the Democrats’ sweep of the midterms hasn’t altered Zillow’s housing forecasts, which call for rates to stay in the 7% range, flat-to-lower sales volume compared to 2026 and home values that rise slightly on paper but decline slightly in real terms after adjusting for inflation.

Could Congress pull any meaningful levers for housing?

When the new Congress is sworn in on Jan. 3, they’ll have their work cut out for them to deliver for voters who made affordability a central election motivation. However, with President Donald Trump already pledging to use the power of his pen to veto Democrat-led bills, will any meaningful housing legislation see the light of day?

“When we have this period where Congress is controlled by one party and the executive branch is controlled by the other party, typically, that doesn’t foretell close collaboration on policy,” Fisher says. “But I think we have seen that in the case of housing, there is a bipartisan agreement that there’s room to improve the environment. That’s what we’re watching to see play out.”

Fisher notes that the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, which passed earlier this year, offers “a real bipartisan blueprint for how policymakers can work together to specifically improve housing.” The timing couldn’t be more crucial as the gap between Americans’ incomes and affordable housing widens.

Kushi adds that Congress should look at policies that make it “easier, cheaper and faster to build and bring more homes to the market.”

While it’s too early to know what lawmakers have in mind to help ease affordability pressures in the housing market, Krimmel cautions that any government stalemates—a shutdown or lapses in government funding—could be disastrous for the 10-year Treasury yield, which directly impacts mortgage rate movements. A government shutdown can also disrupt economic data collection, making it harder to gauge progress on inflation.

“We already have enough pressure on the 10-year,” Krimmel says. “We don’t need anything else.”

All three economists agree that improving housing affordability involves addressing the supply side, among other action items.

The U.S. has an estimated supply gap of 4.03 million homes, according to Realtor.com. Closing the gap, Krimmel says, means boosting new construction, which needs to be “easier to build.” Lawmakers should “encourage states and localities to adopt more permissive local zoning laws and also streamline that permitting process,” Krimmel says, cautioning that it will take time to see any gains.

For now, Realtors® should track local inventory and price trends to help guide their clients more effectively. Fisher notes that affordability-related softness and price pressures will persist in parts of the Mountain West and Sun Belt, while supply-constrained coastal markets where new building isn’t as robust face upward pressure.

Existing-home inventory is still being suppressed by the mortgage lock-in effect, as owners may be reluctant to sell and give up their pandemic-era low rates. More realistic pricing from sellers can help listings go under contract and give buyers more negotiating power. But a more buyer-friendly market doesn’t necessarily mean homes are affordable to more buyers, Krimmel says.

Only time will tell if income growth can keep up with housing costs—and if Congress can act quickly enough to start meaningfully improving affordability to help ease Americans’ financial strain.

Deborah Kearns is a freelance editor and writer with more than 15 years of experience covering real estate, mortgages and personal finance topics. Her work has appeared in The New York Times, Forbes Advisor, The Associated Press, MarketWatch, USA Today, MSN and HuffPost, among others. Deborah previously held editorial leadership and writing roles at NerdWallet, Bankrate, LendingTree and RE/MAX World Headquarters.

#5557. Google Cloud takes aim at the cost of keeping idle AI agents running on Kubernetes

Kubernetes has become the go-to platform for distributed training and inference, but what happens to the compute bill when it runs AI agents that spend most of their time waiting?

When an agent’s container or virtual machine stays provisioned, customers pay for the wait as well as the work. To help customers control those costs and make agent workloads more predictable, Google LLC has donated three projects to the Cloud Native Computing Foundation, according to Allan Naim (pictured, left), director of product management, AI infrastructure, at Google Cloud. For Kubernetes itself, the new challenge is freeing up compute between bursts of activity while letting each agent pick up where it left off.

“Act 2 is a few years back; Kubernetes became the de facto for inference and training,” Naim said. “What’s really interesting right now is we’re embarking on this Act 3 … where the typical patterns are very, very different from how Kubernetes was designed.”

Naim and Gari Singh (right), product manager at Google Cloud, spoke with theCUBE’s Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how Google Cloud is using open-source tools to cut compute costs when AI agents sit idle. (* Disclosure below.)

Cost presents a serious problem in agentic workloads, with agents sitting idle 90% to 95% of the time waiting on models, test runs or human approvals, Naim explained. Google developed Agent Substrate, an open-source runtime that hosts AI agents in isolated environments on Kubernetes. When an agent is suspended, the runtime saves a snapshot of its memory and local files and frees up its compute for other agents. When work resumes, it restores the agent from that snapshot in an available sandbox.

“It helps from an economic standpoint,” Naim said. “We’ve seen 10x reduction in cost in terms of running Agent Substrate on Kubernetes versus running these agents directly on dedicated virtual machines and containers.”

Security is another concern. In response, Google open-sourced gVisor in 2018, which sits on top of the host kernel to block or audit every system call an agent makes, according to Singh.

“Agents and agent harnesses are designed to solve a problem — and to try to solve a problem — until they can’t solve the problem,” Singh said. “They will find all kinds of clever workarounds. They know everything that’s around. You want to make sure that it didn’t go make some low-level change to [your] low-level security, didn’t make an outbound network call, didn’t try to open a file that it shouldn’t.”

Google is also working with Anyscale Inc. on KubeRay, which runs Anyscale’s Ray platform natively on Kubernetes so platform teams can offer distributed training and inference to many research groups, Singh noted. OpenRL brings that approach to reinforcement learning, which teaches post-trained models guardrails, Naim added.

“In the past, to do reinforcement learning, you needed to hire a dozen research scientists with PhDs,” Naim said. “Our goal was, ‘How can we bring reinforcement learning into the world of platform engineering so that you can run reinforcement learning on your Kubernetes environment and take advantage of it to actually do continuous improvement for your agentic workload?'”

#5556. IRS raises 401(k) limit for 2027 to $25,500

The IRS increased the 2027 401(k) deferral limit to $25,500 and raised catch-up limits to $8,500, or $11,750 for ages 60 to 63. IRA limits remain at $7,500, while multiple IRA and Saver’s Credit income thresholds increased.  AI Summary

The IRS has increased the annual contribution limit for 401(k) plans in 2027 to $25,500, up $1,000 from the 2026 limit of $24,500, the agency announced on Thursday.

The higher limit also applies to employees participating in 403(b) plans, governmental 457 plans and the federal government’s Thrift Savings Plan, according to guidance issued by the IRS in Notice 2026-66. The notice outlines cost-of-living adjustments for retirement plans and other retirement-related tax provisions for the 2027 tax year.

The catch-up contribution limit for employees ages 50 and older increased to $8,500, up from $8,000 in 2026. That brings the total annual contribution limit for most eligible participants ages 50 and older to $34,000.

Employees ages 60 through 63 are eligible for a higher catch-up contribution limit under the SECURE 2.0 Act of 2022. For 2027, that limit increased to $11,750, allowing eligible participants to contribute up to $37,250.

The annual contribution limit for individual retirement accounts remains unchanged at $7,500. The IRA catch-up contribution limit for individuals ages 50 and older also remains at $1,100.

“Along with the Working Families Tax Cuts, this increase in the pension limitations will help American families keep more of their hard-earned income,” IRS CEO Frank J. Bisignano said in a statement.

The IRS also increased several income thresholds used to determine eligibility for tax deductions and retirement account contributions.

For traditional IRAs, the income phase-out range for single taxpayers covered by a workplace retirement plan increased to $83,000 to $93,000, up from $81,000 to $91,000 in 2026.

For married couples filing jointly, the range increased to $133,000 to $153,000, up from $129,000 to $149,000, when the spouse making the contribution is covered by a workplace retirement plan.

For IRA contributors who are not covered by a workplace retirement plan but are married to someone who is, the phase-out range increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The income phase-out range for Roth IRA contributions also increased. For single taxpayers and heads of household, the range is now $158,000 to $173,000, compared with $153,000 to $168,000 in 2026. For married couples filing jointly, it increased to $250,000 to $260,000, up from $242,000 to $252,000.

The IRS also raised the annual contribution limit for SIMPLE retirement accounts to $17,500, up from $17,000. Certain eligible SIMPLE plans have a higher limit of $19,100, compared with $18,100 in 2026.

Catch-up contribution limits for most SIMPLE plans remain unchanged at $4,000 for employees ages 50 and older. The limit is $3,850 for certain applicable SIMPLE plans and $5,250 for employees ages 60 through 63.

The income limits for the Saver’s Credit, which benefits low- and moderate-income workers who save for retirement, also increased. For 2027, the limits are $83,000 for married couples filing jointly, $62,250 for heads of household, and $41,500 for single taxpayers and married individuals filing separately.

The IRS said the adjustments are intended to account for cost-of-living changes and help taxpayers and employers plan for the coming year.

#5555. Commission settlement accounts hold $711M as claim payouts await (EXCLUSIVE)

New disclosures show that the settlement fund accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026.

That’s how much money was held in accounts associated with the sweeping real estate commission antitrust settlements as of Sept. 30, according to newly filed federal court documents offering a fresh look at the money from the nationwide agreements.

The disclosures, filed Thursday in federal court in Missouri, show that the accounts received about $17.7 million in interest during the first nine months of 2026, while roughly $5.8 million was transferred out during the same period.

The filings also come amid an ongoing court-ordered audit of settlement administrator JND Legal Administration, which reported earlier this year that it had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions.

The financial accounting follows a series of appellate rulings upholding the commission settlements, although questions remain about when eligible homesellers will receive payments.

According to a declaration signed Oct. 13 by Isaac Lim, a senior vice president and senior risk officer at Morgan Stanley Smith Barney, and filed by plaintiffs Oct. 29, the settlement accounts had a combined balance of $711,251,720.86 as of Sept. 30.

The funds were transferred from Huntington Bank to Morgan Stanley on Oct. 23, 2025, at class counsel’s direction.

Lim reported that $17,705,101.82 in interest was paid into the accounts between January and September 2026, while $5,780,467.43 was transferred out during the same period. The declaration does not identify the purpose of those transfers or establish whether any money has been distributed directly to eligible homesellers.

According to the filing, the money is invested in a BlackRock institutional money market fund yielding about 3.63 percent annually, Morgan Stanley’s preferred savings program paying 4 percent or a combination of both. The yields are estimates and subject to change.

The reported balance represents funds held in the identified Morgan Stanley accounts, rather than necessarily the full amount collected through the broader commission settlements. The declaration does not provide a complete accounting of earlier distributions, expenses or outstanding settlement contributions.

In a June declaration, Jennifer Keough, CEO of JND Legal Administration, said the company had received and processed more than 2.7 million claim submissions. In June 2025, more than 2.5 million claims had already been submitted, while JND had invoiced approximately $32.8 million for its administrative work.

Keough said JND’s original assignment expanded into six separate notification campaigns involving more than 138 million emails and 44 million postcards. Four of those direct-mail campaigns cost about $18.7 million in postage alone, which JND characterized as a pass-through expense.

In May, Missouri-based U.S. District Judge Stephen Bough ordered JND to stop receiving payments while the court considered appointing a special master to audit the company’s past and future bills.

On July 27, the judge appointed Chris Hellums and Randall Sansom as special masters.

Hellums was tasked with overseeing the audit and helping establish future administration arrangements, while Sansom, a certified public accountant, was directed to audit JND’s billing and expenses dating back to the beginning of its work.

The order requires JND to provide detailed financial records, including employee timesheets, vendor invoices, billing records and information about rebates, credits or other financial incentives.

JND opposed the need for an independent audit, arguing in a June filing that the process would be expensive and burdensome and that its work had been performed appropriately. The company said it would cooperate if the audit proceeded, but requested confidentiality protections for commercially sensitive pricing information.

JND also said its responsibilities had expanded substantially at class counsel’s direction and that it had advanced nearly $3 million in out-of-pocket costs on behalf of the class.

The dispute escalated in August when JND sought to disqualify Hellums, alleging he had demonstrated bias against the company through his involvement in a separate antitrust settlement proceeding.

Bough denied the motion Aug. 26, finding that JND, as a nonparty, could not seek disqualification under the applicable rules. He added that even if JND could bring the challenge, it had failed to establish sufficient grounds to question Hellums’ impartiality.

The ruling also examined a question Hellums had raised in the Blue Cross Blue Shield case about potential vendor rebates and credits, which Bough said JND never answered in its email exchange with him and only partly addressed at the Aug. 20 hearing. Keough acknowledged at the hearing that separate vendor agreements govern how rebates and credits are calculated.

JND has maintained in sworn declarations that it has received no rebates, credits or other financial benefits from banks or vendors in connection with the commission settlements.

In its latest accounting, JND reported $155,932 in additional administrative invoices covering July through September, bringing the outstanding balance shown on its October invoice to $494,249.

Keough said JND continues submitting invoices and performing administrative work despite not currently receiving payments.

JND did not respond to Inman’s request for comment by the time of publication.

Despite a series of appellate rulings upholding the real estate commission settlements, it remains unclear when eligible homesellers can expect to receive payments.

On Aug. 19, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 8th Circuit unanimously upheld the landmark Sitzer | Burnett settlement, rejecting seven appeals challenging its scope, fairness and accompanying industry practice changes.

The court subsequently affirmed another $110.6 million in brokerage settlements in the related Gibson litigation on Sept. 1, bringing the total collected for the class to about $1.02 billion, according to the appellate opinion.

After rejecting three additional objector appeals on Sept. 15 and denying rehearing petitions from objectors Robert Friedman and Monty March on Sept. 24, the 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the main Sitzer | Burnett appeals Oct. 2, concluding those proceedings before the appeals court. Objectors may still seek review from the U.S. Supreme Court.

The 8th Circuit issued its mandate in the Gibson appeals Oct. 14.

Despite those developments, the latest financial disclosures do not establish when eligible homesellers will receive distributions or precisely how much of the $711 million held in Morgan Stanley accounts is available for payment.

Eric Dirks, an attorney with the Kansas City-based Williams Dirks Dameron, one of the plaintiffs’ co-lead counsel firms, did not respond to Inman’s request for comment regarding the account balance, interest earnings and anticipated distribution timeline.

#5554. Mortgage industry expects CFPB servicing rule to narrow

The CFPB has sent a revised version of its 2024 “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” rule to the Office of Management and Budget, moving closer to finalizing new loss-mitigation standards under Regulation X. Industry attorneys expect a significantly narrower rule than the original proposal, shaped by President Trump’s directive to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules and broad stakeholder pushback against open-ended requirements.  AI Summary

The Consumer Financial Protection Bureau (CFPB) last week took another step toward finalizing new loss-mitigation standards, sending a revised version of its 2024 mortgage servicing proposal to the White House Office of Management and Budget (OMB) for review.

The final rule, “Streamlining Mortgage Servicing for Borrowers Experiencing Payment Difficulties” under Regulation X, is expected to be narrower than the 2024 proposal advanced when the CFPB was led by Rohit Chopra, according to industry attorneys. The CFPB did not immediately reply to HousingWire‘s request for comments.

The move comes in the wake of President Donald Trump’s March 13 executive order, “Promoting Access to Mortgage Credit,” which directs the CFPB to modernize Dodd-Frank-era rules that lenders and servicers say increase compliance costs. The current standards were finalized in 2013.

“We won’t know the final rule’s content until it is published. But the comment record and the current Bureau’s priorities point toward a significantly narrower rule,”Joseph M. DeFazio and Joe Reilly, partners at Troutman Pepper Locke, wrote in a blog post. “Since President Trump’s second term began, the Bureau has also rescinded prior guidance and signaled that it prefers clear, fixed rules to open-ended frameworks like the one in the 2024 proposal.”

The CFPB received more than 80 comments on the proposal, with what the attorneys described as an “unusual degree of convergence” among groups that rarely agree.

The American Bankers Association (ABA) has urged the CFPB to finalize only a limited portion of the 2024 proposal, pressing the bureau to focus on targeted changes rather than a full rewrite.

“The Bureau’s 2024 proposal was founded on the misconception that servicers prioritize foreclosure over helping borrowers find a successful solution to resolve their payment disruptions,” Teshale Smith, the ABA’s senior counsel for regulatory compliance and policy, said in a letter to the CFPB in June. “In fact, sustained low foreclosure rates and high customer satisfaction rates demonstrate that servicers remain committed to helping struggling borrowers.”

The 2024 proposed rule aimed to make permanent several pandemic-era practices used when large numbers of borrowers needed fast assistance. Industry estimates showed that 8.8 million families were helped, with the re-default rate for loans exiting COVID-19 loss-mitigation programs at about 10%, ABA said in its letter.The proposal allows servicers to evaluate loss-mitigation options before borrowers complete an application, prohibits late fees and other charges while a loss-mitigation review is underway, and makes assistance possible in multiple languages.As it relates to foreclosure, the draft allows a loss-mitigation review cycle to start when the borrower asks for help, not only after a completed application, lasting until the loan is current or all options are ruled out. During that time, servicers could not begin or advance foreclosure, a protection that currently applies only after a complete application is on file. Foreclosure could resume only after options were exhausted or the borrower stopped communicating.

Attorneys at Troutman Pepper Locke expect the final rule to permit sequential review of loss-mitigation options instead of requiring servicers to evaluate all options at once; dropping the proposed ban on fee accrual during loss-mitigation reviews; and removal of the language access provisions that were part of the 2024 draft.

Isaac Boltansky, head of public policy at Pennymac, said the company “supports clear, consistent standards that give servicers the certainty they need to deliver the best possible outcomes for homeowners, particularly those facing financial hardship.”

#5553. Lofty Releases AI Index to Measure the Impact of AI on Real Estate

AI-powered automated real estate analytics and property valuation. Intelligent property management and AI-powered property investment. Man using laptop.

Lofty has announced the release of a new AI Index for Real Estate, which the company describes as the industry’s first AI tracker designed to quantify the amount of time saved by real estate agents who use Lofty AI.

Featuring number breakdowns detailing how agents save time across tasks, based on team or brokerage size, across regions of the country, and per product, Lofty stated that the AI Index offers the industry a view of quantifiable AI results. Grounded in tracking what agents actually do and how AI impacts their activity, in the month of October 2026 Lofty AI completed 1.13 million tasks and saved real estate agents across the country more than 130,000 hours.

“Every AI vendor touts the time-saving nature of their AI product, but almost none of them show the data to confirm that what they say is true,” said Joe Chen, CEO of Lofty. “We decided to eliminate the smoke and mirrors surrounding AI results and create measurable clarity by creating the Lofty AI Index. Each month we’ll put a number to the AI impact, show the calculations, and stand behind it.”

According to NAR’s 2026 Realtors® Technology Report, 81% of agents said that “saving time” was a primary reason they adopted new technology, which is why AI has been hailed as a game changer for the real estate industry. Lofty explained that eliminating much of the manual task-oriented work that keeps agents distracted from big revenue generating activities is an appealing proposition. Yet, few real estate professionals can say exactly how AI delivers results in a tangible way.

Lofty stated that its AI Index closes that gap by counting what AI did, pricing the activity in minutes as compared to how long it takes an agent to execute manually, and calculating the hours saved across products (including three AI agents and Lofty Cowork). With conservative estimates, the first iteration of the Index assessed usage during October 2026 and found 1.13 million tasks were completed by AI saving agents 131,248 hours by handling follow-ups, social media posts, homeowner check-ins, and CRM updates.

Additional October 2026 Lofty AI Index findings include:

“As the industry evaluates how and when to invest in AI, Lofty will continue to not only provide the proven AI innovations that streamline how agents, teams, and brokerages work but eliminate the mystery shrouding AI and showcase its measurable impact on real estate businesses of every size,” said Chen.

To learn more about the data and the results, visit https://lofty.com/ai-index.

#5552. Housing on the ballot: What to watch in the Nov. 3 midterms

Realtor associations in Florida, California and Massachusetts have lined up behind statewide housing measures on the Nov. 3 ballot, led by $18 million from Florida Realtors for a property tax cut.

Those are among six midterm housing ballot measures at the state level in four U.S. states, the most in a single election year since at least 2006, according to Ballotpedia, not counting property tax measures like Florida’s.

Thirty-six states will also elect governors, and candidates in California, Texas and Florida have released housing plans that range from a statewide housing emergency to ending school property taxes on homesteads.

In federal races, housing has surfaced as part of a broader argument about cost of living. Among Americans who plan to vote, 85 percent say housing affordability is at least somewhat important in choosing candidates, but 64 percent don’t know where their congressional candidates stand on housing, according to a Clever Real Estate survey.

Inman’s editorial staff will be watching California, Texas and Florida most closely next Tuesday. Each has a large real estate market and pairs a governor’s race with policy that would affect transactions, property taxes or construction.

In California, Democrat Xavier Becerra would declare a housing state of emergency on his first day, penalize cities that ignore housing element commitments, back local rent control within the statewide framework and seek disclosure of bulk investor purchases. Republican Steve Hilton would cap government fees and mandates on a new home at $50,000 and freeze new housing rules for five years.

In Texas, Republican Gov. Greg Abbott says his plan would cut the cost of a new home by more than $16,000 through faster inspections and pre-approved designs, and he wants to end school property taxes on homesteads. Democratic state Rep. Gina Hinojosa would restrict corporate purchases of single-family homes and pursue an end to residential property taxes.

In Florida, Republican Byron Donalds wants local governments to remove zoning restraints and supports Amendment 3. Democrat David Jolly opposes the amendment and says the state’s Live Local Act has not delivered affordable housing.

Housing is also a campaign issue in governor races in Colorado, Michigan, Massachusetts and Rhode Island. In Colorado, Democrat Phil Weiser has proposed 40,000 more owner-occupied homes by 2035, and Republican Victor Marx would cut state regulations and red tape. In Michigan, Democrat Jocelyn Benson has pitched affordability proposals, and Republican John James says local codes add more than $100,000 to developers’ costs.

Massachusetts Gov. Maura Healey, a Democrat seeking a second term, supports Question 7, a zoning change that could lead to the construction of more single-family homes. In Rhode Island, Democrat Helena Foulkes proposes a $1 billion plan for 20,000 homes over eight years, funded by a millionaire tax; independent Ken Block says the fund would produce no more than 375 units.

Florida Realtors had contributed $18 million to the Vote Yes on 3 committee as of late September, funding the campaign in full, WLRN reported. Amendment 3 would raise the state’s homestead property tax exemption.

“Affordability is on the forefront for every Floridian, and they need meaningful relief,” Florida Realtors President Chuck Bonfiglio Jr. said in a statement.

The California Association of Realtors supports Prop. 37, which would fund second mortgages for buyers of newly built homes, and Prop. 45, which would speed permitting and shorten environmental review. The Massachusetts Association of Realtors supports Question 7.

At the federal level, NAR’s political action committee directed more candidate contributions and independent expenditures to Texas than to any other state through February, according to FEC filings Inman reporters reviewed. NAHB’s BUILD-PAC backs what the group calls pro-housing, pro-business candidates for Congress.

The National Association of Hispanic Real Estate Professionals backed the ROAD to Housing Act in a March letter to Senate leaders, citing its provisions on zoning reform and by-right development.

Florida’s Amendment 3 would raise the homestead exemption on non-school property taxes from about $50,000 to $150,000 in 2027 and $250,000 in 2028, and lower the cap on annual assessment increases for non-homestead properties from 10 percent to 5 percent. It needs 60 percent of the vote.

California voters will decide Prop. 1, an $11.25 billion housing bond; Prop. 37, up to $25 billion in revenue bonds for second mortgages covering up to 17 percent of a new home’s price; and Prop. 45, which would set permitting deadlines and shorten environmental review.

In Massachusetts, Question 7 would require cities and towns to allow a single-family home on residentially zoned lots of at least 5,000 square feet with 50 feet of street frontage and public water and sewer.

Below the statewide level, voters will weigh more than 50 housing-related measures, according to a Shelterforce scan. Inman reporters will track the local questions most likely to touch agents’ markets, including property tax relief for older homeowners, transfer tax changes in San Francisco and Oakland and housing bonds in Charlotte and Raleigh.

Congress passed the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act in July. None of the 12 housing bills Inman reporter AJ LaTrace is tracking have advanced since September, including a bipartisan proposal to double the capital gains exclusion on home sales.

Bills that don’t pass before the current Congressional session ends in January would need to be reintroduced. When lawmakers return after the election, they face a Dec. 11 deadline to fund federal agencies, including HUD, and to reauthorize the National Flood Insurance Program.

Inman reporters will follow how the results shape development, including data center development, which has become a campaign issue in Tennessee. The state has about 60 operating data centers and 15 to 20 more proposed, according to WSMV, and the major-party nominees for governor differ on how to handle them. Republican nominee Sen. Marsha Blackburn has said local communities should decide, and Democrat Jerri Green has called for a moratorium.

Most governors elected Nov. 3 will take office in January as state legislatures convene. That same month, the ROAD to Housing Act’s limits on large investors buying additional single-family homes take effect, and Florida’s higher homestead exemption would follow in 2027 if voters approve it.
