#5532. Legislative risk continues to cloud BTR’s capital outlook; here’s why

Despite a carve-out in the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act, BTR and SFR operators say Treasury implementation and legislative risk is still suppressing capital. NAA Q3 2026 data shows units under construction down 18.5% YoY, completions down 40.2%, and sales volume down 51.5%.  AI Summary

Despite securing carve-outs from the 21st Century ROAD to Housing Act‘s institutional investor ban, build-to-rent (BTR) and single-family rental (SFR) operators continue to grapple with lingering legislative uncertainty that weighs on capital availability and new construction, both of which dramatically lag 2025 levels.

According to the National Apartment Association’s Q3 2026 Market Pulse, released Nov. 5, BTR units under construction fell 18.5% year over year, newly completed units declined 40.2% and sales volume of communities dropped 51.5%. Even against a broader nationwide slowdown in residential construction, the declining BTR pipeline continues to stand out.

The industry’s legislative uncertainty initially stemmed from an earlier version of ROAD, first introduced in March, that would have required investors and developers to sell newly built rental homes to individual buyers after seven years. The provision, among others, threatened the viability of the BTR business model, prompting investors to pull back from committing capital to new projects.

Although the final version of ROAD exempted and protected BTR, uncertainty remains around how Treasury will implement the institutional investor ban, along with the potential for new federal and state legislation that could impose further institutional ownership restrictions. That lingering uncertainty continues to weigh on capital flowing into the industry.

“I would say it hasn’t normalized. In other words, it wasn’t where it was a year ago, where capital was really flowing into the business,” Richard Ross, CEO at QuinnResidences, said when discussing the BTR market, in an interview with HousingWire TBD.

“I almost don’t care what the rules are, as long as you tell me what the rules are,” Ross added. “With uncertainty, people just aren’t going to invest.”

Ross cited the Strait of Hormuz as a timely and illustrative comparison. While oil is still moving through the Strait, traffic remains more restricted than it was a year ago. BTR, he suggested, finds itself in a comparable position.

“Capital’s coming in, but it’s not like it was pre-ROAD. The hope was that the regulatory process would give some clarity. And I think once it gets done, it will provide clarity, but you might remember this was only part one of the regulatory process,” he said, pointing to the prospects of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill. “Until capital knows what the rules are, it’s really hard for them to write checks.

According to Sean Dobson, chairman, CEO and CIO at The Amherst Group, a builder, buyer and manager of single-family rentals, the capital environment for BTR had been flashing signs of softening even before the federal government introduced the idea of an institutional investor ban. New projects often came with modest returns, and rent growth was moderating or even falling across many high-growth Sun Belt markets.

Add a steady drumbeat of policy risk from Washington, and many investors have simply taken their money elsewhere.

“When you add policy uncertainty to the asset, it just doesn’t have the return to pay for that,” Dobson said in an interview.

Invitation Homes CEO Dallas Tanner also acknowledged that the capital environment hasn’t bounced back from an uncertain 2026 during the company’s Q3 2026 earnings call on October 29.

“Capital’s just starting to poke its eyes up after the ROAD Act piece of it. The market’s still trying to find itself,” Tanner said.

In a Q3 2026 Form 10-Q document filed with the United States Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) on November 5, 2026, AMH also called out ongoing legislative uncertainty as a concern.

“Further, the ROAD Act and the prospect of other such laws or regulations have adversely impacted and may in the future continue to adversely impact our access to capital markets and the attractiveness of our securities to certain investors,” the document warned.

The U.S. Department of the Treasury, which implements the institutional investor ban included in ROAD, released a notice of proposed rulemaking in October that would grant BTR communities a range of notable exemptions from the ban. However, concerns remain about some of Treasury’s proposed interpretations.

“If you read the law as a layman, you’d say, ‘all right, built-to-rent is carved out.’ But then you get this rulemaking, and it’s like you have to pat your belly and tap your head and hop on one foot for the built-to-rent to not be banned,” Dobson said.

Quinn Residences, in an open letter to Treasury, outlined several concerns about Treasury’s proposed rulemaking. Chief among them is a proposal to exempt purpose-built BTR communities from the institutional investor ban provided they haven’t been owner-occupied and are purchased within 18 months of receiving a certificate of occupancy.

Ross argued that this timeline isn’t sufficient, as the 18-month certificate-of-occupancy requirement could prevent institutional investors from acquiring purpose-built rental homes that have been operating as rentals for more than 18 months, even if they have never been owner-occupied. And building and stabilizing a community typically takes about 30 months, longer than the rule allows, Ross argued.

The rule, therefore, could prevent subsequent sales of newly built BTR homes among institutional investors, effectively limiting the pool of potential buyers and potentially discouraging investment into new projects.

Ross also signaled his opposition to another one of Treasury’s proposed rulemakings that would fail to exempt single-plat BTR communities zoned for multifamily use, despite congressional record statements indicating lawmakers intended those properties to be excluded from the ban.

For The Amherst Group, uncertainty continues to obscure how Treasury will define the exception for homes requiring substantial repairs under the ROAD institutional investor ban. Many of Amherst’s acquisitions are older homes, typically 25 to 40 years old, that require substantial renovations. While the renovate-to-rent exception could allow Amherst to continue acquiring and renovating these properties for rent, the lack of finalized parameters has left investors uncertain.

“There’s no money to be raised right now,” Dobson said, of capital for financing renovate-to-rent acquisitions.

What’s more, the possibility of a “ROAD 2.0” housing bill raises even more concerns among many BTR operators and developers. They fear they face continued uncertainty and risk over whether future federal or state legislation could restrict the BTR business model.

However, it’s not yet clear whether any such legislation will gain traction in the next Congress. While many successful candidates for the U.S. Senate and the U.S. House of Representatives ran on a platform of opposing institutional ownership of single-family homes, campaign rhetoric and slogans don’t necessarily translate full-stop into policy.

“I worked campaigns for a number of years throughout the country, and the first thing they kind of teach you in campaigning out there is everyone needs a boogeyman. I think you campaign in slogans, and you govern in prose,” Owen Caine, Assistant Vice President of Federal Legislative Affairs at the National Apartment Association (NAA), said in an interview.

Despite the expectation that some members of Congress may push for more aggressive institutional ownership restrictions, Cain was encouraged by the widespread bipartisan pushback against previous provisions that would have undermined BTR. Caine hopes this bipartisan support will keep Congress from passing such far-reaching legislation in the future.

“The fact that we got to where we were with such bipartisan support, and with basically complete industry and nonprofit support, [means] messing around with that at this point, before it’s been fully implemented and before we’ve seen any benefits of the bill whatsoever, doesn’t make a lot of sense from a policy perspective,” he explained.

However, the new Congress comes with another challenge — the sheer size of the incoming freshman class. In the House of Representatives, for example, about 110 new representatives are expected, along with new staff members.

“Those are each offices we have to hit individually to educate about build-to-rent because the odds that the average person has any idea what a build-to-rent development is, is pretty low,” Caine explained.

Ross noted that lawmakers are usually receptive once they learn more about BTR and the legislative challenges facing the industry. A recent meeting with Senator-elect Roy Cooper (D-N.C.) was one example, with Cooper responding positively to those concerns.

“I spent 30 minutes with him personally, explaining what build-to-rent was. He said, ‘Oh, I understand. That makes sense.’ So that’s just something that everyone in this business will have to do again,” Ross explained.

While much of the attention has focused on federal legislation, state-level policy, particularly proposals to restrict institutional investors, may be just as critical an area to watch.

While it’s not clear what the newly elected state legislatures and governors may prioritize, several states have already considered bills limiting the influence of institutional ownership of housing.

In Virginia, for example, state lawmakers from both parties introduced legislation to restrict institutional home purchases. SB 693 and SB 1424 would have prohibited entities with more than $50 million in assets under management from buying single-family homes, but neither bill passed.

In Michigan, however, a similar measure, HB 6074, was signed into law on July 21, 2026. The bill prohibits corporations with a net worth of $375 million or more from owning more than 100 single-family homes in the state, while explicitly exempting build-to-rent (BTR) properties.

As more states consider restrictions on institutional ownership of single-family homes, will BTR secure the exemptions achieved in Michigan, or could operators face a tougher legislative environment in Congress and in other state legislatures?

That’s a key question to watch in 2027 and beyond.

#5531. Leaving VMware starts as a cost decision, but day-two operations decide whether it works

Enterprises leaving legacy hypervisors are finding that moving virtual machines is only half the job, and that a portable data management layer often decides whether a Kubernetes migration succeeds. Rising license costs are pushing teams to run containers and VMs on one platform.

That shift is playing out at Mouser Electronics Inc., one of the world’s largest electronic components distributors. After running Red Hat Inc.’s OpenShift for containers for five to six years, the company is now building a production OpenShift Virtualization cluster to move workloads off Broadcom Inc.’s VMware, according to Ronald Waller (pictured, left), systems engineer at Mouser.

“It doesn’t matter if we’re running containers or VMs, we’re running it on the same foundation, which really works well,” Waller said. “Because we can manage those things with the same tool sets and same skill sets.”

Waller and Jon Owings (right), assistant vice president of global technical presales, cloud and data services, at Portworx by Everpure, spoke with theCUBE’s John Furrier and Rebecca Knight at KubeCon + CloudNativeCon NA, during an exclusive broadcast on theCUBE, SiliconANGLE Media’s livestreaming studio. They discussed how the data management layer helps run VMs and containers on OpenShift. (* Disclosure below.)

Kubernetes already serves as a common control plane for containerized AI workloads, and pulling VMs onto it extends that standard to older applications. Everpure Inc., which rebranded from Pure Storage Inc. this year as part of a data-centric pivot, positions Portworx as the matching abstraction for storage.

“Kubernetes provides that ubiquitous control plane for all of them, and that’s what customers are asking us for,” Owings said. “The one thing that was missing was the same thing but for data.”

The learning curve for VMware administrators moving to Kubernetes is steep, and Waller has climbed it over the last year. Storage turned out to be the easy part when he built Mouser’s proof-of-concept cluster, he explained.

“I asked the storage guy what I needed from him, and he handed me a user ID and an API key. I went to Portworx Central. I configured my spec for the operator and the storage cluster, created my secret, and boom, Portworx Enterprise did everything else on the backend,” Waller said. “I didn’t even have to think about it.”

Portworx keeps building for that use case. It made data management native to OpenShift in May and unveiled new AI and VM capabilities at KubeCon. For teams following Mouser’s path, Owings sees the exit from a legacy hypervisor as a chance to rethink day-two operations on a data management layer that travels across clouds and Kubernetes distributions.

“What can we change that we didn’t like about the last 15 years? … Were we dependent on a vendor? Were we dependent on shell scripts or PowerShell?” Owings said. “We have this great opportunity to do something new, and Kubernetes has that open API that allows you to be creative.”

#5530. Backdoor References: 37% Say Potential Employers Contacted People They Never Listed

New report examines the realities of professional references, as nearly 1 in 3 workers say they've struggled to find enough when applying for a job.

GUAYNABO, Puerto Rico, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- A job reference may seem like a straightforward endorsement, but what happens behind the scenes can be more complicated.

New research from ZetyÂ®, a leading resume builder, shows some references are recommending people despite their own reservations (40%), some candidates are coaching or even faking references (19%), and employers aren't always sticking to the names they're given (37%).

Surveying over 1,000 U.S. workers, the Professional References Report found that 42% believe references should have little to no influence on an employer's final hiring decision, with the results raising broader questions about the role references play in hiring.

How Far Job Seekers Go to Manage References

Rather than leaving references to chance, many candidates take steps to steer the process in their favor.

Candidates may carefully curate their references, but 37% of workers say a potential employer reached out to a former manager or coworker they never listed.

Meanwhile, the references they do provide aren't necessarily contacted: just 15% say their references were contacted every time they were hired, while 47% say sometimes and 38% say rarely or never.

Opinions are divided on whether employers should go beyond the reference list:

Being selected as a reference does not necessarily mean someone is comfortable recommending the candidate. More than half of workers (52%) have been asked to provide a reference for someone they had reservations about, including:

Despite their longstanding role in hiring, professional references do not carry the same value for every worker. Some question their accuracy and influence, while others struggle to meet reference requirements in the first place:

"Rogue reference checks introduce a wild card into the hiring process because candidates have no control over who is contacted or what version of their work history that person may share," said Dr. Jasmine Escalera, career expert at Zety. "Someone outside a candidate's reference list may have an incomplete view of their performance or a perspective colored by office politics, past conflicts, or personal history. Even more concerning, the candidate may never know the conversation took place, much less have an opportunity to provide context."

For detailed insights on the Professional References Report, access the full study at https://zety.com/blog/professional-references-report or contact Skyler Acevedo, at [email protected].

The findings presented are based on a nationally representative survey conducted by Zety using Pollfish on August 24, 2026. The survey collected responses from 1,007 U.S. employees and examined their experiences, perceptions, and attitudes regarding professional references, including how references are selected, provided, and contacted, as well as their perceived accuracy and influence on hiring decisions.

Respondents answered different types of questions, including yes/no; scale-based questions, where they indicated their level of agreement with statements; and multiple-choice questions, where they could select from a list of provided options.

The sample consisted of 56% female, 43% male, and 1% nonbinary respondents, with 21% Gen Z, 27% millennials, 26% Gen X, and 26% baby boomers.

#5529. Bitcoin Price Rebounds Despite Quantum Threat as Nvidia’s Jensen Huang Faces Ouster After Two Affairs

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Bitcoin price has rebounded from recent lows as Nvidia board considers ousting CEO Jensen Huang following revelations about two extramarital affairs. Meanwhile, Glassnode data shows that 7.12 million BTC, worth more than $500 billion, already has publicly visible keys that future quantum computers could potentially exploit.

The developments put two of the technology industry’s biggest names under pressure. Bitcoin faces growing questions about its long-term cryptographic security, while Nvidia confronts a leadership crisis that could draw its AI dominance and ambitions in quantum computing.

Nvidia shares plunged more than 8% in extended trading after reports emerged that directors were preparing to remove Huang. The board is also considering an interim CEO before launching a wider search for a permanent replacement.

Bitcoin price recovered from its November 10 low of $72,600, reaching around $74,000 before easing to $73,700 this morning. The rebound offers bulls some relief after a sharp correction earlier this month. However, Glassnode has identified a potentially huge vulnerability affecting more than a third of Bitcoin’s issued supply.

According to a Glassnode update, approximately 35.4% of Bitcoin’s supply, equivalent to 7.12 million BTC, has publicly visible keys. At current market prices, those holdings are valued at more than $500 billion.

The exposure largely comes from address reuse. When Bitcoin holders spend from an address, their public keys become visible on the blockchain. Any remaining coins associated with those keys could become targets for sufficiently powerful quantum computers. Glassnode also says moving those coins to fresh addresses ends this exposure.

The concern centers on Shor’s algorithm, which could theoretically allow quantum computers to derive private keys from publicly available information. That would undermine the cryptographic security protecting vulnerable Bitcoin holdings.

Bitcoin developers are already exploring ways to address the challenge. BIP 360 proposes new transaction structures designed to reduce public-key exposure, while BIP 361 outlines a potential migration away from vulnerable signature schemes.

Nvidia’s leadership crisis has escalated dramatically after Reuters reported that its board was meeting late Wednesday to decide whether to remove Huang. The 63-year-old founder has led Nvidia for more than three decades, transforming it into the dominant supplier of AI processors. But revelations about two extramarital relationships have triggered an internal investigation and intensified scrutiny of his leadership.

The first controversy involves Alice Huang, a businesswoman whose relationship with Jensen Huang has attracted attention from US intelligence officials. She is reportedly suspected of facilitating Nvidia chip shipments to Chinese companies. The investigation has raised concerns about potential Chinese intelligence involvement and whether Nvidia’s technology reached restricted customers.

BREAKING: Nvidia, $NVDA, is now working with an "outside firm" to find a new CEO to replace Jensen Huang, per Bloomberg.The company is also reportedly weighing naming a temporary CEO while searching for a replacement.

A second relationship emerged through a New York Times report identifying Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare. Powell reportedly worked directly under Huang, creating additional corporate governance questions.

Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife in a message to employees, taking responsibility for his actions. The board’s response has shifted rapidly. Directors previously expressed confidence in Huang, but Bloomberg subsequently reported that Nvidia had engaged an outside firm to identify potential replacements.

It should be noted that Nvidia has 11 directors, with all but Huang considered independent. Its bylaws allow a majority vote to remove the CEO.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has emerged as a potential interim successor, while data-center executive Ian Buck has attracted attention as a possible longer-term candidate. The timing is particularly sensitive, with Nvidia scheduled to release quarterly results on November 17.

Bitcoin’s market recovery remains an important counterpoint for all these developments. Bitcoin price has managed to recover from its November 10 sell-off, with buyers stepping in around $72,700. Reclaiming $74,000 would give bulls another opportunity to challenge higher resistance levels.

The quantum threat is pushing developers to consider changes that could strengthen Bitcoin’s security over the coming years. Nvidia faces a different challenge. Losing Huang would remove the founder most closely associated with its AI dominance, potentially forcing investors to reassess the company’s leadership and long-term strategy.

The $500 billion quantum exposure has added another major scare to the market. But Bitcoin’s ability to adapt could become just as important as its price performance.

#5527. Nearly Half of the Stolen Binance Basket Had a Freeze Button

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Tether, Circle and Ripple could freeze their tokens within hours of the Binance theft, and they did.

There is no one to call for the stolen bitcoin, ether and TRX, which makes up most of the money Binance is unlikely to get back.

In most hacks, the stolen total is the headline. In the Binance breach, the more useful number is how much of the stolen money could be stopped.

On-chain trackers estimate the stolen basket at more than $5.6 billion. Binance itself has put the estimated impact at $6.3 billion and says nearly $3 billion is frozen. That freeze was possible only because of how the stolen money was made up.

Almost half of it was in tokens whose issuers can freeze them. The rest was in assets that no company, foundation or council can stop on their main blockchains.

That second half explains why recovery stalled at about $3 billion despite a fast industry response. It is also the part Binance will most likely have to pay for itself.

The per-asset breakdown from on-chain trackers is:

Sorting by whether the issuer can freeze the token gives a near-even split:

That one division shaped everything that happened after the theft.

The response on the freezable side was unusually fast:

The pattern is the same in every case. A company that issues a token on a public blockchain usually keeps a way to block specific addresses from moving it. Critics see that power as a central point of control, but in this theft it worked. Within hours, the largest dollar-value block of the stolen money could not be moved.

There was one notable intervention outside the token issuers. On Arbitrum, the Arbitrum Security Council took emergency action and moved 74,559,805 ARB and 8,425 ETH, about $30.5 million, out of an address connected to the exploit.

It shows that some layer-2 networks keep emergency powers their base layers lack. The amount was small next to the size of the theft.

The other half is a different story. Bitcoin has no issuer. Ether on Ethereum's main network has no admin key. TRX is Tron's native coin, and no token issuer sits between the holder and the blockchain. Once these assets reached the attacker's wallets, stopping them depended on exchanges refusing deposits and investigators tracking the funds, not on any freeze function.

Together, the $1.45 billion in BTC, $875 million in ETH and $234 million in TRX make about $2.56 billion. That is close to Binance's own numbers: about $3 billion frozen out of a $6.3 billion estimated impact leaves roughly $3.3 billion still in play, and most of it is in assets nobody can freeze.

The bitcoin figure is the most contested part of the basket. Some BTC moving out of Binance-linked wallets during the incident may have been Binance moving its own reserves to safety rather than attacker withdrawals. So the true unfreezable total could be lower than $2.56 billion, but the split between the two groups is unlikely to change much.

The attacker appeared to understand this difference and acted on it right away.

On-chain records show the main sweep on Ethereum used an EIP-7702 delegation. This feature lets a regular wallet hand control to a smart contract. Within minutes, the drained hot wallet's contents, including more than 1.6 billion USDT, had moved to attacker-controlled addresses.

The clearest example of the next step is on Aave. According to Aave's governance forum update from risk manager LlamaRisk, one wallet in the exploiter's cluster acted between 20:58 and 21:01 UTC:

That trade left freezable USDT locked inside Aave as collateral and gave the attacker wrapped ether, which no issuer can freeze. The position stays over-collateralized, and LlamaRisk said it "does not put Aave suppliers at risk." The ETH, however, was already gone.

Aave responded on a large scale. Between 21:42 and 23:04 UTC, its guardian multisigs froze:

The freezes blocked new deposits and borrowing. Reports also describe stablecoins being swapped for ETH on Uniswap.

The race was easy to see in the timeline. Each hour before an issuer froze its token was another hour to swap that token for ether. Tether and Circle reacted within the first hour, so most of the stablecoin stash was frozen before it could be converted.

A freeze stops the attacker, but it does not put money back in Binance's accounts. Frozen tokens stay locked at the attacker's addresses until the issuer decides what to do with them. In past cases, issuers have destroyed frozen tokens and reissued the same amount to the rightful owner, usually after legal or law-enforcement checks. That process takes time, and each issuer has its own procedure.

Binance has said that its initial investigation points to a compromised DevOps engineer's laptop. According to the company, that laptop let the attacker reach a service container and submit unauthorized withdrawal transactions. Binance said it found no evidence that wallet private keys were leaked, and that it has revoked the affected address authorization and is working with law enforcement and blockchain intelligence firms.

Deposits and withdrawals were suspended while security checks continue. Binance has not yet given a date for reopening them.

Binance has said it will cover all losses using its SAFU fund and its own money. Grouping the stolen basket by freezability gives a rough picture of what that bill could be.

The roughly $3 billion that is frozen should eventually be recovered, depending on how and when each issuer releases or reissues the tokens. The bitcoin, ether and TRX are another matter. Unless exchanges block deposits and investigators recover funds as they are laundered, that part is effectively gone. It accounts for most of the money Binance will have to cover from its own reserves.

The theft also raises a question for the whole industry. The assets that limited the damage were the issuer-controlled tokens that crypto purists often criticize. The assets that caused the real loss were the ones built so that no one can stop them. Exchanges have long decided hot-wallet sizes by liquidity needs. After this theft, they may also consider which assets in those wallets can still be stopped once they leave.

VANCOUVER, BC, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Stock Preachers News Commentary - Wall Street closed out a volatile week with every major index still higher versus last Friday, even after a broad Friday retreat. The Nasdaq Composite led decliners with a 1.24% drop on the session, while the S&P 500 fell 0.75% and the Dow slipped 0.14%. For the week, the S&P 500 gained 2.15%, the Nasdaq rose 1.92% and the Dow added 1.83%, as chip-driven strength carried the market even as Friday gave back some ground heading into the weekend. Active Companies from around the markets with current developments this week include: Eli Lilly and Company (NYSE: LLY), vVardis (NYSE: VVVV), NVIDIA Corporation (Nasdaq: NVDA), Caterpillar Inc. (NYSE: CAT), and Bank of America Corporation (NYSE: BAC).

The S&P 500 closed at 7535.72, down 56.68 points on the day but up 158.86 points, or 2.15%, from last Friday's 7376.86 close. The index touched a week high of 7652.76 and a week low of 7422.24, and sits up 10.08% year to date. Its RSI14 reading of 45.6 points to a market that cooled off from overbought conditions during the week.

The Nasdaq Composite fell 315.80 points, or 1.24%, on Friday to 25050.29, trimming its weekly gain to 1.92% from the November 6 close of 24579.43. The index ranged between 24762.57 and 25649.85 during the week and carries an RSI14 of 41.6, the weakest among major indices. The Dow Jones Industrial Average slipped 75.29 points to 52221.80, still up 1.83% on the week and 8.65% year to date, while the Russell 2000 eased 17.98 points to 2781.08, up 0.98% for the week.

The VIX rose 1.14 points to 19.84 on Friday, essentially flat on the week, while the VXN volatility gauge climbed 1.33 points to 29.88 but ended the week down 4.14 points. The 10-year Treasury yield rose 3 basis points on the day and 27 basis points on the week to 5.13%. Gold fell 5.56% for the week to $3,885.70 an ounce, silver dropped 6.66% to $49.06, and WTI crude added 1.92% to $88.52 a barrel.

#5524. Sovereign or not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

BREAKING ANALYSIS by David Vellante and Amit Eyal Govrin

Sovereignty is everywhere right now, and most people still can’t agree on what it means and, just as importantly, what it all means to them.

This week theCUBE Research releases its new market report, Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide. In this Breaking Analysis, we’re joined by its author, Amit Eyal Govrin, lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, to talk about why he wrote it, what sovereignty is and what it isn’t, and what surprised him most in the findings.

The full scores are in the report. Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide https://siliconangle.com/sovereign-or-not

Dave: As someone who’s been leading the thought leadership in this domain, how did you come up with the inspiration to research this topic and write the report?

Amit: To understand the how, it helps to understand the why. I’ve been thinking about this subject for a while now. It hasn’t always been called “sovereignty,” but the tenets have always been the same.

It all started around four years ago, as I’ve been a builder in this space for that long. First with Kubiya, one of the industry’s first agentic implementations, deploying agents in enterprise production environments as early as September 2023, before agents were even an industry term.

We were deploying as a software-as-a-service company, and many of those concerns were legitimate. As a software company, we got to keep our intellectual property and license it out. If we were successful, we would create dependency, which effectively meant customers lost control of their crown jewels.

When we started Agentcy Labs earlier this year, customers familiar with our work approached us, and many of these points crystallized for us. What they told us: We’re relieved you are no longer at Kubiya. It’s not that we ever doubted your technology or the value it brings. Quite the opposite. That was what they were afraid of. Kubiya creates a dependency, adoption balloons, and they lose control of their costs. Or a vendor changes the meter on them because of shareholder pressure or regulatory controls.

What clicked for us is that their resistance was never about Kubiya or our technology. It was about the loss of control of their alpha. Namely, the Agentic Operating System, the key driver of their artificial intelligence transformation, which falls under our technological pillar.

It doesn’t matter if the vendor is a startup, an AI lab or a hyperscaler. No enterprise can afford to mortgage its entire business on an external dependency on such a key issue. It’s far too strategic not to own outright.

That finding forced us to rethink the model behind software, dig deeper into sovereignty as an issue of control, and help the industry define it in a more standardized way.

Dave: So control is the heart of it. But when most people hear sovereignty, they think about where the data sits. Is that the wrong way to look at it?

Amit: Sovereignty goes well beyond territory, which is often the most misunderstood aspect. People hear sovereignty and immediately revert to the sovereign state: government initiatives, national security, on-premises air-gapped environments. That can be true in some cases. But by and large, our sovereignty discussions involve enterprises and regulated industries that have sovereignty as a core tenet of their AI initiatives.

It goes beyond buzzwords and sovereign-washing claims. Think back to the explosive Alex Karp interview on CNBC claiming enterprises are losing their alpha to frontier labs. I largely agree with that claim, by the way. Only he finished his pitch by offering customers to move it over to Palantir. In other words: Stop mortgaging your alpha to Anthropic and OpenAI, come rent it from us.

That interview was my trigger point to take up arms and educate the industry on sovereignty: what it is, what it isn’t, and most importantly, what you, as a buyer of AI, can do about it.

Dave: And you’ve been out in the field with buyers ever since. What did those conversations teach you, and how did that shape the framework?

Amit: Since then, we’ve been included in dozens of engagements with enterprises, governments and policymakers around the world, from Washington to Brussels, New Delhi, Sydney and even Riyadh. We are in the room when sovereignty discussions happen. That helped us shape our view, tease out the concerns, and focus on what really matters and why. From those discussions came the 5 Pillars of Sovereignty framework. We use it today to assess all vendor relationships, policy and regulation, and geopolitical events.

Dave: Which brings us to the report. You started with the hyperscalers. Walk us through how you approached it.

Amit: In our first edition, Sovereign or Not? The Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide, we take the buyer’s lens and assess each hyperscaler by its sovereignty posture.

Hint: By definition, working with any hyperscaler means ceding a good portion of control over your Operational, Technological, Legal and Financial pillars. Oftentimes that’s the reality in the real world.

My view: Sovereignty is not a purity test. It’s perfectly acceptable to go with a hyperscaler, as long as it’s a known dependency you priced in as an acceptable risk. If that’s the case, let us guide you through these considerations to the best path forward for your organization.

Dave: OK, let’s get to the part everyone wants to know. Who scored what, and why?

Amit: We looked at seven hyperscalers and 40 of their offerings, from the point of view of buyers in five regions: the U.S., Europe, Asia-Pacific, Latin America and the rest, including the Middle East and Africa. Everything is scored out of 5.

The short version: The most sovereign product a hyperscaler sells is the one the hyperscaler itself can’t reach.

On these tests, sovereignty often runs inverse to how a hyperscaler is built. A shared global control plane and services the vendor runs for the customer make a cloud easy to adopt, but every layer the vendor runs is a layer the buyer does not control. Amazon Web Services and Google built their platforms around that abstraction, which becomes a hindrance once a buyer needs to run the stack without them. The grades measure how much control a buyer can take back, not the quality of the cloud.

Who came out on top, who came in last, and by how much, is in the report. And every score is backed by a source. Don’t like your grade? Publish the document and we’ll re-score it.

Dave: What surprised you most when you went through the findings?

Amit: None of the hyperscalers has a practical solution for the U.S. CLOUD Act, and that alone has created a real legal clawback on non-U.S. companies.

In plain English: The U.S. government can ask an American cloud company for data it controls, no matter which country the data sits in. A sovereign cloud in Brandenburg, run by a German subsidiary, doesn’t change the answer. It’s still owned by an American company.

The vendors aren’t hiding it. AWS told us as much on the record. Microsoft’s own lawyer in France told the French Senate he couldn’t guarantee French data would never reach U.S. authorities. That’s honesty, and we don’t penalize honesty. It’s the law, and it applies to every American cloud the same way.

The fixes buyers are being sold, like keeping data local, holding your own encryption keys, or a contract promise to fight requests, don’t change who the government can go to.

Dave: So what’s a non-U.S. buyer supposed to do about that?

Amit: There’s no perfect answer today, only partial ones.

Going with a hyperscaler is fine, as long as you know the risk and priced it in. What’s not fine is believing a data center in Brandenburg, on its own merits, solved your sovereignty problem.

Dave: And this is just the first of several. Where do you go from here?

Amit: This is the first of a series: neoclouds, OEMs, telcos and specialized sovereign initiatives, wherever you happen to be, whether you’re a U.S., EU, Latin American, APAC or Middle Eastern buyer. Every edition covers the 5 Pillars, plus security, regulation and exit costs. Readers will be surprised by how deep we got, including quotes from the hyperscalers themselves and surveys of actual buyers. I truly think this will be valuable to everyone listening and reading.

Dave: That’s phenomenal, Amit. This is a cutting-edge report on a truly important and timely subject. If previously you were building on the frontier, you’re now squarely on the frontier of research. The scores, the vendor answers and the buyer data are all in the full report.

Read the full report online: Sovereign or Not? The 2026 Hyperscaler Buyer’s Guide

Amit Eyal Govrin is lead analyst for sovereign AI at theCUBE Research and CEO of Agentcy Labs, which designs and builds sovereign AI platforms for enterprises and governments. His research for theCUBE Research is conducted under theCUBE Research’s editorial standards and is not sponsored or directed by Agentcy Labs. #5523. Alwaleed Philanthropies and The Research, Development and Innovation Authority Sign Strategic Partnership valued at SAR 10 million to Advance Innovation and Technology Solutions

RIYADH, Saudi Arabia, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Alwaleed Philanthropies, chaired by HRH Prince Alwaleed bin talal Al Saud and the Research, Development and Innovation Authority (RDIA) have signed a strategic partnership agreement in the presence of HRH Princess Lamia bint Majed Al Saud, Secretary General of Alwaleed Philanthropies, and HE Dr. Munir bin Mahmoud Eldesouki, Acting Governor of RDIA, to strengthen Saudi Arabia's research, development and innovation ecosystem, empower researchers and innovators, and advance technology solutions with meaningful impact.

The partnership will also promote a culture of research and innovation, build national capabilities, and enable the development of programs and initiatives aligned with the Kingdom's priorities in key technology fields.

As part of the partnership, Alwaleed Philanthropies will play a role in enabling the Open RAN Technology Challenge and contributing to the ongoing oversight of the participating startup. Four startups were selected as winners after presenting innovative and deployable technology solutions. The partnership will enable the winning startups to further develop their solutions, accelerate their transition to deployment, launch their products, and measure their impact.

Alwaleed Philanthropies will also contribute to promoting a culture of research, development and innovation and strengthening its presence within the local community. The Research, Development and Innovation Authority will coordinate with relevant stakeholders across the RDI ecosystem, monitor the startups' performance and periodic reports, share updates with Alwaleed Philanthropies, and assess the initiative's outputs and impact.

The partnership includes the formation of a joint working group to oversee implementation, fulfil shared commitments, monitor the participating startups, and facilitate the launch of products developed through the initiative. The two organizations will also explore and develop joint programs and initiatives in research and innovation, strengthening collaboration between the public and nonprofit sectors and creating sustainable impact in Saudi Arabia and internationally, in line with applicable laws and regulations.

The strategic partnership builds on the successful collaboration between Alwaleed Philanthropies and the Research, Development and Innovation Authority. Their first joint initiative enabled 96 women to pursue postgraduate studies in fields of the future, including artificial intelligence and renewable energy, at universities ranked among the world's top 30, contributing to the development of highly qualified national capabilities.

The partnership represents a sustainable model for empowering national talent, advancing innovation, and developing technology solutions with tangible impact. It will help address national challenges and transform ideas and research into products and solutions that create lasting knowledge and economic value, supporting the Kingdom's transition toward an economy powered by knowledge and innovation.

#5522. Europe will release 42 million barrels of oil reserves over three months, France says

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Half of the volume will be diesel, France's economy minister said, as E.U. energy ministers meet over fuel prices and winter supply

French Economy Minister Roland Lescure said Thursday that over the coming three months, Europe will put 42 million barrels of its oil reserves on the market to help ease prices, according to Bloomberg. Half of the volume will be diesel, he said.

Lescure made the remarks before E.U. energy ministers gathered in Luxembourg, according to Bloomberg. The ministers are set to discuss energy security before the winter heating season, according to Reuters.

Lescure said France’s previously announced drawdown of 10 million barrels of diesel would arrive on the market within days, according to Bloomberg. He said prices would begin reacting as early as next week. He said the reserves would be sold without markup, lowering prices by 12 to 18 euro cents per liter.

Diesel is "at the heart of our challenges," Lescure said, according to Bloomberg. He said he was hopeful that the present crisis would be settled "slowly, but surely," and that Europe would leave the door open to additional releases from its stockpiles.

The Group of Seven nations agreed on Oct. 2 to release 100 million barrels of oil and diesel from emergency reserves, with the International Energy Agency overseeing a drawdown spread over four months. The Trump administration had pressed European countries to tap their stockpiles as fuel prices climbed.

The IEA's Governing Board agreed to accelerate the release of remaining volumes under its March 2026 Collective Action on Oct. 15, the agency said. About 330 million barrels had been released at that point, with around 100 million barrels remaining. The board said specific plans were in place for more than 20 million barrels of diesel to be released as soon as possible.

The board also noted the IEA Secretariat's assessments pointing to continued tightness in oil markets, notably for diesel. It encouraged members with oil production and refining capacity to boost supply of crude and refined products, particularly diesel.

#5521. CNFinance Announces Change of Auditor

GUANGZHOU, China, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- CNFinance Holdings Limited (NYSE: CNF) ("CNFinance" or the "Company"), a leading home equity loan service provider in China, today announced the change of auditor, effective November 13, 2026. HTL International, LLC ("HTL") has served as the Company's independent registered public accounting firm since December 2024. HTL declined to stand for re-election to serve as the independent registered public accounting firm for the audits of the Company's financial statements for the financial year ending December 31, 2026. The decision was not a result of any disagreement between the Company and HTL on any matter of accounting principles or practices, financial statement disclosure, or auditing scope or procedure. The audit committee of the Company's Board of Directors has approved the change of auditor and appointed Guangdong Prouden CPAs GP ("Prouden") as the Company's independent registered public accounting firm for the fiscal year ended December 31, 2026.

The appointment of Prouden was made after a careful and thorough evaluation process and has been approved by the audit committee of the Company's board of directors.

Prouden succeeds HTL, the Company's previous independent registered public accounting firm. The reports of HTL on the Company's consolidated financial statements for each of the fiscal years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025 did not contain an adverse opinion or a disclaimer of opinion and were not qualified or modified as to uncertainty, audit scope or accounting principle.

During each of the fiscal years ended December 31, 2024 and 2025 and the subsequent period through November 13, 2026, there have been no disagreements between the Company and HTL on any matter of accounting principles or practices, financial statement disclosure, or auditing scope or procedure, which disagreements, if not resolved to the satisfaction of HTL, would have caused HTL to make reference to the subject matter of the disagreements in its report on the consolidated financial statements, and there have been no "reportable events" as the term is described in Item 16F(a)(1)(v) of Form 20-F.

The Company is working closely with HTL and Prouden to ensure a seamless transition.

The audit committee would like to express its sincere gratitude to HTL for its quality of services rendered to the Company over the past years.

CNFinance Holdings Limited (NYSE: CNF) ("CNFinance" or the "Company") is a leading home equity loan service provider in China. CNFinance, through its operating subsidiaries in China, conducts business by connecting demands and supplies through collaborating with sales partners and trust companies under the trust lending model, and sales partners, local channel partners and commercial banks under the commercial bank partnership model. Sales partners and local channel partners are responsible for recommending micro- and small-enterprise ("MSE") owners with financing needs to the Company and the Company introduces eligible borrowers to licensed financial institutions with sufficient funding sources including trust companies and commercial banks who will then conduct their own risk assessments and make credit decisions. The Company's primary target borrower segment is MSE owners who own real properties in Tier 1 and Tier 2 cities and other major cities in China. The Company's risk mitigation mechanism is embedded in the design of its loan products, supported by an integrated online and offline process focusing on risks of both borrowers and collateral and further enhanced by effective post-loan management procedures.

#5520. SoftBank Corp. might launch its U.S. AI cloud business in other countries first

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The mobile carrier's CEO is gauging the effect of the Democratic midterm sweep and rising anti-data center sentiment

SoftBank, the mobile unit of SoftBank Group, may roll out its AI cloud business in other countries before the U.S. if American conditions deteriorate, CEO Junichi Miyakawa said, according to Bloomberg.

Speaking to investors in Tokyo as the company reported its results, Miyakawa said recent developments in the U.S. will not help the company. Should conditions in the U.S. deteriorate sharply, he said, "we may launch in other countries first," according to Bloomberg. He added that, worldwide, customers still want plenty of AI data center capacity.

The company had been preparing to build AI cloud operations in the U.S., according to Bloomberg. It is now working out the effect of last week's Democratic midterm sweep and mounting resistance to data centers, Bloomberg said.

The Democratic win has led observers to anticipate stricter regulatory oversight and slower construction of data centers, according to Reuters.

SoftBank on Monday announced its consolidated earnings results for the six months ended Sept. 30. The company raised its annual profit outlook, and its cloud and AI-related revenue rose 37% in the six months through September.

SoftBank is Japan's third-largest wireless carrier, according to Bloomberg. It has branched out into AI services and data center operations to meet growing demand among Japanese businesses. Its plans call for up to 10 gigawatts of U.S. capacity.

SoftBank Group has also been looking at Asia for AI infrastructure. Malaysian Prime Minister Anwar Ibrahim said last month that the group intends to put $50 billion into Malaysia for AI, data centers and other emerging technologies. Anwar said SoftBank Group founder and CEO Masayoshi Son had chosen sites in Kuching, Sarawak, and in peninsular Malaysia.

SoftBank Group is discussing the plan as it works to bring to Asia the AI infrastructure buildout it has pursued in the U.S. and Europe.

#5519. Freightos Receives Nasdaq Notice Regarding Minimum Bid Price Requirement

BARCELONA, Spain, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Freightos Limited (NASDAQ: CRGO) ("Freightos" or the "Company"), the leading vendor-neutral global freight pricing, booking and procurement platform, today announced that on November 10, 2026, it received a written notification letter (the "Notification Letter") from the Listing Qualifications Department of The Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") notifying the Company that it is not in compliance with the minimum bid price requirement set forth in Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) for continued listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market.

Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of $1.00 per share, and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet this requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. The Notification Letter indicated that the closing bid price of the Company's ordinary shares had been below $1.00 per share for 30 consecutive business days, from September 29, 2026 through November 9, 2026.

In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), the Company has been provided an initial period of 180 calendar days from the date of the Notification Letter, or until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement. The Company will regain compliance if, at any time during this compliance period, the closing bid price of its ordinary shares is at least $1.00 per share for a minimum of 10 consecutive business days, unless Nasdaq exercises its discretion to extend this period under Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(H). If the Company regains compliance, Nasdaq will provide the Company with written confirmation and the matter will be closed.

If the Company does not regain compliance by May 10, 2027, the Company may be eligible for an additional 180-calendar-day compliance period.

The Notification Letter has no immediate effect on the listing of the Company's ordinary shares. The Company's ordinary shares will continue to be listed and to trade on the Nasdaq Capital Market under the symbol "CRGO" during the compliance period. The Notification Letter does not affect the Company's business operations.

The Company intends to monitor the closing bid price of its ordinary shares and is evaluating available options to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement within the applicable compliance period, which may include, if necessary, effecting a reverse share split, subject to any required shareholder approval. There can be no assurance that the Company will regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement or maintain compliance with any other Nasdaq continued listing requirement.

#5518. Honda plans $3 billion Ohio hybrid plant, its first new U.S. mass-production plant since 2008

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The plant is expected to begin production in 2029 with capacity for 240,000 vehicles a year and more than 2,000 jobs

Honda $HMC announced plans to build a $3 billion factory in central Ohio, with production slated to start in 2029 pending final government approvals.

The plant will create more than 2,000 jobs and have capacity for 240,000 vehicles a year, the company said. It will sit on land between Honda's existing East Liberty and Marysville auto plants and become the fourth Honda auto plant in Ohio. The project is part of investments that will expand Honda's yearly vehicle-building capability in the U.S. to roughly 1.3 million units and across North America to roughly 1.9 million.

Honda said the plant will be able to build multiple vehicle types and powertrains, including hybrid, gasoline-powered and battery-electric vehicles. Honda would not name the models planned for the site. It would be the automaker’s first large-scale U.S. factory for assembling vehicles since an Indiana facility began operating in 2008, according to CNBC.

"We are making one of the most significant commitments in our history to position Honda for the next 50 years," Bob Nelson, executive vice president of American Honda Motor Co., said in a statement.

Nelson told CNBC that although tariffs affect the business, the plant mainly reflects a drive for expansion in the U.S. "Tariffs are an impact to us, even with the high localization rate that we have," he said. "But the real impact is that we have customers out there wanting Honda product and we can't give it to them."

Honda also plans investments at existing facilities in Ohio, Alabama and Georgia to expand production of hybrid vehicles, engines and hybrid systems. In Alabama, the company will add equipment for producing a hybrid V6 engine of a new design. In Ohio, it is retooling the Anna Engine Plant for a next-generation four-cylinder engine and a transmission plant to raise hybrid system capacity by 250% in the coming years. Honda also will update its Alliston, Ontario, operations and reintroduce engine manufacturing there.

In May, Honda unveiled a plan to roll out 15 more hybrids across its Honda and Acura lineups around the globe by 2030, with North America expected to be the primary market for many of them.

Honda had warned in August that it might not build a new North American assembly plant if the U.S., Canada and Mexico failed to extend the USMCA trade agreement. The agreement remains unextended as a deepening trade conflict pits the U.S. against Canada, according to Reuters.

OSAKA, Japan, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- FiEE, Inc. (NASDAQ:FIEE) ("FiEE," the "Company," "we," "our," or similar terms), a technology company that leverages IoT, connectivity, and AI to deliver SaaS solutions for content creation and brand management, along with phygital art advisory services that connect artists, collectors, and brands, today announced its unaudited financial results for the three and nine months ended September 30, 2026.

Operational and Financial Highlights for the Nine Months Ended September 30, 2026

Operational and Financial Highlights for the Three Months Ended September 30, 2026

Rafael Li, Chief Executive Officer and President of FiEE, commented, "We delivered solid financial results during the period and made meaningful progress in building a more diversified, scalable digital services platform. #5516. OPEC crude oil output is nearing pre-war levels as Saudi Arabia rebounds

Free daily briefing on global business news.

OPEC production rose 930,000 barrels a day in October to 22.8 million, about 88% of February levels, a Bloomberg survey shows

Andrey Rudakov / Bloomberg via Getty Images

OPEC pumped 22.8 million barrels of crude a day in October, a gain of 930,000 barrels a day that leaves output at about 88% of its February level, according to a Bloomberg survey.

Saudi Arabia was responsible for the bulk of the increase, according to Bloomberg. The kingdom boosted output by 970,000 barrels a day to 9.2 million, leaving it roughly 800,000 barrels daily short of the pace it held when the year began. Saudi oil exports ran at an average of 7 million barrels daily in October, according to tanker-tracking data compiled by Bloomberg. Bloomberg attributed the gain to Saudi Arabia routing a larger number of tankers via the Strait of Hormuz and loading cargoes along its Red Sea coast, despite hostilities connected to the U.S.-Iran conflict.

Iraq added 140,000 barrels a day to reach 4.15 million, and Kuwait added 130,000 to reach 2 million, according to Bloomberg. Those gains were canceled out by lower output in Nigeria and Iran.

Iran's output dropped 120,000 barrels daily to 1.9 million, the weakest reading in Bloomberg's monthly records going back to 1989. Bloomberg said satellite imagery has not captured a single tanker at Iranian export terminals, Kharg Island among them, since late August, with the U.S. blockade of Iran's ports still in force.

Brent crude traded near $98 a barrel this week.

Saudi Aramco's CEO, Amin Nasser, said at an Abu Dhabi industry conference earlier in the week that the firm intends to "maximize production going forward in the fourth quarter," according to Bloomberg.

Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Iraq and Kuwait exported a combined 15.53 million barrels of crude a day in October, a 10% increase that put volumes in line with levels at the start of the year. Kuwait's shipments of 1.44 million barrels a day were the highest since before the war began. Iran's exports stayed at zero for a second month.

JPMorgan $JPM estimates Middle East oil exports now stand near 20.7 million barrels a day, up from 9.8 million in March, although they have yet to return to where they were before the conflict erupted in late February, according to Reuters.

OPEC and its allies are examining the volumes each member is technically capable of producing, as groundwork for 2027 output targets to be set at a ministerial meeting on Nov. 29, according to Bloomberg.

#5515. Reconciling the OCC’s Final Stablecoin Reserve Floors Against the Fed’s Proposal

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The OCC's final GENIUS Act rule sets a 5% cash floor and a 40% cap on any one counterparty. The Fed's open proposal uses neither figure, and its comment window runs until November 30.

Issuers now face two sets of reserve rules that share a redemption deadline and differ on almost everything else.

Ask a stablecoin issuer what its reserves must look like in 2027, and the honest answer is now: it depends which regulator you ask.

The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency (OCC) gave its answer on October 21, the final rule implementing the GENIUS Act. Our October 19 piece on staggered agency filings expected that rule "before the end of October," and it came two days later. The rule sets specific numbers: at least 5% of reserves in demand deposits or similar instant-access funds, and no more than 40% of reserves with a single counterparty.

The Federal Reserve's answer is still a proposal. Its GENIUS Act rulemaking remains open for comment until November 30, and it contains neither of those numbers. Until the Fed finalizes its rule, any company planning to issue under both agencies' rules, or deciding which one to apply to, is working with one fixed set of numbers and one open-ended set of principles.

The OCC's final rule was published in the Federal Register on October 23 and takes effect on January 18, 2027, the same day as the GENIUS Act itself. Comptroller Jonathan V. Gould called it "a clear, practical framework for payment stablecoin innovation, with strong standards for reserve backing, redemption, and risk management."

The reserve rules are looser than the March proposal in several places:

The OCC also removed the rebuttable presumption that some affiliate yield arrangements break the GENIUS Act's ban on paying interest, though it kept its broader anti-evasion powers. The agency received about 328 comments.

For existing issuers, the timeline is short. Under OCC Bulletin 2026-51, firms already operating in the United States that file a "substantially complete" application by January 18 can generally expect a waiver of the prior-approval requirement.

The Fed released its two proposals on September 24. They were published in the Federal Register on September 29 under Docket No. R-1899, and comments are due November 30.

The main requirements proposal would require Board-supervised issuers to "fully back their stablecoins with certain permissible reserve assets". The reserves' fair value would have to equal or exceed the stablecoins' outstanding value at all times. Permissible assets include:

On diversification, however, the Fed sets no numbers. Reserves must be "sufficiently diverse" to keep one-to-one backing at all times, and issuers must manage concentration in uninsured deposits and repo counterparties. The Board says it generally expects reserves to be mostly Treasuries, but it sets no cash floor and no counterparty percentage.

Redemption is where the two agencies agree most closely. Both define timely redemption as no later than two business days after a request. The difference lies in what happens under stress.

The FDIC, in its own proposal, uses a third approach: issuers would report on their own when redemption requests exceed 10% of issuance within 24 hours.

The clearest conflict is not about how much cash an issuer must hold, but how each agency treats bank deposits.

Under the OCC rule, at least 5% of reserves must be held in demand deposits or similar balances. That is a direct requirement to hold bank money.

The Fed proposal has no deposit floor. Instead, it would charge 2% capital against reserves held as uninsured deposits at an insured bank, and the same charge applies to undercollateralized reverse repo. One agency requires a minimum amount in deposits, and the other makes issuers hold extra capital against the deposits they choose to keep.

Concentration works the same way. An issuer with 60% of its deposit reserves at one bank would breach the OCC's 40% cap, unless one of the custodian or government exemptions applies. Under the Fed's current text, that issuer would face only a judgment by its supervisor about whether it has managed concentration risk properly.

The rules for a reserve shortfall also differ:

The difference is largest on capital. The OCC sets an individualized capital requirement measured in GAAP tangible equity. It has a $5 million floor that now lasts for the issuer's whole life, plus an operational backstop equal to 12 months of total expenses, up to half of which can be funded with qualifying subordinated debt.

The Fed proposes a fixed formula. On top of the 2% charges on deposits and repo, it adds an operational-risk charge on outstanding issuance:

It also adds 25% of three-year average revenue from sources other than reserves, adjusted by a loss scalar.

For an issuer with $50 billion in circulation, the issuance charge alone works out to $850 million under the Fed's proposal, before the revenue add-on. The OCC rule has no comparable fixed figure. Its capital depends on the issuer's own risk profile, with the $5 million floor as the only set minimum.

For now, the OCC's figures are final and the Fed's are not. Issuers and banks that hold reserves can still argue for changes until the Fed's comment period closes on November 30, and the Fed has asked 277 questions.

The decisions that matter most are clear from the comparison above:

Both sets of rules apply from the same date, January 18, 2027. If the Fed's final rule keeps its current approach, the United States will begin regulating stablecoins with a common redemption deadline and two different reserve rulebooks, decided by which agency charters the issuer.

#5514. NeuralSat raises $3.2M to bring high-speed data connectivity and compute to space

German startup NeuralSat GmbH announced Thursday that it has raised €2.9 million, about $3.2 million, in pre-seed funding to develop a 72-satellite data-relay processing network aimed at speeding up the flow of data from space.

Capnamic and Bayern Kapital co-led the round. Other investors participating in the round included ZOHO.VC, Robin Capital, BAB – Die Förderbank für Bremen und Bremerhaven, Mission E and KIEMIS Holding.

Founded in early 2026, NeuralSat’s satellite constellation will allow operators to offload computing and communications. According to the company, its network will deliver up to 50 gigabits per second via optical and high-frequency radio links.

The network will support real-time edge processing, hosted workloads for commercial and defense clients and provide for time-critical missions like Earth observation and signals intelligence.

“We believe the next major evolution in space will… come from connecting satellites to shared infrastructure that enables them to communicate, access computing resources, and operate together,” Chief Executive Mohd Bilal said in a statement. “Just as the internet transformed how computers interact on Earth, we intend to transform how intelligence is connected and delivered in space.”

The company said the funding will help it accelerate plans to launch its first in-orbit demonstration node, planned for October 2027. After that, NeuralSat plans to begin rolling out commercial operational satellites.

The race to develop and build better connectivity and compute capabilities in space is on. Canadian startup Kepler Communications Inc. launched its first commercial space data relay service in January, allowing resilient data transfer and onboard computing, with a next-gen optical relay network announced in August. Skyloom, acquired by quantum computing firm IonQ Inc. in early 2026, deployed 84 optical terminals and a relay architecture in low Earth orbit.

Space is not the optimal place to run processors because heat dissipation becomes a major issue with no air to carry it away. But space technology firms have developed solutions to radiate it from giant sails and other surfaces. Space-based compute may not replace terrestrial data centers, but it can enable edge compute given payload weight restrictions for orbital launch.

Starcloud Inc., formerly known as Lumen Orbit, raised $250 million in August at a $2.3 billion valuation. The company has already tested an Nvidia H100 graphics processing unit in orbit in late 2025, proving that it can scale to multi-satellite AI “data centers.” The company is now collaborating with Nvidia Corp. on upcoming space-grade chips.

Currently, data relay and compute processing in space reduce the need for other satellites to send data to Earth to complete workloads. Talking to a nearby satellite for edge compute can shave significant time off data transfers. Sending data down to Earth can take a round trip of four to more than 30 milliseconds; satellite-to-satellite is slightly faster, at three to 30 milliseconds.

The real boost comes from relaying between satellites rather than routing long distances on the ground to a data center and back, often via optical cable ground networks, which add additional lag. Over long distances across the globe, inter-satellite links are around 30% to 50% faster than sending signals down to Earth for processing.

Companies such as NeuralSat hope to use the advantage of being right there, near the data production, to provide processing capabilities, or swift relay to a satellite closer geographically to terrestrial data center processing to reduce delays.

Brent crude fell 16% last week, while Iran's foreign minister said talks with Washington had made no progress

President Donald Trump said Sunday that he considered additional U.S. strikes on Iran improbable while negotiations to wind down the war kept advancing, and oil prices dropped on Monday.

Brent crude futures traded below $100 a barrel. Brent was down 3.5% at $94.93, and West Texas Intermediate was down 3% at $88.13.

Trump had suggested he might resume attacks on Iran once last week's midterm elections were over, but there was no indication of a major American military campaign, according to Reuters. Iran has warned that it would retaliate against U.S. and Israeli targets.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said negotiations with Washington had yielded no headway, while Tehran was waiting to find out whether the U.S. administration would shift its stance once the elections were over, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Saxo Bank analyst Ole Hansen said the slide in oil reflects optimism about a U.S.-Iran peace agreement more than any tangible evidence of headway, according to Reuters. Brent fell 16% last week, marking its sharpest weekly decline since the COVID-19 pandemic began.

Attacks and shipping incidents continued over the weekend. An administrative office run by Saudi Aramco in Riyadh was lightly damaged on Sunday, according to The Wall Street Journal. The Saudi Energy Ministry said the building was hit by debris raining down after an attempted attack, with no casualties reported. The Iran-aligned Houthis claimed responsibility for the attack, according to Reuters.

The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations said an unidentified projectile hit a tanker leaving the Strait of Hormuz on Sunday, according to The Wall Street Journal. The crew was safe. The U.K. Maritime Trade Operations also relayed a report from military authorities of a burning tanker roughly eight nautical miles to the northwest of Khasab, Oman, where the crew was evacuated. The origin of the blaze was not disclosed.

Trump said the United States had no immediate plans to strike Iran last Wednesday, the day after Democrats won majorities in the House and the Senate. Brent crude futures traded at $101.02 that day.

The U.S. military had conducted defensive strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island the day before, aimed at anti-aircraft missiles fired at American assets, a U.S. official said. A senior Iranian official said Tehran and Washington were a long way from an agreement to end the war.

#5512. Greenland Technologies Holding Corporation Receives Nasdaq Notification Regarding Minimum Bid Price Deficiency

HANGZHOU, China, Nov. 13, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Greenland Technologies Holding Corporation (Nasdaq: GTEC) ("Greenland" or the "Company"), a technology developer and manufacturer of electric industrial vehicles and drivetrain systems for material handling machineries and vehicles, today announced that the Company received a written notification (the "Notification Letter") from the Nasdaq Stock Market LLC ("Nasdaq") on November 10, 2026, notifying the Company that it is not in compliance with the minimum bid price requirement set forth in the Nasdaq Listing Rules for continued listing on the Nasdaq.

Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2) requires listed securities to maintain a minimum bid price of US$1.00 per share, and Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A) provides that a failure to meet the minimum bid price requirement exists if the deficiency continues for a period of 30 consecutive business days. Based on the closing bid price of the Company's Class A ordinary shares for the 30 consecutive business days from September 29, 2026 to November 9, 2026, the Company no longer meets the minimum bid price requirement.

The Notification Letter does not impact the Company's listing on the Nasdaq Capital Market at this time. In accordance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5810(c)(3)(A), the Company has been provided 180 calendar days, or until May 10, 2027, to regain compliance with Nasdaq Listing Rule 5550(a)(2). To regain compliance, the Company's Class A ordinary shares must have a closing bid price of at least US$1.00 for a minimum of 10 consecutive business days. In the event the Company does not regain compliance by May 10, 2027, the Company may be eligible for additional time to regain compliance or may face delisting.

The Company's business operations are not affected by the receipt of the Notification Letter. The Company intends to monitor the closing bid price of its Class A ordinary shares and may, if appropriate, consider implementing available options, including, but not limited to, implementing a share consolidation, to regain compliance with the minimum bid price requirement under the Nasdaq Listing Rules.

#5511. Binance said North Korean hackers used fake job interviews in $6.3 billion heist

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Binance's incident report traces the Oct. 29 theft to a tampered coding tool, a fraudulent recruitment process and an internal AI tool

Binance said Tuesday that hackers it attributes to North Korea used fake job interviews and malicious software to steal $6.3 billion from the exchange, according to Bloomberg. The company called the breach a "sophisticated, multi-stage campaign" in an incident report published Tuesday, Bloomberg reported.

The attack began in June, when a staffer who builds Binance's wallets installed a doctored AI tool, according to Reuters. Binance spotted the problem, swapped out the device and reset credentials, though the hacker still learned the employee's role and those of teammates on the wallet team, Reuters reported.

In September, someone posing as a project director approached a second software engineer through a job hunting platform, according to Bloomberg. That engineer then took part in an interview on a social messaging app with someone posing as the CEO of an invented company, and was told to download an assignment that held a "malicious code repository."

On Oct. 20, the attackers leveraged an internal AI tool along with the second engineer's infected computer to seize command of the devices belonging to two other engineers, according to The Block $SQ. Then on Oct. 29, the attackers logged in with stolen credentials, set up a container and ran a malicious script that kicked off the theft from the wallet, The Block reported.

“This was not a single mistake or a single breach. It was a campaign built over many months,” Binance Co-CEO Richard Teng said, according to Bloomberg. Teng said the attackers blended sham hiring interviews, malware posing as genuine developer tools, hijacked devices and AI-driven methods.

About $2.85 billion in assets has been frozen or intercepted by Binance, which has also restored 98% of the affected assets, according to The Block. Binance has said it is reimbursing every customer who lost money, according to Reuters.

The exchange paused withdrawals after the incident and began letting users take out funds again on Sunday, according to Bloomberg. By Tuesday, deposits per hour had begun to outpace withdrawals per hour, Bloomberg reported.

Binance said it has shut the entry points the attackers exploited, replaced or rebuilt the systems that were hit, tightened controls on devices and broadened its AI-based anomaly detection, according to The Block. It also said it caught and stopped 57 attacks in 2026 that it suspects were tied to North Korea, many of which relied on comparable methods.

The FBI has attributed the breach to North Korean hackers, according to Bloomberg. North Korea has denied the claim. On Monday, the sister of North Korean leader Kim Jong-un called the FBI's claims a "grave political provocation," according to The Block.
