#5485. 10 executives who left their companies and later returned as CEO

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 boomerang CEOs, from Steve Jobs at Apple to Pat Gelsinger at Intel, left the companies they once led or worked for and later returned to run them

When a board picks a new chief executive, it sometimes chooses someone who has already left the company once. That person knows the business, its products and many of its people. They also bring a record from their first stint, including whatever ended it.

Executives who take that route are often called boomerang CEOs. The term covers anyone who returns to run a company they founded, led or worked for earlier. The paths back vary, and each one reflects a different kind of succession decision.

Some returns involve founders who handed the CEO title to a successor and later took it back. Michael Dell $DELL gave up the role in 2004 but stayed on as chairman, then reclaimed it in January 2007. Larry Page passed Google $GOOGL's top job to Eric Schmidt in 2001 and resumed it in April 2011. Jack Dorsey, Charles Schwab $SCHW and Mark Pincus also returned to companies they had founded or co-founded after other executives ran them.

Other comebacks start with a board reversing its own succession plan. Disney $DIS's board brought Bob Iger back as CEO on November 20, 2022, replacing Bob Chapek, the executive who had succeeded him. Some executives return more than once. Howard Schultz took back the Starbucks $SBUX CEO job in January 2008, then came back again as interim CEO in April 2022.

A few routes run outside the company altogether. Steve Jobs left Apple $AAPL in 1985 and came back after Apple bought NeXT, the company he ran after leaving. He became interim CEO in September 1997. Pat Gelsinger joined Intel $INTC in 1979, left in 2009 for EMC and became CEO of VMware in 2012. He returned as Intel's CEO in February 2021. Michael Bloomberg stepped away from the company he founded to serve as mayor of New York City, then returned to run it in January 2014.

The 10 executives here span technology, consumer brands, entertainment, media and financial services. They are a selection, not a ranking or a complete list of CEO comebacks. Each slide sets out when the executive left, who held the job in between and how the return came about.

Steve Jobs became Apple $AAPL's interim CEO in September 1997, after Apple bought NeXT, the company he ran after his first exit. His route back to the top job ran through an acquisition rather than a direct appointment.

Jobs co-founded Apple in 1976. He left in 1985 after a power struggle with John Sculley, who was then Apple's CEO.

Jobs held the chairman's title at the time, not the chief executive's. The 1985 dispute ended with him giving up that seat and leaving the company altogether.

During his years away, Jobs ran NeXT. Apple bought that business in a deal that spanned 1996 and 1997. The purchase put Jobs back inside the company he had co-founded before any change at the top.

The CEO job opened when Gil Amelio resigned. Jobs stepped into the role on an interim basis in September 1997, 12 years after his 1985 exit.

That sequence set his return apart from a board hiring a former leader from outside. By the time the post came open, Jobs was already back at Apple through the NeXT deal.

He later dropped the interim label and led Apple as its permanent chief executive.

Apple released the iMac, the iPod and the iPhone during his second tenure. All three arrived after a return that began with the acquisition of NeXT.

Howard Schultz returned as CEO of Starbucks $SBUX in January 2008, then came back again as interim CEO in April 2022. He retook the top job at the coffee chain on two separate occasions.

Schultz held the chief executive title at Starbucks until 2000. His first return to the post came more than seven years after that exit.

In January 2008, he replaced Jim Donald as CEO. Starbucks was struggling at the time. The move put the company back under a leader who had run it before.

That tenure lasted until 2017, about nine years in all. When Schultz stepped down that year, Kevin Johnson took over as CEO.

The two returns opened up in different ways. In 2008, Schultz took the seat from a sitting chief executive. In 2022, the vacancy followed Johnson's retirement. One comeback displaced a successor, while the other filled a seat a successor had left.

The titles differed as well. His 2008 return carried the full CEO title. In April 2022, he stepped in as interim CEO, a label that set the arrangement up as temporary. It meant a permanent successor still had to be named.

That interim stint ran until March 2023, a span of less than a year. Laxman Narasimhan then succeeded him as Starbucks CEO. This exit came much sooner after his return than the 2017 one had.

In total, Schultz held the Starbucks CEO role in three distinct periods. The first ended in 2000. The second ran from 2008 to 2017, and the third covered 2022 to 2023. Jim Donald, Kevin Johnson and Laxman Narasimhan each held the job directly before or after one of those stints.

Michael Dell $DELL returned as CEO of Dell, the computer company he founded, in January 2007. He took the job back after Kevin Rollins $ROL resigned.

Michael Dell led the company as its founder and chief executive until 2004. That year, Rollins became CEO.

The founder did not leave the business when he gave up the top executive title. He stayed on as chairman.

The 2004 change split the two most senior posts between two people. Rollins held the chief executive title. Michael Dell kept the chairman's seat.

That structure shaped how his return worked. He did not come back from another employer or after time away from the company. He was still chairman when Rollins resigned in January 2007.

His route back was a move within the company's own leadership. The founder who had handed over the chief executive's title in 2004 resumed it while still serving as chairman.

Twitter $TWTR co-founder Jack Dorsey returned as the company's interim CEO in July 2015 and became its permanent CEO that October. The appointment put him back in a job he had held once before, as Twitter's first chief executive.

Dorsey's first run in the role ended in October 2008. He was pushed out, and Evan Williams became CEO in his place.

Nearly seven years passed before Dorsey came back. The opening came when Dick Costolo left the CEO post in July 2015. Dorsey stepped in that month, but under an interim title rather than a permanent one.

His return filled a vacancy. Costolo had already left. Dorsey did not displace a sitting chief executive to get the job back.

The interim label marked the appointment as temporary. That changed in October 2015, when Twitter made Dorsey its permanent CEO. About three months separated the interim appointment from the permanent one.

Dorsey did not give up his other job to take the role. He was running Square $SQ at the same time. He led the two companies in parallel during his second tenure at Twitter.

That arrangement set his return apart from a move between employers. He kept Square and added Twitter to his responsibilities, rather than resigning from one company to join another.

His second tenure lasted until November 2021, when he stepped down. Parag Agrawal succeeded him as CEO. Measured from the permanent appointment, the second stint ran a little over six years.

That put the length of his second run close to the length of his time away. Each exit also ended with a different executive taking over: Williams in 2008 and Agrawal in 2021.

Dorsey's path at Twitter ran through four stages. He was the first CEO, then a co-founder pushed out of the job, then an interim chief and finally the permanent chief executive again.

Bob Iger returned as CEO of the Walt Disney $DIS Company on November 20, 2022. Disney's board brought him back to replace Bob Chapek, the executive who had succeeded Iger in the top job.

Iger first held the Disney CEO post from 2005 to 2020. Chapek took over as chief executive when Iger gave up that role.

Iger stayed at the company after handing over the CEO title. He became executive chairman and held that position through 2021.

The succession unfolded in two stages. The CEO title passed to Chapek first. Iger's executive chairman role ended later.

The board's November 2022 decision reversed that plan. It replaced the executive it had chosen to follow Iger. It then gave the job back to the leader Chapek had succeeded.

Iger did not found Disney. His return rested on his earlier tenure in the same office.

The gap between his roles was short. His executive chairman term ran through 2021. The board called him back to the CEO post the following year.

Disney's CEO succession began and ended with the same executive. Chapek's tenure sits between Iger's two terms as chief executive.

Google $GOOGL co-founder Larry Page became the company's CEO again in April 2011, taking over from Eric Schmidt. Google announced the change in January 2011, roughly three months before it took effect.

Page had run Google before. He was its first CEO, holding the role from 1998 until 2001. About a decade separated the end of his first stint from the start of his second.

Schmidt became Google's chief executive in 2001. He was not one of the company's founders. His appointment put an executive from outside the founding team in charge of the company Page had co-founded. Schmidt held the CEO title for the entire stretch between Page's two tenures.

The 2011 change kept Schmidt at Google. He moved into the role of executive chairman. Page took the CEO title back.

That path differs from cases where a board removes a sitting chief executive. Google announced the handoff in advance. The outgoing CEO stayed on in a senior role. The top job also passed between the same two people in both directions. It went from Page to Schmidt in 2001, then from Schmidt back to Page in 2011.

The early announcement meant Google's next CEO was public knowledge while Schmidt still held the title. For that stretch, the company operated with a named successor already in place. That successor was also the executive who had held the job first.

Page's second tenure included a change to the corporate structure. In 2015, he led the creation of Alphabet, which became Google's parent company. Page then served as Alphabet's CEO.

Alphabet did not exist during Page's first stint as CEO. The 2015 restructuring gave him the top job at a holding company that sat above Google itself. By 2015, Page held a broader title than the Google role he had handed to Schmidt in 2001.

Charles Schwab $SCHW returned as CEO of Charles Schwab Corporation in 2004, after the company's board removed David Pottruck from the role. Schwab founded the brokerage, which carries his name.

Pottruck held the CEO job when the board acted. His removal left the top post open, and the board filled it with the firm's founder.

That sequence sets this return apart. It came through a board decision to remove a sitting chief executive. It was not a planned handoff or a successor's voluntary exit.

The move also meant the board did not run an outside search for Pottruck's replacement. It turned instead to the person who had built the company.

Schwab's second stint as CEO lasted until 2008. That year, Walt Bettinger took over the role, and the founder handed the top job to a new chief executive for a second time.

Pat Gelsinger returned to Intel $INTC as chief executive in February 2021, replacing Bob Swan. He had not founded Intel. He was a career employee who came back to take a job he had never held.

Gelsinger joined Intel in 1979. He stayed for 30 years and rose through the company to become its chief technology officer.

That title put him among Intel's senior technical leaders. It did not make him chief executive. Other executives held the top seat throughout his first run at the company.

His first stint ended in 2009, when he left Intel to join EMC. In 2012, he became CEO of VMware.

The VMware job gave him something his Intel career had not. It was his first experience running a company as its chief executive. He gained it outside Intel, at a different business.

His route back did not depend on a founder's title or a chairman's seat. He held neither at Intel. The company instead turned to a former employee who had spent the intervening years at other firms.

Intel brought him back 12 years after he left. He returned with two kinds of experience. One was his long technical career inside Intel. The other was his time leading VMware.

Michael Bloomberg came back to run Bloomberg LP in January 2014, after his time as mayor of New York City ended. He had left the company 12 years earlier, in January 2002, to take that office.

Bloomberg founded the business in 1981. It did not start out under his name. Its original name was Innovative Market Systems.

His departure came 21 years after that founding. The cause was specific. He stepped away from the company to become mayor of New York City.

That sets his exit apart from the usual routes out of a corporate top job. He was not leaving after a board decision about the company's leadership. He was leaving for elected office.

He served more than one term as mayor. His return to the company followed once those terms were over.

The result is a timeline set by public office rather than by a corporate succession process. The date he left and the date he came back both tracked his time at City Hall. Other returning CEOs came back after a successor resigned or a board reversed course. Bloomberg's gap in leadership was the length of his mayoralty.

Mark Pincus, the founder of social-games company Zynga, returned as its CEO in April 2015. He had stepped aside from the role in 2013, when Don Mattrick became chief executive.

Pincus started Zynga in 2007. He was CEO until the 2013 handover to Mattrick.

That handover put an outside hire in charge. Mattrick came to Zynga from outside the company rather than rising through its ranks. Pincus no longer held the CEO title.

In April 2015, Pincus took the title back. The founder again led the business he had started.

His return followed a specific sequence. He stepped aside for an executive hired from outside, then resumed the role himself. Zynga's leadership went from founder to outside CEO and back to founder.

#5483. 10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare

Free daily briefing on global business news.

These 10 major tech outages of the 2020s, from Google to CrowdStrike to Cloudflare, show how a single fault could disrupt flights, payments and everyday apps

One routine change inside one company can stop planes from taking off, block card payments at checkout and silence messaging apps at once. That is a common thread running through the major tech outages of the 2020s. The failures in this list did not come from one dramatic attack on the internet. Several began with something ordinary: a quota setting, a configuration update, a maintenance job or a software release.

This selection covers 10 outages, ordered by date from December 2020 to November 2025. It is not a ranking. No single source measures these incidents against one another. Some hit consumer apps used for chat and video. Others reached airports, hospitals, banks and emergency phone lines.

The causes repeat. Google $GOOGL traced its December 2020 sign-in failure to an automated quota system. Meta $META said a configuration change on its backbone routers took Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp offline in October 2021. The company also said it was not a malicious attack. Cloudflare said its November 2025 disruption came from an internal change rather than an attack. In the U.S., the Federal Aviation Administration's preliminary finding on its January 2023 Notice to Air Missions failure pointed to a damaged database file. Amazon $AMZN Web Services' post-event summary on its October 2025 cloud outage cited a DNS problem in its Northern Virginia region.

Another pattern is concentration. Several of these incidents started at one provider and spread to the services built on top of it. A software bug at Fastly, a content delivery network, knocked out sites including Reddit $RDDT and Gov.uk in 2021. A faulty CrowdStrike $CRWD update in July 2024 crashed Windows machines at airlines, hospitals and banks. Microsoft $MSFT estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected. Telecom failures followed a similar shape on a national scale. Rogers in Canada and Optus in Australia each had network failures that disrupted emergency calling.

Each slide that follows explains what failed, when it happened and what is known about its cause. Where a company or agency published an incident report or public explanation, the slide names it and keeps to what that organization said.

Read together, the 10 cases span social and consumer apps, cloud platforms, content delivery networks, telecom carriers, security software and the U.S. flight-notice system.

On Dec. 14, 2020, Google $GOOGL's sign-in system failed for roughly 45 minutes, and Gmail, YouTube and Google Drive stopped working for users who were logged in. Google's incident report traced the failure to its automated quota system, which cut the capacity of its User ID Service.

The outage hit services that look separate to the people using them. Gmail handles email. YouTube streams video. Google Drive stores files. All three depend on Google confirming who the user is before anything else happens. When that check failed, the products built on top of it failed along with it.

That check is called authentication. It is the step in which a service confirms an account's identity before granting access to it. Google runs one shared account system across its consumer products. A single Google account opens Gmail, YouTube, Drive and the company's other services. The design spares people from managing a separate login for each product. It also means a fault in the sign-in layer reaches every product that relies on it.

The User ID Service is part of that sign-in layer. Once the automated quota system reduced its capacity, authentication requests arrived without enough resources to be processed. Requests that could not be verified went unanswered. The email, video and file services waiting on them stopped responding.

Quota systems are a standard tool in large computing operations. They divide capacity among internal services and cap how much any one of them can draw. That keeps a single service from consuming resources that others need. In this case, the automated system responsible for allocating resources was the component that took them away.

The episode shows that a safeguard can become a single point of failure. The quota system governed a service that every signed-in product needed, so its error did not stay in one place. Email, video and file storage failed together during the same short window. Products that look independent shared one hidden dependency, and that dependency decided whether any of them worked.

On June 8, 2021, a software bug in Fastly's content delivery network knocked major websites offline, including Reddit $RDDT, The New York Times and the U.K. government's Gov.uk. The bug was triggered when a Fastly customer changed a configuration setting.

A content delivery network, or CDN, is a distributed system of servers that stores copies of web content in many locations. When a reader requests a page, the CDN serves it from a server close to that reader instead of from the publisher's origin server. That setup makes pages load faster. It also absorbs traffic spikes that could overwhelm a single site.

The same setup creates a dependency. Publishers that route their traffic through a CDN rely on it to deliver their pages at all. When the CDN fails, readers can lose access to a site even though the site's own servers keep running.

That is the pattern this outage followed. The problem did not start inside Reddit, The New York Times or Gov.uk. It started at the shared provider that sat between those sites and their readers.

The change itself came from one customer, not from Fastly. CDN customers typically control the settings for their own content, such as which files are stored and for how long. In this case, one customer's adjustment exposed a flaw in Fastly's software. The effect reached sites far beyond that customer's own.

Fastly said 85% of its network was back to normal within 49 minutes. The company then issued a fix for the bug.

The affected sites serve very different audiences. Gov.uk is the U.K. government's central website for public services such as tax, benefits and passports. Reddit hosts user-run discussion communities. The New York Times publishes news and opinion. A government portal, a discussion platform and a news publisher all went offline because they depended on the same provider.

Facebook $META, Instagram and WhatsApp went offline together for about six hours on Oct. 4, 2021. Meta traced the outage to a configuration change on its backbone routers.

A backbone is the internal network that carries traffic between a company's data centers. Routers on that network direct data from one location to another. Meta said the faulty change cut its data centers off from one another.

The effect reached beyond the company's own facilities. Meta said the same change made its network unreachable from the wider internet. People who opened any of the three apps during the outage could not connect to the servers behind them.

The three services failed at once because they depended on the same company network. One change to that shared infrastructure took a social network, a photo-sharing app and a messaging service offline together.

Meta placed the cause inside its own operations. The company said the outage was not a malicious attack. In its account, the trigger was a change it made to its own routers rather than an intrusion from outside.

Rogers Communications lost wireless and internet service across Canada on July 8, 2022. The nationwide failure followed a maintenance update to the company's core network. It disrupted debit payments and some emergency calling.

Rogers is one of Canada's major telecommunications carriers. It sells mobile phone plans and home internet service. Businesses also depend on its network to move data. A failure at that scale reached well beyond people trying to place a call or load a web page.

A carrier's core network is the central part of its system. It directs traffic between cell towers, home connections and the wider internet. A problem at that level can take down wireless and wired service at the same time. That is what happened in July 2022, when both failed together across the country.

Debit payments were among the most visible effects. Card terminals at checkouts need a working network connection to approve a transaction. With that connection gone, debit purchases at affected businesses could not go through.

Some emergency calling was also disrupted. For some people in Canada, the outage cut off a route to emergency services as well as everyday phone and internet use.

Service did not return all at once. Rogers' wireless and internet services came back over the following day.

The Federal Aviation Administration's Notice to Air Missions system failed on Jan. 11, 2023, and the failure led to a nationwide ground stop on departing domestic flights in the U.S. The FAA's preliminary finding pointed to a damaged database file.

The outage did not take down a website or a messaging app. It held aircraft at airports across the country. The system that failed is one of the ways pilots learn about conditions that could affect a flight before departure.

A NOTAM alerts pilots and other flight personnel to conditions at an airport or along a route. Common examples include closed runways, temporary airspace restrictions and navigation aids that are out of service. Each notice is short and written with standard abbreviations. Flight crews and dispatchers review the relevant notices while planning a trip.

NOTAMs are not only an American tool. The International Civil Aviation Organization sets the standards that member countries use to issue them.

Preflight review is a legal duty in the U.S. Federal Aviation Regulations require the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning a flight before it begins. NOTAMs are one part of that information.

The FAA changed the name of these notices in December 2021. They had been known as Notices to Airmen. The agency adopted the gender-neutral Notice to Air Missions and kept the NOTAM abbreviation.

A ground stop holds aircraft at their departure airports instead of letting them take off. Flights already in the air are outside its scope. The FAA uses ground stops at individual airports for reasons such as weather or congestion.

The January 2023 order was different in scope. It applied to the whole country rather than a single airport. It was widely reported as the first nationwide halt of its kind since the September 2001 attacks.

Microsoft $MSFT 365 services, including Teams and Outlook, went down on Jan. 25, 2023, along with parts of the Azure cloud platform. Microsoft said a change to its wide-area network disrupted connectivity.

That explanation places the trigger in Microsoft's network rather than in any one app. A fault at the network level can affect every service whose traffic crosses that network. Workplace tools and cloud infrastructure went down on the same day.

A wide-area network, or WAN, links computers and data centers spread over long distances. A local network typically covers a single building or campus. For a cloud provider, the WAN connects its facilities to one another. It also connects them to the people and businesses using its services.

Microsoft 365 is the company's subscription bundle of productivity software and online services. Teams is its workplace chat and video meeting app. Outlook is its email and calendar service.

Azure is Microsoft's cloud computing platform. Businesses use it to run their own software and store data. A disruption to Azure can reach the customers of companies that build on it, not only the people who use Microsoft's own apps.

About 10 million Optus customers in Australia lost service on Nov. 8, 2023, in an outage that lasted roughly 12 hours. Optus attributed it to a software upgrade at one of its international peering networks.

That account places the starting point outside Optus' own network, on a network connected to it. A peering network is a separate network that links directly with a carrier's network so the two can exchange traffic. Carriers use these direct connections to pass data to and from other parts of the internet.

Optus said that after the upgrade, routing information exceeded preset safety limits on its core routers. Routing information is the data routers use to decide where traffic should go. A preset safety limit caps how much of that data a router will accept. Network operators set these limits in advance as a guard against overload.

Core routers sit at the center of a carrier's network. They carry traffic for the customer base as a whole rather than for a single neighborhood or cell tower. A problem at that layer can reach customers far from the point where it started.

Emergency calling was also affected. Failures in emergency calls were widely reported during the disruption. In Australia, emergency services are reached by dialing 000.

Those failures drew regulatory scrutiny of Optus.

On July 19, 2024, a defective content update to CrowdStrike $CRWD's Falcon sensor crashed computers running Microsoft $MSFT Windows. Microsoft estimated that 8.5 million Windows devices were affected.

Microsoft published that estimate in a blog post on its official site. It also put the number in context. The company said the affected machines made up less than 1% of all Windows machines. That share still included computers at airlines, hospitals and banks.

In the airline industry, the effects reached passengers directly. Delta Air Lines canceled flights.

CrowdStrike is a cybersecurity company, and Falcon is its endpoint security platform. An endpoint is an individual device, such as a laptop, desktop or server, that connects to a network. The Falcon sensor is the software installed on those devices. Organizations deploy tools like this to detect and block threats on each machine. Falcon also runs on macOS and Linux, but computers running those systems were not affected by this update.

Microsoft was not the source of the defect. The faulty update came from CrowdStrike, a separate company whose software runs on Windows. Security software typically receives frequent updates so it can respond to new threats. In July 2024, an update meant to help protect machines instead left them unable to run.

Unlike outages that leave a website or cloud service unreachable, this one stopped the computers themselves from running.

Amazon $AMZN Web Services suffered a major outage on Oct. 20, 2025, in its us-east-1 region in Northern Virginia. AWS's post-event summary traced the failure to a DNS problem affecting the endpoint for DynamoDB, its database service.

The disruption reached well beyond Amazon. Snapchat, Venmo and Fortnite were among the apps and services that reported problems. Each depends on infrastructure that AWS runs.

DNS, short for Domain Name System, works like the internet's address book. It translates a name that software asks for into the numerical address of the machine that answers. An endpoint is the address a program contacts to reach a cloud service. When DNS cannot return a working address for that endpoint, software that calls the service cannot find it. That can happen even if the servers behind it are still running.

DynamoDB is a managed database that AWS runs on behalf of its customers. Applications use it to store and retrieve data without operating their own database servers. A lost connection to it can stop an app from loading accounts, records or settings.

AWS's summary located the root of the problem in DynamoDB's own DNS management. It described a race condition. In software, a race condition occurs when two or more processes act on the same data at nearly the same time. The outcome then depends on which one finishes first. If the timing goes the wrong way, the system can end up in a state its designers did not intend.

A cloud region is a cluster of data centers in one geographic area. Many unrelated companies build their products on the same regional services. A fault in one widely used component can therefore surface at a messaging app, a payments app and a video game at the same time. AWS lets customers spread workloads across several regions. That design can limit exposure to a failure in any one of them.

A database permissions change inside Cloudflare caused the company's outage on Nov. 18, 2025. The change made a feature file used by its bot management system grow beyond its expected size. That oversized file crashed the software that routes traffic across Cloudflare's network. Sites including X $TWTR and OpenAI's ChatGPT were affected.

Cloudflare sits between many websites and the people trying to reach them. Customer sites route their incoming requests through its network, which provides services such as content delivery and protection against attacks. Visitor traffic passes through Cloudflare's systems before it reaches the site itself. A failure in that layer can make a working website unreachable.

Bot management is one of the Cloudflare products that operate inside that layer. It tries to separate automated traffic, such as scrapers and credential-stuffing bots, from requests made by people. The system depends on a feature file, a set of data the software consults when it evaluates incoming requests. On Nov. 18, that file became the point of failure.

The damage did not stay inside one Cloudflare product. The crash hit the component that moves requests through the network, not a single add-on feature. Websites that relied on Cloudflare to carry their traffic lost that path to their visitors. The fault sat inside Cloudflare's systems, not on those sites' own servers.

Cloudflare said the outage was not an attack. The company attributed it to an internal change of its own. The bot filtering at the center of the incident is itself one of the tools Cloudflare offers to screen out unwanted traffic.

Cloudflare later published a post-incident explanation. It traced the outage step by step, from the permissions change to the oversized file to the crash in the traffic-routing software. That sequence shows how a change to database permissions reached all the way to the system that carries visitor requests.

#5482. JPMorgan and Mastercard back Seattle startup Firmly’s bet on AI shopping agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 7, 2026 at 10:23 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:47 am

Firmly, a Seattle-area startup that helps online retailers sell through AI shopping assistants, raised a $15 million Series A round led by Squarepoint Capital, with participation from J.P. Morgan Payments, Mastercard, Samsung Next and others.

The company, founded in 2019, connects retailers’ existing online stores to AI assistants, marketplaces and other shopping channels, so people can buy products inside those third-party apps and services without going to retailers’ websites. Retailers keep their own payment providers and customer relationships.

“Every new AI assistant, marketplace or shopping platform is another place to sell. But connecting to each one can take serious engineering, because catalogs, inventory, payments, and checkout all have to work together,” wrote Kumar Senthil, Firmly’s co-founder and CEO, in a blog post announcing the round.

Mastercard is a commercial partner as well as an investor. Firmly handles the merchant side of Mastercard Agent Connect, a service launched in September to link merchants, AI agents and payment providers through a single integration.

Senthil told Axios Pro that Mastercard is recruiting merchants for the service, giving Firmly a route to new customers.

Firmly charges merchants $2,000 to $15,000 a month, depending on the total value of merchandise they sell, Senthil told Axios. He said connecting a merchant took four to six weeks in 2024 and now takes a day or less, including testing.

The company lists Best Buy, Furniture.com and Backcountry among its retail customers. RetailMeNot and an AI shopping app called Wizard also use its technology.

The funding comes as AI shopping agents move into the mainstream. Meta’s Muse assistant can browse retail sites and buy items with a user’s approval. Amazon has blocked Muse from its site and is suing Perplexity over a shopping agent in the startup’s Comet browser.

Firmly takes a different approach from those agents. Instead of having software click through a retailer’s web pages, it connects directly to the retailer’s systems with its permission.

The company this week also launched Ask Agent, an AI shopping assistant for retailers’ own websites. Shoppers describe what they want, get product recommendations and can check out without leaving the chat.

Other investors in the round include Alumni Ventures, ARK Invest, Benhamou Global Ventures, Granada Funds, Hike Ventures, The Mercantile Companies and Versus Ventures.

The round brings Firmly’s total funding to about $20 million. The company had raised $5.2 million when it partnered with Perplexity in March 2025 on shopping features inside the AI search app.

Senthil spent eight years at Microsoft and later led e-commerce products at Samsung. He co-founded Firmly with Damien Balsan, a co-founder of LoopPay, the mobile payments startup acquired by Samsung, and Murali Krishnamurthy, Firmly’s CTO and a former chief technical architect for Samsung’s U.S. and global e-commerce business. Firmly is based in Issaquah, Wash., and its engineering leaders work in Seattle. The company also has engineering teams in Sao Paulo, Brazil, and Chennai, India.

#5480. How GTA Online makes money: free updates, Shark Cards and 10 moments

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How GTA Online makes money comes down to Shark Cards, free updates and console and PC re-releases, traced here through 10 moments from 2013 to 2022

GTA Online gives away its new content and sells the currency players spend inside it. New missions, vehicles, properties and game modes arrive as free updates. Many of the biggest items in those updates carry steep prices. Players pay those prices in GTA$, an in-game currency they can either earn through play or buy with real money.

That arrangement explains how GTA Online makes money. It turned a multiplayer mode into a business built on content that players never pay for directly. Each new update gives players something else to spend on. Each purchase helps fund the next round of free updates.

The mode came from Rockstar Games, the studio that developed Grand Theft Auto V, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, its publisher and parent company. GTA V went on sale Sept. 17, 2013. Take-Two reported that the game passed $1 billion in sales within its first three days. That figure covers GTA V as a whole, not GTA Online on its own. The online mode opened on Oct. 1, two weeks later, inside a game that had already reached a large audience.

The start was rough. Connection failures and characters that would not save marked the first weeks. Rockstar gave affected players GTA$500,000 as an apology. From there the model took shape one piece at a time. Shark Cards, added in the weeks after launch, gave players a direct way to buy GTA$. Heists, businesses and a casino added new things to do and new things to buy. Releases on newer consoles and PC kept bringing fresh players into the same online world.

The 10 slides that follow are a selection of those moments and mechanisms, arranged in chronological order. They run from the October 2013 launch to the March 2022 release on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S. That release arrived alongside a new subscription called GTA+. These slides are not a ranking, and they are not the complete story. Each one covers a specific update, release or business decision in the mode's history.

GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013, two weeks after Grand Theft Auto V went on sale on Sept. 17. The online mode was not sold separately. It arrived as part of a game that players had already bought.

Rockstar Games developed both the story campaign and the online mode. Rockstar North, the studio's team in Edinburgh, Scotland, led the work. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published GTA V and is Rockstar's parent company.

GTA V first went on sale for PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. GTA Online opened on those same two consoles. On those consoles, a single session held up to 16 players.

The story campaign follows three playable leads: Michael, Franklin and Trevor. Their story plays out in Los Santos, a fictional city modeled on Los Angeles, and in the countryside of Blaine County. GTA Online uses the same map. Players build their own character instead of controlling the three story leads.

That shared setting tied the two halves of the package together. Players who spent the first two weeks in the campaign already knew the streets, the vehicles and the layout of the city. The multiplayer side did not have to introduce a new world.

Some faces carried over as well. Characters from the campaign, including Lamar Davis and Lester Crest, hand out jobs to online players. Those jobs sit alongside races, deathmatches and other modes that pit players against each other or put them on the same team.

Progress in the online mode runs on two tracks. Reputation points, known as RP, raise a character's rank and unlock weapons, clothing and activities. GTA$, the in-game currency, pays for cars, apartments and gear. Completing jobs earns both.

The release order also shaped how the mode found its audience. GTA Online did not need to attract buyers on its own. Its potential player base was everyone who already owned GTA V on PlayStation 3 or Xbox 360.

GTA Online launched in October 2013 with serious connection failures and lost character saves. Rockstar Games answered by giving affected players GTA$500,000 in in-game currency as an apology.

The trouble began on day one. GTA Online went live on Oct. 1, 2013, on PlayStation 3 and Xbox 360. Those were the same consoles Grand Theft Auto V had reached two weeks earlier. Players opened the online mode from inside GTA V and did not buy it separately. Many could not connect at all. Others got in, only to find the game had failed to save the characters they had built.

Lost saves struck at the core of the mode. GTA Online characters are created by players and are separate from Michael, Franklin and Trevor, the three protagonists of the GTA V story mode. Each one is a persistent character who earns money, buys property and climbs in rank over time. A failed save erased that progress. A player who lost a character in the first week had to start again from the beginning.

Rockstar released patches over the following weeks to address the connection and save problems. The compensation was part of that recovery. Instead of cash refunds, the studio paid players in GTA$, the fictional currency used throughout GTA Online. GTA$ exists only inside the game and cannot be exchanged back into real money.

The payment fit the way the mode works. Players spend GTA$ on cars, weapons, apartments and other items in Los Santos, the game's fictional version of Los Angeles. Apartments also serve as a base, with garage space for the cars a player collects. A payment of GTA$500,000 gave affected players a head start on those purchases.

The broken start did not end GTA Online. The mode recovered from its October 2013 failures and kept its players. Rockstar went on to support it with new content for years.

Shark Cards let GTA Online players spend real money to receive GTA$, the in-game currency. That currency buys the cars, weapons, apartments and clothing sold inside the game. The cards form the direct link between GTA Online's virtual economy and real-world revenue.

Rockstar Games added Shark Cards in the weeks after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. The online mode came included with Grand Theft Auto V at no extra charge. The cards gave Rockstar a way to earn money from players after the initial game sale.

The cards are sold in tiers named after sharks, including Red Shark, Great White Shark and Megalodon. Larger tiers deliver more GTA$ for a higher price. Megalodon takes its name from an extinct prehistoric shark and sits at the top of the range.

The purchase itself is simple. A player picks a card, pays in real currency and sees the GTA$ added to their in-game balance. Cards can be bought through a platform's digital storefront or through the store menu inside the game.

The GTA$ is then spent at in-game shops and on the game's fictional websites. Legendary Motorsport, the in-game site for high-end cars, is one example. Property and vehicle purchases go through these same menus whether the money was earned or bought.

Shark Cards do not unlock a separate catalog. GTA$ bought with a card is the same currency players earn by completing jobs, missions and races. A player who never spends real money can reach the same items by playing longer.

That earn-or-buy choice defines how the cards work. Players with limited time can skip hours of repeated jobs. Players with more time can earn the same currency without paying.

Take-Two Interactive $TTWO, Rockstar's publisher and parent company, reports this kind of ongoing in-game spending under a category it calls recurrent consumer spending. The cards turned GTA Online into a product that could keep earning money long after a player bought the base game.

The Heists update arrived in GTA Online on March 10, 2015, about a year and a half after the mode opened. It added cooperative, multi-stage robberies that a crew plans and carries out together. Each stage feeds into a final job.

Heists were not new to the Grand Theft Auto series. The single-player campaign of Grand Theft Auto V is built around them, with its three protagonists planning and pulling off large scores. Online players waited until 2015 for a version of that structure designed for groups.

The update shipped with five heists: The Fleeca Job, The Prison Break, The Humane Labs Raid, Series A Funding and The Pacific Standard Job. Each one follows the same basic pattern. A crew completes a set of setup missions, then attempts a finale that carries the main payout. Setup missions range from stealing vehicles to collecting equipment the finale depends on.

Most of the heists call for four players. The Fleeca Job, the first in the sequence, needs only two. Lester Crest, a character from the story mode, offers the jobs.

Planning happens on a board inside a high-end apartment. A player has to own one of these properties to host a heist. Apartments are bought with GTA$. The host also pays the setup costs before any missions begin.

That host acts as heist leader. The leader assigns players to roles and decides what share of the final payout each crew member receives. Roles change from one job to the next. One player might fly or drive while another hacks a security system or provides cover.

The update came out on PlayStation 3, Xbox 360, PlayStation 4 and Xbox One at the same time. It gave every console version of the online mode the same new long-form content on the same day. Grand Theft Auto V had not yet reached PC at that point.

Rockstar Games releases new GTA Online content as free updates instead of selling it as paid expansions. Revenue comes afterward, when players spend GTA$ on the vehicles, weapons, properties and other items those updates introduce.

That arrangement differs from a paid add-on. A player downloads an update at no cost and gets access to its new missions and activities. Many of the items inside it carry an in-game price tag, though. To own them, the player needs enough GTA$ in the bank.

There are two ways to get that money. Players can earn GTA$ by completing missions, races and other jobs inside the game. They can also buy it with real money through Shark Cards, the currency packs Rockstar sells for GTA Online. Both routes lead to the same GTA$ balance.

This structure links each content release to Shark Card sales. A new car or property gives players a specific GTA$ target. A player short of that total can keep earning through jobs or buy the difference with real money. The update costs nothing, but what it unlocks can lead to a real-money purchase.

Free updates also keep the online player base together. Paid expansions divide players into those who bought the add-on and those who did not. When every player receives the same content, new missions and items reach the whole audience at once. A new vehicle or activity is open to everyone who plays GTA Online, not only to buyers of a specific pack.

Rockstar used the paid model with its previous game. Grand Theft Auto IV received two paid episodic expansions in 2009, The Lost and Damned and The Ballad of Gay Tony. GTA Online took a different path, offering its additions as downloads with no separate charge.

The approach has carried through the mode's major releases. Large cooperative missions, property and business updates and later content drops all arrived without a purchase price of their own. Each one added new items with GTA$ prices attached.

Three GTA Online updates pushed players toward buying property and running criminal businesses inside the game. They were Executives and Other Criminals in 2015, Gunrunning in 2017 and After Hours in 2018.

Each update added expensive properties and businesses. Players paid for them with GTA$, the currency used throughout the mode. The updates themselves came free. The price sat inside the game rather than at the point of release.

Before these releases, a GTA Online player mostly took on jobs and finished them. The business updates added ownership to the mode. A player now had property to buy and an operation to run.

Executives and Other Criminals came first. As its name signals, the update cast the player as the head of a criminal enterprise. The player was no longer only a lone operator picking up work.

Gunrunning followed in 2017. Its theme was arms dealing. It carried the ownership idea into a second line of illegal work.

After Hours arrived in 2018 and became known as the nightclub update. Its new content revolved around a nightclub that players could own. That made it the third business type in the series, after the criminal enterprise and the arms trade.

Price links the three releases. Each one put a large GTA$ cost on the property or business at its center. Those costs gave players a concrete target for the currency. A player saving for a business had a specific item in mind, not just a growing balance.

The updates also built on one another. Each arrived as a new business type rather than a replacement for the last one. A player who bought into an earlier business did not lose it when the next update arrived. Each release instead added another option to spend GTA$ on.

From 2015 to 2018, owning an in-game business became a recurring theme of new GTA Online content rather than the subject of one release.

Grand Theft Auto V and GTA Online were re-released for PlayStation 4 and Xbox One in November 2014, then for PC on April 14, 2015. Each new version brought another group of players into the same online mode.

The console re-release came about 14 months after the original game went on sale. The PC version followed roughly 19 months after that first launch.

None of these releases created a separate online game. Players on the new platforms entered the same GTA Online that had opened in October 2013. They joined its missions, its in-game economy and its GTA$ currency.

That meant newcomers did not arrive at a blank start. By November 2014, the mode had been running for more than a year. Its missions, prices and GTA$ economy were already in place when the new versions went on sale.

That structure ties each re-release to the mode's revenue model. GTA Online earns money when players use real money to buy GTA$ through Shark Cards. Those cards were already on sale when the new versions arrived. A new platform adds more people who can make those purchases. Rockstar Games did not have to build a new multiplayer game to reach them.

The PC release also followed a major content drop. The Heists update came out on March 10, 2015. The PC version arrived about five weeks later. PC players joined with the cooperative heist missions already live. They could plan and carry out those multi-stage missions with other players from their first weeks. The newest content and the newest platform reached players within weeks of each other.

Rockstar Games developed each version, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO published them. The same online mode carried on across every format. Players on every system bought the same GTA$ and spent it on the same kinds of in-game items. Each release widened its audience without changing how it made money.

The Diamond Casino & Resort update arrived in GTA Online in July 2019. It added an in-game casino that served two roles: a social space where players could gather, and a new source of content inside the mode.

Rockstar Games, which develops GTA Online, released the update nearly six years after the multiplayer mode opened on Oct. 1, 2013. Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes the game and is Rockstar's parent company.

Many earlier updates centered on missions, properties and businesses. The casino offered a different kind of content. It was not another job to finish or another business to manage. It was a destination inside the game world where players could meet and spend time together.

The update also sits at a specific point in the mode's timeline. It came the year after After Hours, the 2018 nightclub update. It arrived before the Cayo Perico Heist, which followed in December 2020.

Like other GTA Online content, the casino reached players as a free update to the existing mode. It was not sold as a separately priced expansion.

The Cayo Perico Heist launched in GTA Online on Dec. 15, 2020. It was set on a private island, and players could complete it alone or with a group.

That solo option broke from how GTA Online heists had worked before. The Heists update of 2015 was built around a crew. Its missions were cooperative jobs that players planned and carried out together. Cayo Perico made those other players optional rather than required.

The change removed a practical hurdle for players without a regular crew. A heist no longer depended on finding teammates, matching schedules or waiting for others to join. Players who preferred company could still bring a group along.

The design widened the audience for a major piece of content. A crew-only heist served players who already had organized groups. A heist one person could finish was open to anyone who logged in to the mode.

The private island also gave GTA Online a new setting for a heist. Earlier updates had expanded the mode with businesses, properties and a casino. Cayo Perico added a destination of its own.

The release date shows how long the mode had stayed active. The heist arrived more than seven years after GTA Online opened on Oct. 1, 2013. It came about five years and nine months after the original Heists update of March 10, 2015. It followed the Diamond Casino & Resort update of July 2019 by about 17 months.

Those gaps point to a mode that kept growing rather than being replaced. Rockstar Games added a new heist to the same online world that had opened in 2013, instead of moving players to a new game.

Cayo Perico reached players the same way as other GTA Online content. Rockstar Games delivered it as a free update. Players did not buy the heist as a separate expansion. Like other GTA Online activities, the heist paid out in GTA$, giving solo players a way to earn the currency through play.

GTA V and GTA Online arrived on PlayStation 5 and Xbox Series X $TWTR|S on March 15, 2022. Rockstar Games paired the release with two changes to how players could get into the online mode and pay for it. The first was a standalone GTA Online download on PlayStation 5. The second was a subscription called GTA+.

The release moved GTA Online onto a newer generation of home consoles than the PS4 and Xbox One versions of November 2014. The mode had opened on Oct. 1, 2013, so the new versions came about eight and a half years into its life. Rockstar Games developed the game, and Take-Two Interactive $TTWO publishes it.

The standalone version split the multiplayer mode off from the GTA V story campaign. On PS5, a player could download GTA Online by itself instead of buying the full game. For the first three months after release, that download was free.

The free entry point fit a game that earns its money from spending after the download. Every new player joins the same online world, where GTA$ pays for vehicles, properties and businesses. Players can earn that currency through play or buy it with real money through Shark Cards. Under that model, the revenue comes from what players buy once they arrive, not from the download itself.

Rockstar launched GTA+ the same month. It is a paid subscription service for GTA Online that bills players on a recurring basis. It added another way to pay, alongside buying the game and buying Shark Cards.

Both changes kept the core of the model intact. New content stays free to play, and spending happens inside the game. The standalone download widened the way in, and GTA+ added a recurring way to pay once there.

#5479. Trevor Noah on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 8, 2026 at 9:52 amNovember 8, 2026 at 9:52 am

On Oct. 19, Trevor Noah launched Luminaries, a science conversation series at Boston’s Museum of Science. I joined him onstage, and Rana el Kaliouby moderated. Rana is a pioneer of emotion AI, software that reads human emotion, and the host of the Pioneers of AI podcast. She wrote afterward that she expected Trevor to be witty and funny, but “didn’t expect to be so blown away by his humanity and depth of ideas.”

Here are a few of his insights with his own words highlighted.

When an AI matchmaker Rana built in ChatGPT picked Trevor as her match, he pointed out that it knew very little about either of them. It assembled a plausible answer from what’s on the internet.

Trevor added that when you tell AI it made a mistake, it thanks you but often fails to correct the error: “It’s like a friend who’s been to a lot of therapy but doesn’t actually change.”

When asked how we protect ourselves from AI’s downsides, Trevor said the answer “goes back to something that is very un-technological and very un-AI.” He cited Robert Putnam’s book Bowling Alone, noting that places where communities form accrue many surprising benefits including more accountable governments.

I pushed back that communitarianism, the 1990s movement my father helped found to foster communities, had failed. Trevor responded that we hand too many ideas to intellectuals, who then “apply too much academia” to them. Communitarianism failed, he deadpanned, “because it’s called communitarianism.” An overly academic name.

He noted that nobody calls a phone a failure when the first version doesn’t sell; companies keep re-releasing it. He vowed never to stop investing in community.

Despite his concerns, Trevor has “yet to see a technology that blew up and then left everyone behind.” Cars, computers and the internet all spread to ordinary people.

AI has reached what he calls “work intelligence”: it can do the jobs we invented, but we keep inventing new ones. Salt and ice used to be precious. Now restaurants hand them out for free. What we value changes, and in Trevor’s view, we’re expendable only if we define being human by the tasks we value today.

Our conversation turned to AI’s impact on jobs.

Touring as a comic, Trevor saw towns hollowed out after Kodak and the automaker Studebaker left. Factory workers were told automation was progress. “White-collar workers are now experiencing what many blue-collar workers experienced for decades,” he said. The difference, he argued, is that white-collar workers are closer to power, so newspapers are covering it.

Trevor is confident new jobs will come, as they did after telephone exchange operators disappeared. What worries him is the gap. His analogy is the highway, where the following distance is the space that lets you stop before you hit the car ahead:

Trevor tells tech leaders that “it’s easier to be patient when you are in a position of privilege,” and added, “But ironically, they don’t have patience when it comes to quarterly earnings.”

After ChatGPT took off, show hosts kept telling him weak jokes that ChatGPT had written in a pale imitation of Trevor’s style. He rattled off four reasons AI struggles with humor: there isn’t enough comedy data, the model is a frozen snapshot while what society finds acceptable keeps shifting, comedy depends on knowing your audience (there are jokes you know are funny but you wouldn’t tell your mom), and companies have made models risk averse.

In addition to being the former host of The Daily Show, an award-winning author and a sought-after comedian, Trevor Noah is Microsoft’s Chief Questions Officer.

I reminded him of Picasso’s famous verdict on computers, “They are useless. They can only give you answers,” and joked that as Chief Questions Officer he has something rare these days: job security. He chuckled. Of course, his real job security comes from his depth and humanity, which feed his exceptional humor and wit.

Rana noted that everybody’s getting replaced by AI, but Trevor had played an AI, voicing Griot in Black Panther: Wakanda Forever.

He quipped: “Yeah, I’m coming for AI’s job.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
