#5478. Jensen Huang's failed bid and Rene Haas's IPO: 10 things to know about Arm

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How Arm chip licensing works, explained in 10 parts covering architecture licenses, core designs, royalties, Jensen Huang's failed Nvidia bid and Rene Haas's leadership

Arm Holdings does not manufacture a single chip, yet its technology runs inside processors designed by Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung. The company, based in Cambridge, U.K., sells something less tangible than silicon. It licenses the rules a processor follows and, in many cases, ready-made blueprints for the processor cores themselves. Partner companies turn those designs into finished chips. Contract manufacturers such as TSMC $TSM then fabricate them.

That division of labor lets a company with no factories of its own shape the design of chips that other companies build and sell. Arm leaves the expensive work of building and running fabrication plants to others.

Understanding how Arm chip licensing works starts with two kinds of payment. A company that wants to use Arm technology generally pays an upfront license fee. It then pays a royalty on each chip it ships. Arm earns money when a partner signs on and again when that partner's products reach customers.

The rights a company buys vary. Some companies license ready-made core designs and build their chips around them. Others, such as Apple, hold an architecture license that lets them design their own cores to Arm's instruction set. The choice affects how much control a company has over its chip's design. It also sat at the center of a legal dispute between Arm and Qualcomm.

The business has changed hands and leaders in recent years. In September 2020, Nvidia agreed to buy Arm from SoftBank for $40 billion. Jensen Huang, Nvidia's co-founder and CEO, led the company at the time. The U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the purchase in December 2021. U.K. and EU regulators had also raised concerns. Nvidia abandoned the deal in February 2022. That same month, Rene Haas became Arm's CEO, succeeding Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ in September 2023, and SoftBank kept a majority stake.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of the pieces that make up the Arm licensing model. They explain what an instruction set architecture is, how the company began and which license types chipmakers choose. They also look at how RISC-V and x86 compete with Arm. Each slide covers one part of what Arm does and can be read on its own.

Arm does not manufacture semiconductors. The company, based in Cambridge, U.K., creates processor designs and sets the rules those processors follow. It then sells other companies the right to use that work.

Arm owns no chip factories. What it produces is intellectual property — detailed specifications and circuit designs that exist as digital files rather than as physical silicon. A customer receives those files, not a box of finished parts.

Other companies design the chips that carry Arm technology. Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Nvidia $NVDA and Samsung are among the companies that build chips on Arm's foundation. Each one takes Arm's work as a starting point and turns it into a product of its own.

A finished processor for a phone or laptop usually contains far more than Arm's contribution. Chip designers combine Arm-based processor cores with their own graphics units, memory controllers and other circuits on a single piece of silicon. The industry calls that combined design a system-on-chip. The Arm portion handles general computing tasks. The rest of the chip reflects each company's own engineering.

Manufacturing is a separate step, handled by yet another company. When a chip designer finishes its layout, it sends the design to a foundry for fabrication. TSMC $TSM, short for Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co., is a contract foundry that fabricates chips for other companies. Its customers include many of the same companies that license Arm technology.

Companies that design chips but outsource production are described as fabless. Qualcomm and Nvidia work this way. Arm sits one layer further back in the chain. It supplies the designs that those chip companies start from.

The three-way split lets each company specialize. Arm concentrates on processor design. Chip companies concentrate on complete products. Foundries concentrate on production technology. A single Arm design can appear in chips from many different companies at the same time.

Arm's revenue comes from that same chain. The company collects money from the businesses that use its technology, not from selling hardware. Its income therefore depends on what its partners design, build and ship.

Arm started in 1990 as Advanced RISC Machines Ltd, a joint venture formed by Acorn Computers, Apple $AAPL and VLSI Technology. The company grew out of processor work at Acorn, a British computer maker. Its name was later shortened to Arm.

Acorn was based in Cambridge, U.K. It was best known for the BBC Micro, a home computer used widely in British schools during the 1980s. For its next generation of machines, Acorn designed its own processor instead of buying one from another supplier. Sophie Wilson and Steve Furber led that design work. The first chip, the ARM1, ran its first code in 1985.

At that stage, the letters ARM stood for Acorn RISC Machine. Acorn used the chip family in its Archimedes computers, launched in 1987. Its simple design also meant the chip drew relatively little power. That trait later suited battery-powered devices.

The 1990 spinout changed who the processor was for. The design moved out of Acorn and into a separate company that could supply it to others. Each of the three founders brought something different. Acorn contributed the processor design and the engineers behind it. Apple was a prospective customer for the chips. VLSI Technology, a U.S. chip company, brought manufacturing capability.

Apple's interest centered on the Newton, its handheld personal digital assistant. The Newton MessagePad, released in 1993, ran on an ARM processor. The device never sold in large numbers. It still gave the young company an early commercial product in the market.

Robin Saxby became the company's first chief executive. Under his leadership, the company licensed its designs to other firms instead of building and selling chips itself. In 1998, it listed its shares in London and on Nasdaq $NDAQ.

That period as a listed company ended in 2016. SoftBank, the Japanese technology investor, acquired Arm that year for about £24 billion, or roughly $32 billion. The deal took Arm private.

The Arm instruction set architecture is the list of basic commands an Arm processor understands and carries out. It acts as the shared language between software and hardware. Any program meant to run on an Arm chip must first be translated into those commands.

An instruction set architecture is usually shortened to ISA. It defines operations such as adding two numbers, loading data from memory or jumping to another part of a program. It also sets out the registers a processor exposes and how memory is addressed.

The ISA is a specification, not a physical circuit. Two chips can look very different inside and still run the same software, as long as both follow the same ISA.

This separation explains why compilers matter. A compiler converts code written in a language such as C or Rust into machine instructions for one specific ISA. A program compiled for Arm will not run natively on an x86 processor from Intel $INTC or AMD $AMD. The reverse is also true. Developers either recompile their code for each architecture or rely on translation software.

The Arm architecture follows RISC, short for reduced instruction set computing. The RISC approach favors a small set of simple instructions that each do one job. Arm is also a load/store design. Arithmetic happens on values held in registers, and separate instructions move data to and from memory.

The x86 family follows the complex instruction set computing, or CISC, approach. Some of its instructions combine a memory access and a calculation in a single step. Its instructions also vary in length.

Arm's 64-bit era began with Armv8, which introduced the AArch64 execution state. AArch64 instructions are a fixed 32 bits long. A fixed size makes them simpler for a processor to decode. AArch64 also provides 31 general-purpose registers. Armv8 kept a separate 32-bit state, called AArch32, so older software could still run on many chips.

Armv9 was announced in 2021 as the next major version of the architecture. It includes Scalable Vector Extension 2, known as SVE2. This feature lets a single instruction work on many pieces of data at once. That style of processing is used in machine learning, image handling and signal processing.

Each new version builds on the previous one rather than replacing it. Software written for earlier 64-bit Arm chips generally continues to run on newer ones.

Arm earns money in two stages. A company pays an upfront license fee to gain access to Arm's designs, and then it pays a royalty on each chip it ships that uses that technology.

The license fee comes first. A chip company pays it when it signs an agreement, long before any product reaches a customer. The fee buys the right to use Arm's intellectual property. That property can be the instruction set itself or a finished processor core design. With it, the licensee can start building a chip around Arm technology.

The royalty comes later. It applies to each unit the licensee sells once its chip is in production. A processor in a smartphone, a microcontroller in a household appliance and a server chip in a data center can each generate a royalty for Arm.

That timing creates a gap between a deal and the money it produces. Designing a chip, verifying it and moving it into manufacturing at a foundry takes time. An agreement signed today may not produce royalty income until the resulting chip ships. That can be years later.

The gap runs the other way at the end of a product's life. A chip design can stay in production for years after launch. Every unit shipped during that time adds to the royalty stream. An older license can keep paying Arm long after the original fee was collected.

The two streams track different things. License fees reflect how many companies are starting new projects with Arm. Royalties reflect how many chips those companies actually sell. A licensee that ships chips in large volumes generates more royalty income than one that ships few.

This structure ties Arm's income to its partners' sales. When companies such as Apple $AAPL, Qualcomm $QCOM, Samsung and Nvidia $NVDA ship more Arm-based processors, Arm collects more in royalties. When demand for those products slows, royalty income slows too.

The specific fees and royalty terms are set in contracts negotiated between Arm and each licensee. The basic two-part model applies whether a company licenses a ready-made core or designs its own cores to Arm's instruction set.

An Arm architecture license gives a company the right to design its own processor cores from scratch, as long as those cores run Arm's instruction set. Apple $AAPL and Qualcomm $QCOM are two of the best-known companies that use this route to build custom CPU designs.

Fewer companies take this path than license Arm's ready-made cores. Many Arm customers do not design cores at all. They license finished core designs from Arm and place them inside their chips. An architecture licensee takes on that engineering work itself. It decides how the core is organized internally, how it processes instructions and how it balances speed against power use.

Compatibility is the part that does not change. A custom core built under this license must execute the same Arm instructions as any other Arm processor. Software compiled for Arm can therefore run on it. The licensee gains control over the hardware design without giving up access to the wider pool of Arm software.

Apple is one example. Its M1 chip, announced in November 2020, used Apple-designed cores built to Arm's instruction set. The M1 began Apple's shift away from Intel $INTC processors in its Mac computers. The custom approach lets Apple shape its chips around its own devices and operating systems.

Qualcomm is another. Its newer custom CPU designs trace back to Nuvia, a chip startup that Qualcomm acquired. Nuvia held its own architecture license with Arm before that deal.

Those designs became the subject of a court fight. Arm sued Qualcomm in 2022 in a dispute over which license terms applied to the Nuvia-based designs after the acquisition. A jury in Delaware returned a verdict in December 2024 that went mainly in Qualcomm's favor.

The case put the terms of an architecture license in public view. It showed that the specific wording of such a license, including which company holds it, can decide who may use a design after a change in ownership.

The custom route also carries practical trade-offs. Designing a competitive CPU core requires large engineering teams and years of development. The companies that take this path are generally those that want processors tuned closely to their own products rather than a design shared with competitors.

A core license gives a chip company a finished processor design from Arm that it can place directly into its own chip. Arm sells these ready-made cores in families aimed at different markets. They include Cortex-A for phones, Cortex-M for microcontrollers and Neoverse for servers and data centers.

The licensee does not have to design a processor core from scratch. It takes Arm's completed core and builds a larger chip around it. That chip can also include graphics processors, memory controllers, wireless modems and other circuits the company designs or sources elsewhere.

Cortex-A is the family built for application processors. These are the chips that run full operating systems, such as Android on a smartphone or tablet. Phone chips often combine several Cortex-A cores of different sizes on one piece of silicon. Larger cores take on demanding work. Smaller cores handle lighter tasks and use less power.

Cortex-M targets microcontrollers. These are small, low-power chips that control a single device or a narrow set of tasks. They show up in appliances, sensors, wearables and industrial equipment. They typically run simple firmware or a small real-time operating system. That is far lighter than the software found on a phone or laptop.

Arm also sells Cortex-R cores for real-time systems. These are used where a chip must respond within strict time limits, such as in automotive systems and storage controllers.

Neoverse is Arm's line for servers, cloud computing and networking infrastructure. It is meant for chips that sit in data centers rather than in consumer devices. Amazon $AMZN's Graviton processors, which power servers in Amazon Web Services, are one example. Amazon designs the Graviton chips itself but builds them around Neoverse designs.

A ready-made core removes a large engineering task from a licensee's project. Creating an original processor core requires a specialized engineering team and extensive testing. Licensing a finished core lets a company focus its effort on the surrounding circuits instead.

The trade-off is control over the core. A company using a standard Arm core gets the same core design that its competitors can license. It can still set its product apart through the other components on its chip, its software and its manufacturing choices. Companies that want to change the internal design of the core itself take a different route, through an architecture license.

Arm Flexible Access, launched in 2019, lets a company try out a wide range of Arm designs before signing a full license for any of them. Compute Subsystems take a different approach to a related problem: they bundle several Arm designs into one pre-integrated package that a chip team can build around.

Both programs aim to lower the cost and effort of building an Arm-based chip. Under the traditional model, a company negotiates a license for a specific design and pays for it before engineering work goes far. For a large chipmaker, that is routine. For a startup, a university lab or a small device maker, it can mean committing money before knowing which design fits.

Flexible Access changes the order of those steps. A participant gets access to a portfolio of Arm intellectual property, along with tools and design support. Engineers can evaluate cores, run simulations and build prototypes using several options side by side. The company pays a license fee only for the designs it decides to take into production. Royalties still apply once finished chips ship.

The program is built for companies that have not yet settled on a processor. A maker of connected sensors, for example, might compare several microcontroller-class cores before choosing one. Under a conventional arrangement, each of those comparisons could require its own license negotiation.

Compute Subsystems address a later stage of the design process. A modern processor is more than its CPU cores. The cores have to connect to each other, to memory and to other parts of the chip. Integrating and verifying those pieces takes significant engineering time.

A Compute Subsystem packages Arm cores with surrounding components that Arm has already integrated and tested together. A licensee starts from that working foundation instead of assembling the pieces itself. The aim is to cut the integration and verification work a chip team would otherwise do on its own.

The trade-off is control. A company that builds on a pre-integrated bundle accepts more of Arm's design choices. A company that assembles individual cores, or designs its own under an architecture license, keeps more room to differentiate its chip.

Nvidia $NVDA's $40 billion agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank, announced in September 2020, was abandoned in February 2022 after regulators in the U.S., U.K. and EU objected. Their central worry was that one chipmaker would own the designs its rivals license.

Jensen Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led it as CEO since then. The company built its business on graphics processors. Those chips later became widely used hardware for training AI models. Buying Arm would have added a widely licensed CPU architecture to a company already known for GPUs.

SoftBank had owned Arm since 2016. SoftBank does not design or sell chips. Under the proposed deal, Arm would have moved to an owner that designs and sells chips in large volumes. That change sat at the center of the regulatory fight.

Arm's model depends on licensing the same technology to many companies, including firms that compete with one another. Several of those licensees also compete with Nvidia. The deal raised the question of whether Arm could stay neutral under an owner with its own chip products to sell.

In December 2021, the U.S. Federal Trade Commission sued to block the acquisition. The agency's complaint argued that the merger would give Nvidia control over computing technology and designs that its rivals rely on. The lawsuit meant the deal faced a court process in the U.S. on top of reviews in other jurisdictions.

Regulators in the U.K. and the EU had also raised concerns. Arm's headquarters in Cambridge, U.K., placed the deal under British review. With objections on several fronts, the companies walked away from the agreement. That came about 17 months after the deal was announced.

The collapse did not end Nvidia's use of Arm technology. Nvidia remains an Arm licensee. Its Grace CPU, designed for data centers, is built on Arm designs. Nvidia kept access to the architecture through the same licensing route that other chip designers use, rather than through ownership of Arm itself.

Rene Haas has run Arm as chief executive since February 2022, when he succeeded Simon Segars. Under Haas, Arm listed on Nasdaq $NDAQ on September 14, 2023, under the ticker ARM, with shares priced at $51.

Haas was promoted from inside the company. Before becoming CEO, he led Arm's IP products group. IP stands for intellectual property. At Arm, that term covers the processor designs and instruction set rights the company licenses to chipmakers. The group Haas ran was responsible for the products Arm sells to its customers.

Earlier in his career, Haas worked at Nvidia $NVDA. Jensen Huang co-founded that company and serves as its CEO. Nvidia is one of the chip designers that license Arm technology.

Haas took charge in the same month that Nvidia abandoned its agreement to buy Arm from SoftBank. With that sale off the table, SoftBank, which had acquired Arm in 2016, remained the owner. The Nasdaq listing followed in September 2023.

That listing was an initial public offering. In an IPO, a privately held company sells shares to outside investors. Those shares then trade on a stock exchange. The $51 figure was the offering price, set before trading began. Once trading opened, the share price was set by buyers and sellers on the market.

SoftBank kept a majority stake after the offering. Holding more than half the shares means SoftBank owns more of Arm than all other shareholders combined. Public investors gained a piece of the company, but control stayed with SoftBank.

The ticker ARM is the short code investors use to buy and sell the stock on Nasdaq. Nasdaq is a U.S. exchange based in New York. Arm's shares trade there even though the company's headquarters are in Cambridge, U.K.

The listing changed who owns Arm. It did not change the licensing business at the center of the company. A public listing does add a daily share price. That price gives investors a running measure of how they value the business Haas oversees.

Arm faces competition from two architectures that sit at opposite ends of the licensing spectrum. RISC-V is an open instruction set that companies can use without paying license fees. x86, at the other end, is a closed architecture made by Intel $INTC and AMD $AMD.

RISC-V began as a project at the University of California, Berkeley. Like Arm, it follows the reduced instruction set computing approach, which relies on a small set of simple instructions. The difference lies in ownership. The RISC-V specification is published openly. Any company can design a processor that implements it without signing a license with an architecture owner.

That openness offers a direct alternative to the Arm licensing model. Arm charges companies for the right to use its instruction set and designs. A chipmaker that builds on RISC-V does not pay an architecture owner for the instruction set itself.

Free access to the specification does not mean free chips. A company choosing RISC-V still has to design its own processor cores or obtain finished designs from another supplier. It also has to make sure compilers, operating systems and applications run properly on the result. That engineering work carries real cost. It is also part of what Arm sells when it offers ready-made designs.

x86 presents a different kind of competition. Intel created the architecture, and Intel and AMD are its principal makers. The two companies design and sell their own x86 processors. They do not license designs to a wide pool of customers the way Arm does. Decades of desktop, laptop and server software were written for x86. That installed base keeps the architecture entrenched in PCs and in many data centers.

Arm's position against both rivals rests less on any single chip than on its ecosystem. Operating systems, development tools and applications have been compiled for Arm over many years. Software is built for a specific instruction set. A large library of programs that already runs on Arm makes switching away more costly for device makers.

The same principle works against Arm where x86 holds the advantage. Moving PC or server software to Arm requires recompiling it or running it through translation. The contest among these three architectures turns largely on which software already runs where. It also turns on what it costs a chip designer to change.

#5477. From paper routes to fighter jets: Shield AI’s bet on Seattle is a homecoming for its co-founders

by Todd Bishop & John Cook on Nov 9, 2026 at 6:36 amNovember 9, 2026 at 6:36 am

As a kid on Mercer Island, Brandon Tseng delivered The Seattle Times and the Mercer Island Reporter for extra cash. Now he and his older brother, Ryan Tseng, are making news of their own in the Seattle region.

Shield AI, the San Diego defense tech company the brothers co-founded in 2015, announced a deal last week to buy Kirkland, Wash.-based radar maker Echodyne for up to $5.3 billion. Shield, now valued at $28.8 billion, had already unveiled plans in September to build its AI-piloted X-BAT fighter jet at a factory south of Seattle.

“I believe we will become one of the largest, or at least the fastest-growing employer in this region over the next several years,” Brandon Tseng said in an interview with GeekWire in the hours after the Echodyne acquisition was announced.

The company projects that it will employ about 4,000 people in the Seattle area by the early 2030s. It estimates the X-BAT could support about 8,000 jobs across the region in all, including jobs at Shield and its suppliers, according to an economic analysis drawing on company figures.

Tseng said Shield expects to have “well north of a million square feet” in the area before long, up from its initial 420,000-square-foot facility in Des Moines, Wash.

“That will really just be the beginning,” he said.

Brandon Tseng said the biggest reason Shield chose the Pacific Northwest for X-BAT production was the region’s “density of engineering and manufacturing talent,” pointing to Boeing, Microsoft and Amazon.

Inside the Echodyne deal: Shield believes the defense tech companies that succeed will need products that “sense, think, and act,” Tseng said. Its Hivemind autonomy software handles the thinking, and its V-BAT drone and X-BAT jet will handle the acting.

Echodyne becomes “the cornerstone of the sensing piece,” he said.

Tseng said Shield got a closer look at the market for sensors when it bought Australian optics company Sentient Vision Systems in 2024. That led the company to start looking seriously at other sensor makers, and eventually to Echodyne.

Shield and Echodyne had first crossed paths in 2016, when both were fledgling companies in the Department of Homeland Security’s Silicon Valley Innovation Program.

Nearly a decade later, the two companies’ teams were talking about working together when Echodyne began exploring a sale, Tseng said. The deal came together over several months. Tseng was at Echodyne the day it was announced last week, as the companies held all-hands meetings with their teams.

It’s an unusual deal: one venture-backed startup buying another, funded in part by a new venture round. Shield is raising $2.5 billion to help pay for the deal, including $1 billion in new funding at the $28.8 billion valuation — more than double what it was worth in March.

Echodyne has about 400 employees, after opening a $40 million radar factory in Woodinville in July. No layoffs are planned, the companies said. Eben Frankenberg, Echodyne’s co-founder and CEO, will stay in that role, reporting to Shield CEO Gary Steele. The combined company will have about 2,700 employees.

The deal is expected to close in early 2027, pending regulatory approval. Tseng said Shield plans a light touch for roughly the first year after that. Echodyne will keep selling radar to other manufacturers, many of them in counter-drone systems, while pursuing performance targets that could add $500 million to the price.

Deeper product integrations will be announced later, he said.

“They’ve been on a tear growth-wise, and we don’t want to get in their way,” Tseng said. “We don’t want to slow them down. We just want to supercharge them.”

He called the two companies’ cultures a strong match, describing both as mission-oriented and engineering-first. Echodyne’s best-selling radar, EchoShield, is designed to protect U.S. and allied service members from incoming drones.

Echodyne spun out of Intellectual Ventures, the Bellevue invention lab, in 2014 with a $15 million round led by Bill Gates and Madrona. Madrona and other Echodyne investors will become significant Shield shareholders.

Tim Porter, the Madrona Venture Group managing director who has served on Echodyne’s board since 2014, called the deal another sign of the defense tech industry’s rapid growth in the Pacific Northwest.

Echodyne “rarely, if ever, showed up on lists of the hottest defense tech companies,” he wrote. Now it’s “under the radar no longer.”

X-BAT bet: Much of Shield’s growth in the region depends on an aircraft that hasn’t flown yet. Shield unveiled its first full-scale X-BAT prototype this month and shipped it to Kansas for flight testing, with first flight targeted by the end of the year. Shield has said low-rate production will start in Des Moines in mid-2027, with the first locally built jet due in early 2028.

The Pentagon and Shield have committed a combined $400 million to X-BAT’s development, but Shield hasn’t announced any production orders.

Ryan Tseng, speaking to Breaking Defense on the sidelines of the International Fighter Conference in Munich last week, said Shield expects to announce European X-BAT orders and partnerships but declined to discuss quantities, saying only, “Watch this space.” Andrew Hawkes, Shield’s X-BAT director for Europe, told Breaking Defense the company has “several active” sales campaigns there but declined to name customers.

Asked about the X-BAT schedule in the interview last week, Brandon Tseng acknowledged the challenge but pointed to the engineering and manufacturing teams that brought the prototype together in about a year. “There was no quit in them,” he said.

“It’s hard as hell, right? Just to move out on production that fast, but you have to be confident,” he said. “I’m confident.”

Tseng, a Naval Academy graduate who deployed twice to Afghanistan as a Navy SEAL, compared Shield’s pace to that experience, when small, mission-driven groups with the right tools and resources would “do things that people didn’t think were possible.”

Ryan Tseng, an electrical engineer, previously founded wireless charging company WiPower, which was acquired by Qualcomm. The brothers started Shield with Andrew Reiter, Shield’s first CTO, who returned to the company this year.

Seattle roots: The Tseng brothers and their sister grew up on Mercer Island. Brandon Tseng spent summers swimming in Lake Washington and played water polo for Mercer Island. Ryan Tseng, who was Shield’s CEO for about a decade, graduated from Mercer Island High School, and their sister graduated from the University of Washington.

Their father, Carlos Tseng, was CEO of Seattle-based Foss Maritime from 1996 to 2001, according to Tseng and Shield. He would stop at Pike Place Market on the way home from work, and the family “probably ate salmon every other day,” Brandon Tseng said.

The family moved to Florida in 2001. None of the Tsengs live in the area anymore, but Brandon Tseng still has friends here from middle school and high school and stops by Mercer Island when he has time on his visits to the region.

Shield’s Washington state connections go further. Steele, the company’s CEO since May 2025, grew up in Yakima and graduated from Washington State University.

Brandon Tseng called Shield’s expansion in the region “a fun homecoming” for him, his brother and Steele. He is based in Washington, D.C., but expects to spend more and more time in the Seattle area.

Tseng delivered the Times, then the afternoon paper, seven days a week from age 10 to 14, making his rounds every day after school and on weekends. He credits those routes with teaching him about hard work.

“It’s always felt like home,” he said. “It’s great to be back here.”

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5476. From interim CEO to Form 8-K: 10 steps boards take after a sudden CEO exit

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit, from naming an interim chief executive to running a board search and filing the required disclosures

A sudden CEO exit tests a board's preparation more than its judgment. When a chief executive resigns without warning, dies, falls seriously ill or is dismissed, directors rarely have time to deliberate from scratch. The decisions they make in the first days are shaped by work they did, or failed to do, long before.

The stakes reach well beyond the boardroom. Employees want to know who is in charge and whether their projects will survive. Investors want evidence that the company has a plan and that strategy will not drift. Customers and suppliers watch for signs of disruption. For a U.S. public company, regulators also expect prompt disclosure of the change.

Understanding how companies replace a CEO after a sudden exit means looking at several moving parts at once. Boards must put an accountable leader in place quickly. They must decide whether that person is a placeholder or a contender for the permanent job. They also need a process for finding a successor that staff and shareholders find credible.

The tools available to directors are well established. Many boards keep an emergency succession plan alongside their longer-term CEO succession planning. They can promote a sitting executive or ask a director to step into an executive role. They can also bring in an outside search firm to build a slate of candidates. Each route carries tradeoffs between continuity and change.

The legal and financial side matters too. A departing chief executive usually leaves behind an employment agreement, equity awards and possibly severance terms that the board must review. The interim leader and the eventual successor each need a pay package. Public companies must also manage what they say, when they say it and to whom.

The 10 slides that follow cover a selection of common steps boards take during an emergency CEO succession. They are not a complete or ranked list, and the order is not fixed. In practice, many of these steps run in parallel during the first weeks of a chief executive transition. Each slide explains one step, why boards use it and what it involves.

When a chief executive leaves without warning, the board's first move is usually to name an interim CEO. That appointment gives employees, investors and customers one accountable leader while the search for a permanent successor begins.

A company cannot run for long without someone holding the chief executive's authority. Contracts need signatures and budgets need approval. Managers need a person who can settle disputes and make final calls. Payroll, regulatory obligations and customer commitments do not pause for a leadership change. Naming an interim closes that gap and makes clear who is in charge.

Speed matters outside the company as well. Investors, lenders, customers and suppliers watch a leadership change closely. An announcement that pairs the departure with a named replacement shows that the board has acted. A long silence between the two can invite speculation about why the previous CEO left.

Interim chief executives usually come from one of two places: the board or the senior management team. A director tends to know the company's strategy, finances and governance history. A senior executive brings day-to-day knowledge of operations, staff and customers. The board weighs which of those strengths the business needs most in the moment.

The interim holds the CEO's authority, but the board usually sets the terms of the role through a formal resolution. Those terms cover whom the interim reports to and how long the arrangement is expected to last. Some boards also require their own approval for transactions above a set size.

Some interims state from the start that they will not seek the permanent role. That clarity can let other executives focus on the transition instead of on competing for the top job. Other interims stay open to the position. In those cases, the board may evaluate the interim alongside outside and internal candidates in the formal search.

The title varies from company to company. Some boards use "interim CEO," while others prefer "acting CEO." A few split the job temporarily between two senior executives as co-CEOs. That structure requires the board to spell out which parts of the business each executive oversees and how they resolve disagreements.

Many boards keep a confidential emergency succession plan that names who takes charge if the chief executive leaves without notice. Putting that plan into action lets directors carry out a decision they made in calm conditions, rather than improvising one in a crisis.

An emergency plan usually answers a short list of practical questions. It names the person or people who can step in on short notice. That is often a senior executive or a sitting director. The plan may also say who convenes the board, who speaks for the company and which outside advisers get called first.

This document differs from long-term CEO succession planning. A long-term plan develops candidates over years and prepares for an orderly retirement. An emergency plan deals with a narrower problem: who runs the company tomorrow.

The person named for an emergency is not always the board's preferred permanent successor. Keeping the two roles separate lets the board fill the gap without locking in a long-term choice. It also leaves directors room to run a fuller search later.

Confidentiality is part of the design. Boards generally keep the plan private to avoid signaling who is in line for the top job. A leaked name can unsettle other executives or create expectations the board never meant to set.

A plan works only if it stays current. Executives change roles, get promoted or leave the company. A name on the plan can go stale as a result. Boards review and update these plans periodically, often through the full board or its governance or nominating committee. Directors may also confirm that the named stand-in is still willing and able to serve.

The absence of a plan carries its own cost. Without one, directors must debate who leads while employees, customers and lenders wait for answers. That debate can stretch from hours into days. It also leaves room for internal rivalries to surface during the transition.

After a sudden CEO exit, boards commonly set up a small committee of directors to run the search for a permanent successor. The committee manages the process day to day and brings a recommendation back to the full board, which keeps the final vote.

A full board is too large, and meets too rarely, to run a search on its own. A smaller group can schedule interviews quickly and review candidates in detail. It can also keep sensitive information within a tight circle. Some boards hand the job to an existing nominating and governance committee. Others create an ad hoc committee for this search alone and dissolve it once a new chief executive is in place.

Independent directors usually make up the committee. These are directors who are not company employees and have no material business ties to the company. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often leads the group. That person typically serves as the main contact for candidates, advisers and the rest of the board.

Membership comes with a conflict rule. A director who wants to be considered for the CEO job generally steps off the committee. The same applies to an interim chief executive who may compete for the permanent role. Keeping candidates off the committee separates the people doing the judging from the people being judged. It also strengthens the board's ability to defend its choice later.

One of the committee's first tasks is to write a candidate profile. This document sets out the experience, skills and leadership qualities the next CEO needs. It reflects the company's strategy, its current challenges and the circumstances of the departure. A profile agreed early gives the committee a fixed standard for comparing candidates.

The committee then sets the process and the timetable. It decides how candidates will be sourced, who interviews them and in what order. It also oversees reference and background checks on finalists. Those checks carry extra weight after an abrupt exit tied to misconduct.

Confidentiality shapes the committee's work. Candidate names, interview notes and deliberations stay inside the committee and its advisers. A leak can cost the company a candidate who is employed elsewhere.

The committee reports to the full board at regular intervals throughout the search. Its decision rights stop short of the appointment itself. It recommends a finalist, and the full board votes to name the new CEO.

Promoting a sitting executive, such as the chief operating officer or chief financial officer, is a common way for a board to fill a sudden CEO vacancy. An insider already knows the business, the people and the numbers. That shortens the time before the company has a working leader.

The appeal starts with familiarity. A COO typically oversees day-to-day operations and already manages many of the teams that report up to the chief executive. A CFO knows the balance sheet, the lenders and the investor base. Either one can step into the top job without a long orientation period.

Existing relationships also count. Customers, suppliers, lenders and major shareholders often already deal with the internal candidate. That prior contact can make the leadership change easier to explain to each of them. Employees may read an internal appointment as a sign that the company's direction is not about to be overturned.

An insider also brings a track record the board has watched directly. Directors have usually seen the executive present at board meetings, defend budgets and respond to problems. That direct view removes some of the guesswork that comes with a candidate the board has met only in interviews.

The tradeoff is change. An executive who helped build the current strategy may be less inclined to question it. If the exit followed poor results or misconduct, a board may judge that an insider is too close to the problem.

Promotion also creates a second vacancy. If the COO becomes chief executive, someone still has to run operations. Companies often fill that seat with an acting appointment from the next management layer. Others split the duties among existing leaders for a period. A company that promotes its CFO must keep financial reporting and internal controls running without a gap. A public company also faces periodic filing deadlines that do not pause for a leadership change.

Readiness is the last test. Running one function is different from running the whole company. A COO may have limited experience facing investors. A CFO may have little exposure to product development or sales. Boards weigh those gaps before deciding. Some pair the new chief executive with an experienced chair or outside adviser. Others set out a defined development plan covering the areas where the executive has less experience.

A board sometimes asks its chair or another director to take on a temporary executive role after a sudden CEO exit. The appeal is speed and familiarity. The cost is that the person meant to supervise management now helps run it.

Directors who step in already know the company's strategy, finances and open risks from board meetings. They have usually worked with the senior team and the largest investors. That background lets them take charge without the orientation an outside hire would need. It also gives the board a leader whose judgment it has already seen up close.

The arrangement takes two main forms. In one, the chair becomes executive chair and takes on operating duties alongside the remaining executives. The CEO seat then stays vacant or goes to an internal officer. In the other, the chair or another director is named interim CEO outright. Both forms place a board member inside management, and both are meant to be temporary.

The tension is built into the board's role. Directors hire, oversee, evaluate and, when necessary, remove the chief executive. A director serving as interim leader ends up overseeing their own work. Questions about performance, pay and strategy become harder for the board to examine at arm's length.

Boards use several safeguards to manage that conflict. A common step is naming a lead independent director, or strengthening the role if one exists. That director runs executive sessions of the non-management directors and acts as a check on the interim leader. Under NYSE and Nasdaq $NDAQ listing standards, audit committee members must be independent. A director who takes on paid executive duties generally steps off the audit committee and often the compensation committee as well.

Time limits are another safeguard. Boards often set a defined term or tie the role to the end of the permanent search. A stated end point tells employees and investors that the arrangement is a bridge, not a new leadership structure. It also keeps a split role from becoming the default.

The board also has to settle whether the director in the executive seat is a candidate for the permanent job. Boards often decide that early. A director who is a contender generally steps away from the search committee's deliberations. A director who is not can say so publicly. That statement tells internal candidates the search is open.

Once a permanent CEO arrives, the director typically returns to a non-executive role. Some boards keep the director on as executive chair for a set period to support the handoff. The board then revisits committee assignments and independence determinations. The specifics depend on the company's bylaws, governance guidelines and listing requirements.

Boards often retain an executive search firm to find and vet candidates for a permanent chief executive. Spencer Stuart, Russell Reynolds Associates, Heidrick & Struggles and Korn Ferry are among the firms that take on this kind of board-level assignment.

The firm works for the board, not for management. It typically reports to the committee of directors that oversees the search. That reporting line matters after a sudden exit, when an interim leader may also be a contender for the permanent job.

A search usually begins with a role specification. The firm and the directors agree on what the next CEO needs to deliver. That brief draws on the company's strategy, its financial position and the circumstances of the previous leader's departure. The resulting document shapes which industries, functions and backgrounds the firm targets.

The firm then maps the market. Consultants identify executives who fit the profile, including sitting CEOs, division heads at larger companies and leaders at competitors. Many of those people are not looking to move. The first approach is therefore typically discreet and framed as a conversation rather than a job offer.

Confidentiality runs in both directions. Candidates employed elsewhere often cannot afford to have their interest become public. The hiring company, for its part, may not want rivals or its own employees to learn who is under consideration before the board decides.

Assessment goes beyond the résumé. Search firms conduct structured interviews and check references. They also examine how a candidate performed in situations similar to the one the company now faces. Some boards ask the firm to evaluate internal candidates as well. That gives directors a common yardstick for comparing insiders and outsiders.

CEO searches are generally run on a retained basis. Under that model, the firm is paid for conducting the search rather than only when a candidate is hired. Fee terms are set in each engagement letter and vary by firm and assignment.

Boards also ask about conflicts. Search firms commonly observe off-limits arrangements that restrict them from recruiting executives out of their own current clients. A large firm's client list can therefore narrow the pool of executives it is able to approach.

The firm's output is a short list of finalists, not a decision. Directors interview the candidates, often over several rounds, and the full board votes on the appointment. The board, not the search firm, remains accountable for the final choice.

The choice between an internal and an external CEO candidate turns on one question: does the company need continuity or a change in direction? No fixed rule settles it. Boards weigh each sudden exit on its own circumstances.

The reason for the departure shapes the answer. A CEO who leaves because of illness or death may leave behind a strategy the board still supports. In that case, a leader who already knows the plan can carry it forward with less disruption.

A dismissal tied to misconduct or weak results points the other way. If the board has lost confidence in the direction of the business, an insider may look too close to the decisions that caused the problem. Directors then have to judge whether a familiar face can credibly signal a break with the past.

Internal candidates come with a known record. Directors have usually watched them present to the board, manage budgets and lead teams. They already understand the company's products, customers and culture. That familiarity lowers the risk of a poor fit. It can also limit fresh thinking.

External candidates offer a different set of tradeoffs. An outsider arrives without loyalty to past strategy or to particular executives. That independence can make it easier to restructure, exit a business line or reset relationships with investors.

The cost is a learning curve. A chief executive hired from outside has to learn the organization, its people and its informal ways of working. Until that happens, acting with confidence on major decisions is harder.

Culture adds another layer to the comparison. A company with a strong internal culture may resist a leader who does not share it. A company whose culture contributed to the exit may need someone willing to challenge it.

The depth of the internal bench also narrows or widens the field. If no executive is ready for the top role, the debate moves quickly toward outside candidates. If several insiders are credible, the board can compare them directly against an external slate rather than choosing one pool at the outset.

Timing is another variable. An insider can usually step into the permanent role faster. A wider external search can take longer. That extends the period the company spends under interim leadership.

A U.S. public company generally must report a CEO departure, and the appointment of an interim or permanent replacement, on SEC Form 8-K under Item 5.02. The standard filing deadline is four business days after the triggering event.

Form 8-K is the Securities and Exchange Commission's current report. Companies file it to tell investors about significant events that occur between quarterly and annual reports. Item 5.02 governs the departure and appointment of directors and certain senior officers. The principal executive officer, usually the CEO, falls within it.

A typical filing states who is leaving, when the change takes effect and who is taking charge. For a newly appointed officer, the disclosure includes background such as age and business experience. It also describes any material compensation arrangement tied to the appointment.

The four-day window is a deadline, not a waiting period. Companies often announce the news by press release on the same day and attach that release to the 8-K as an exhibit. A quick announcement shortens the stretch in which rumors circulate without an official account.

Regulation Fair Disclosure, known as Reg FD, shapes how the news goes out. The rule bars a public company from selectively sharing material nonpublic information with analysts or certain investors ahead of the general public. A sudden change at the top can be material. That pushes companies toward one broad public announcement rather than a round of private calls.

Foreign companies listed in the U.S. as foreign private issuers follow a different route. They generally furnish reports on Form 6-K rather than Form 8-K. Companies without SEC reporting obligations file no 8-K at all. Their boards still decide how and when to inform lenders, investors and staff.

Inside the company, timing is a practical problem. Employees who learn about a leadership change from a headline may question whether anyone is in control. Boards and communications teams therefore tend to schedule an all-staff message close to the public announcement.

That message usually names the person now in charge and explains what happens next. It often confirms that the board has started a search, without committing to a date. Companies generally avoid speculating about the reasons for an exit, especially while lawyers are still reviewing the circumstances.

Customers, suppliers and lenders form a third audience. Sales teams and account managers may need prepared language for their contacts. The board may also need to check whether any financing or commercial agreements require formal notice of a leadership change.

After a sudden CEO exit, the board reviews the departing executive's employment agreement to settle severance, equity awards, clawback rights and any non-compete. It also sets pay for the interim leader and, later, for the permanent successor.

The compensation committee usually leads this work, often with outside legal counsel. Its first task is to establish what the contract actually says. Employment agreements differ from company to company. The signed documents set the baseline, and departing from them usually means negotiating new terms with the former executive.

The reason for the departure shapes almost every term. Chief executive agreements commonly treat a termination "for cause" differently from one "without cause." A resignation for "good reason," as the contract defines it, often carries the same benefits as a dismissal without cause. Death and disability usually have their own provisions. A board that labels an exit incorrectly can invite a legal dispute with the former executive.

Equity awards are often the largest piece of value at stake. Unvested stock options and restricted shares may be forfeited, continue to vest or vest immediately. The outcome depends on the equity plan and the individual award agreements. Performance-based awards can carry separate rules tied to whether targets are met after the executive leaves.

Clawback provisions let a company recover pay that should not have been awarded. In the U.S., stock exchange listing standards adopted under SEC Rule 10D-1 require a clawback policy. That policy must cover erroneously awarded incentive pay after an accounting restatement. Some company policies reach further and cover misconduct.

Restrictive covenants come next. These can include non-compete, non-solicitation and confidentiality clauses. Whether a non-compete can be enforced depends on the jurisdiction. The board's lawyers assess that question for each case.

Many departures end in a negotiated separation agreement. In exchange for severance, the former CEO typically signs a release of legal claims against the company. The agreement may also cover a short transition period, a consulting arrangement or a mutual non-disparagement clause.

The committee then turns to the interim leader. An executive who steps up temporarily may receive added cash pay, a one-time equity grant or both. Those terms reflect the extra duties and the uncertainty of a temporary role. The permanent successor's package is negotiated later, as part of the search itself.

Public companies also face scrutiny of the payout. U.S. proxy statements describe the potential payments named executive officers would receive on termination. Shareholders can compare that disclosure with what the departing CEO actually receives.

During a CEO transition, an interim leader usually keeps strategy steady, holds the senior team together and leaves major long-term bets for the permanent chief executive. Retention arrangements for key executives are a common tool for limiting departures while the search runs.

A sudden exit leaves a gap at the top, and the people just below it often feel the uncertainty first. Senior executives may wonder whether the next CEO will keep them, reshape their roles or bring in a new team. Some may hear from recruiters or competitors during this period. Losing several leaders at once would add to the disruption the board is trying to contain.

The interim CEO's job is partly to answer that uncertainty. An interim leader often meets early with each member of the executive team to clarify reporting lines and decision rights. Those conversations confirm which projects continue and who owns them. That clarity lets managers keep running their units rather than wait for direction.

Retention pay is another lever. A board may offer selected executives cash bonuses or additional equity. These awards pay out only if the person stays through the transition or for a set period after it. The terms vary by company and by individual. The aim is to give critical leaders a concrete reason to stay until the new CEO is in place.

On strategy, interim leaders typically focus on carrying out the existing plan. They tend to defer decisions that would bind the next CEO for years. Examples include large acquisitions, major restructurings or a shift in the company's core direction. Routine operations, approved budgets and customer commitments continue. Postponing the biggest choices preserves options for whoever takes the permanent role.

That caution has limits. A business facing a crisis, a regulatory deadline or a fast-moving competitor cannot simply pause. In those cases the board and the interim leader decide which time-sensitive matters must move forward. The board often stays more involved than usual while those decisions are made.

The final stage is the handoff. Once the permanent CEO is named, the interim leader typically briefs the successor on open issues, pending decisions and the state of the executive team. An interim drawn from management may return to a previous role or leave the company. An interim drawn from the board may go back to serving as a director. The new chief executive then sets the longer-term direction. That includes any changes to the leadership team or strategy that the transition period left open.

#5475. New tax incentives give Washington’s sustainable aviation fuel industry a boost

Challenges, breakthroughs and big ideas in the race to protect our planet. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 9, 2026 at 9:38 amNovember 11, 2026 at 7:41 am

Washington has cleared a milestone in its effort to become a hub for lower-carbon jet fuel, unlocking tax incentives aimed at attracting production to the state.

Gov. Bob Ferguson announced Friday that Washington has reached the capacity to produce at least 20 million gallons of sustainable aviation fuel annually. That triggers incentives taking effect Jan. 1, including a tax credit starting at $1 per gallon for qualifying fuel. The credit rises to as much as $2 for fuels with greater emissions reductions.

The Department of Ecology recently surveyed potential producers and confirmed that Phillips 66’s Ferndale refinery alone has enough capacity to meet the threshold. The benchmark measures production capacity, not actual output.

Sustainable aviation fuel, or SAF, is widely seen as one of the most promising near-term options for cutting aviation’s carbon emissions because it can be blended with conventional jet fuel and used in existing aircraft. But it remains more expensive than petroleum-based fuel, and production is orders of magnitude below the industry’s needs.

“We have so many unique assets in Washington that position us to be global leaders in the SAF transition, and this tax incentive is the final element needed to really unleash the tidal wave of opportunity,” said Jake Gentry, executive director of the Cascadia Sustainable Aviation Accelerator, in a GeekWire interview.

The accelerator launched in January, bringing together airlines, SAF producers, public officials, researchers and others to promote the industry in the Pacific Northwest. Its work includes helping producers secure financing, develop feedstock supplies and connect with customers.

SAF can be produced from used cooking oil, grease and fats, plants and agricultural waste, and captured carbon. Its climate benefits depend on the raw materials and energy used to make it.

The fuel still produces carbon dioxide when burned. But unlike petroleum-based jet fuel, which releases carbon that would otherwise stay trapped underground, SAF recycles carbon already in circulation in plants, animals and the atmosphere. Washington’s per-gallon tax credit requires emissions at least 50% below those of conventional jet fuel.

Washington’s production capacity is below that of some larger facilities elsewhere. A Diamond Green Diesel plant in Texas can produce up to 235 million gallons of SAF annually, according to its partner Valero. That figure also represents capacity, not actual production.

With the minimum threshold being met, all Washington SAF producers will be eligible for the tax credit regardless of their volumes.

A startup called Twelve is already making the fuel in the central Washington city of Moses Lake. The company opened its AirPlant One facility last year and began commercially producing SAF this summer from captured carbon dioxide and water. The technology has the potential to create the most climate-friendly SAF available, potentially unlocking the largest state tax credits.

Nicholas Flanders, Twelve’s CEO and co-founder, welcomed the announcement.

“This is an extraordinary signal of support for our industry,” Flanders said via email. “Washington is building the leading foundation in the country for next-generation domestic fuel production, and Twelve is ready to build upon it.”

Twelve’s first-of-its-kind facility is designed to make up to 50,000 gallons of SAF per year. AirPlant Two, a much bigger plant that would make tens of millions of gallons a year, is in development. The company hasn’t said where it will be located.

Dutch-owned SkyNRG is building a SAF facility in Walla Walla, Wash., and plans to use renewable natural gas that’s captured at landfills and from dairy waste as a feedstock. Earlier this year, leaders said the company had secured key environmental approvals and plans to start commercial operations in 2030.

Washington’s relatively affordable hydroelectric power has historically helped attract climate tech companies. But growing electricity demand, including from data centers, is putting pressure on the region’s power supply.

Washington also faces competition from other states offering SAF tax incentives. Illinois and Minnesota already offer credits, and Nebraska’s program starts next year. Meanwhile, a federal credit was reduced from $1.75 per gallon to $1 after President Donald Trump returned to office.

Washington leaders tout other perks that could attract SAF production. It’s the only state that offers both a SAF tax credit and a clean fuel standard. Together, the policies help make cleaner jet fuel more cost-competitive by providing tax benefits and allowing SAF producers to earn credits they can sell to other fuel suppliers that need to meet the state’s emissions requirements.

The accelerator also supports efforts with Washington State University to develop regional feedstock supplies, including waste from logging and agriculture.

“Between our long history of aviation innovation, our intentional investments into the sector and our climate-forward policies, we’re making sure Washington is the best state in the country to produce sustainable aviation fuels,” Ferguson said in a statement.

The Climate Pledge is a commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040, co-founded by Amazon and Global Optimism in 2019.

Seven years later, the community has grown to over 700 signatories across 62 industries and 49 countries and territories, reducing emissions, scaling emerging climate solutions, and addressing challenges across operations and value chains.
