#5474. How MLB's qualifying offer works, from salary formula to pick compensation

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The MLB qualifying offer ties a one-year salary to draft pick compensation, and these 10 explainers cover who gets it, what it pays and what happens when players decline

A club about to lose a free agent can turn his departure into draft pick compensation. The price of that option is the risk that he accepts a one-year salary instead. For the 2023-24 offseason, that salary was $20.325 million. The mechanism behind the trade-off is the MLB qualifying offer, a one-year contract a team can extend to its own impending free agent.

The offer cuts both ways. A club collects compensation only if the player declines and signs with another team. If he accepts, the club owes him the one-year salary. A player who declines gives up a guaranteed salary to test the open market. He also enters that market carrying a cost for any rival club that signs him.

The system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement between the league and its players. It replaced the older Type A and Type B classifications, which relied on player rankings. The salary is not negotiated player by player. It is pegged to the average salary of the 125 highest-paid players in the majors and recalculated every offseason. That formula ties the offer to the top of the market rather than to any one player's performance.

A player generally must spend the full season with the same club to be eligible. A player traded midseason is not eligible. A player can also receive an offer only once in his career. When a player declines and signs elsewhere, the signing club gives up draft picks and, in some cases, international bonus pool space. The exact cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue-sharing money or pay the luxury tax. The size of the contract also matters.

Those costs have shaped individual free agencies. Kyle Lohse, a free agent after 2012, remained unsigned into spring training 2013. The draft pick cost attached to him was a factor. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales each turned down the 2013 offer of $14.1 million. Both signed in June 2014, after the draft, when the pick compensation no longer applied. Drew went to the Red Sox, and Morales went to the Twins.

The 10 slides below cover the offer piece by piece, from its definition and salary formula to eligibility, acceptance, departure and the compensation rules.

The MLB qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a team may extend to one of its own players who is about to become a free agent. The player then chooses between two paths: accept the deal and stay, or decline it and test the open market.

The offer is optional. A club decides player by player whether to make it. Nothing requires a team to extend one to any departing free agent.

The arrangement exists to give clubs something back when a player leaves. If the player turns the offer down and then signs with a different team, his former club receives draft pick compensation.

That conditional link sits at the center of the system. Declining alone does not trigger anything for the original club. Compensation depends on whether the player goes on to sign with another team, not on the rejection itself.

For the player, the offer is a fallback and a decision point at once. Accepting locks in a one-year salary with his current club. Declining keeps every other option open. It also attaches a cost in draft selections to any other team that signs him.

For the team, the calculation runs the other way. Making the offer creates a path to compensation if the player walks. It also carries the possibility that he says yes. In that case, the club is committed to a one-year salary it chose to put on the table.

The qualifying offer arrived with the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It took the place of an older approach to free agent compensation that sorted players into Type A and Type B classes based on rankings.

The newer system ties compensation to a team's decision to make an offer, rather than to where a player sat in a ranking. A player becomes subject to compensation because his club offered him the one-year deal and he turned it down.

The qualifying offer salary equals the average salary of MLB's 125 highest-paid players. The league recalculates that average every offseason.

The player receiving the offer has no effect on the amount. A team cannot lower it for a modestly paid player or raise it for a star. Every qualifying offer made in a given offseason carries the same one-year salary.

The figure is also the same for every club. A team with a small payroll and a team with a large one face an identical number. That single salary takes up a bigger share of a smaller budget. The same offer can therefore be a heavier commitment for one club than for another.

That makes the offer a fixed price rather than a negotiated contract. A club considering one is not bargaining over terms. It is deciding whether the player is worth that single figure for one more season.

A fixed price also means a club has to be prepared to pay all of it. A player who accepts receives the full amount, whatever he earned the year before.

The benchmark draws on the highest salaries in the sport. When the largest contracts rise, the average rises with them. When pay at the top levels off, the figure follows.

Because it is an average across 125 salaries, no single contract sets the figure. One record-setting deal shifts the average by only a fraction of that deal's size. Broad movement across many top contracts is what moves the number.

The yearly recalculation means the price can change from one winter to the next. A club weighing an offer in one offseason may face a different figure than a club weighing a similar player a year earlier.

For a player, the formula provides a known number. He can compare that guaranteed one-year salary with the offers he expects from other clubs before he responds.

A qualifying offer can go only to a club's own impending free agent. That player generally must have spent the entire season with the same club. A player who changes teams in a midseason trade is not eligible to receive one.

Both conditions have to be met. The first is contract status. The offer is meant for a player whose deal is ending and who is about to reach the open market. A player still under contract for the following season falls outside the system, no matter how long he has been with his club.

The second condition is tenure. The rule generally ties eligibility to a full season with one organization. The club extending the offer has to be the club the player spent the whole year with.

A midseason trade breaks that link. A pending free agent who is dealt during the season cannot receive a qualifying offer from his new team. His old team cannot make one either. He is no longer its own free agent when the offseason arrives.

That limit carries over to trades of pending free agents. A club that acquires one during the season gets his play for the rest of that year. It does not gain the option of making him a qualifying offer once the season ends. The club that trades him away loses that option as well.

Eligibility also decides whether draft pick compensation is possible. Compensation goes only to a club whose offer was declined and whose player then signed with another team. A player who was never eligible for an offer carries no such cost. The club that signs him does not forfeit draft selections under this mechanism.

Eligibility does not oblige a team to act. A club may extend the offer to an eligible player. It may also let him leave without one, in which case no draft pick compensation follows.

A Major League Baseball player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. After a club makes him that one-year offer, no team can make him another, whether he accepted it or turned it down.

The limit follows the player, not the club that made the offer. It does not reset when he changes teams. A club that signs him later cannot extend a fresh offer to a player who has already had one.

The limit shapes his later free agency. Draft pick compensation for a departing free agent flows only through a declined qualifying offer. A player who can no longer receive one carries no pick cost the next time he hits the open market.

A club that wants to sign him at that point does not give up draft picks or international bonus pool space to do it. His former club, in turn, cannot collect compensation when he leaves.

The rule applies to players who accept. An accepted offer is a one-year contract. The player can return to free agency a season later. When he does, his club cannot issue a second offer.

Joc Pederson and Martin Perez accepted offers in the 2022 offseason, as did Hyun-Jin Ryu in 2019 and Brandon Belt in 2021. Each of those acceptances used up that player's single offer.

The same limit covers players who decline. Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales both turned their offers down. Having received one, neither could be given another later in his career.

The limit also holds as the offer's value climbs. A player who received an offer at an earlier, lower amount cannot be tagged again when the figure is higher.

For a player, the compensation attached to his name is a one-time event. For a club, making the offer is a single chance to tie draft pick compensation to that player's departure.

The MLB qualifying offer was worth $13.3 million in 2012, the year the system began under that year's collective bargaining agreement. By the 2023-24 offseason, the figure had climbed to $20.325 million.

Two more figures mark points along the way. The offer was $14.1 million in 2013. For the 2022-23 offseason, it was $19.65 million.

Those four numbers are snapshots rather than a full year-by-year record. Two sit at the start of the system, in its first two years. The other two come from back-to-back offseasons much later. Read in order, each figure is higher than the one before it.

The direction follows from how the number is set. The offer is an average of top salaries, so it moves when that group of salaries moves. Bigger contracts at the high end of the market push the next offer up. A quiet offseason for top-end deals would hold the figure down. The number reflects where elite pay stood in a given offseason. It is not a reward tied to any single player.

The same sum applied to every club that made a qualifying offer in a given offseason. A team with a modest payroll faced the same one-year figure as a team with a large one. That fixed figure takes up a bigger share of a smaller payroll than of a larger one.

A higher number changes what is at stake on both sides. It means a larger guaranteed salary for any player who accepts. It also means a larger one-year bill for the club that made the offer.

That raises the bar for extending an offer. A club has to be willing to pay the full figure for one season if the player says yes. A player weighing the offer compares that one-year sum with what he expects to find on the open market. The higher the figure, the more the guaranteed side of that comparison is worth.

A player who accepts the qualifying offer signs a one-year contract with his current club at that offseason's set salary. He skips the open market, and the club keeps him for one more season instead of collecting draft pick compensation.

Joc Pederson and Martin Perez both took that route in the 2022 offseason. Each accepted $19.65 million, the qualifying offer figure for the 2022-23 offseason. Two players signed at an identical salary in the same winter because the offer carries one price for everyone who receives it that year.

Hyun-Jin Ryu accepted a qualifying offer worth $17.8 million in 2019. Brandon Belt accepted $18.4 million in 2021. Both figures sit below the $19.65 million that Pederson and Perez took. The amount a player accepts depends on the year he receives the offer, not on his own salary history.

Acceptance also changes what happens on the club side. Draft pick compensation exists only when a player declines and then signs with another team. Once a player accepts, that path closes. His club receives no extra draft selection. No rival club forfeits picks or international bonus pool space to sign him.

What the club gets instead is another season of the player's services at a fixed, known price. The deal covers one year only, with no multiyear commitment attached to the offer itself.

For the player, accepting means trading the uncertainty of free agency for a guaranteed salary. He gives up the chance to test what other clubs would pay him. In return, he avoids a market where any signing team would have to give up draft picks to land him.

The choice also carries a career-long consequence. A player can receive a qualifying offer only once in his career, and a player who accepts has used that one offer. When his one-year deal ends, his club cannot attach a second qualifying offer to him. He reaches his next free agency without that draft pick cost following him.

A player who turns down the qualifying offer becomes a free agent on the open market. His former club receives draft pick compensation only if he signs with a different team.

The decline alone earns the original club nothing. Compensation depends entirely on where the player lands. If no other club signs him, no picks change hands.

Turning down the offer means walking away from a guaranteed one-year salary. In exchange, the player can negotiate terms with any club in the league.

That single trigger shapes the calculation for the club that made the offer. Extending it places a price on the player's departure. The club collects that price only when a rival team decides to sign him.

The decline also travels with the player. Any team weighing a contract with him has to account for what it would give up to sign him. The size of that cost varies from club to club.

Each side makes its own trade-off. The player exchanges a guaranteed salary for access to the open market. The original club exchanges its hold on the player for the possibility of draft picks. The signing club gives up some of its draft capital to add him.

When a player turns down a qualifying offer and signs with a new team, that new team gives up draft picks. In some cases it also surrenders international bonus pool space. The size of that cost depends on whether the clubs involved receive revenue sharing or pay the luxury tax, and on how large the contract is.

The forfeiture is one half of an exchange. The club that made the offer receives draft pick compensation, but only if the player signs with a different organization. If he never signs elsewhere, no picks move in either direction.

Three variables shape the exchange. The first is whether a club is a revenue-sharing recipient. The second is whether a club is a luxury-tax payer. Both questions apply to each club in the transaction — the team that loses the player and the team that signs him. The third variable is the size of the contract the player signs.

Those factors mean the price of signing a player who declined a qualifying offer is not uniform across MLB. Two clubs pursuing the same free agent can face different forfeitures based on their financial standing. The compensation that flows back to the team that lost him also depends on that club's own status.

None of the three variables is a direct measure of the player's performance. Two describe the finances of the clubs involved. The third reflects the deal he signs.

The possible loss of international bonus pool space means the penalty for some signings reaches beyond the draft. A single free-agent signing can draw down two separate resources at once.

For a front office, the cost of a free agent tied to a declined offer has two parts. One is the contract itself. The other is the picks, and in some cases the bonus pool space, that the club gives up to sign him. The size of that contract can also change the second part.

Kyle Lohse, Stephen Drew and Kendrys Morales are three examples of how draft pick compensation can weigh on a free agent's market. All three stayed unsigned for long stretches while pick compensation was attached to them.

Lohse reached free agency after the 2012 season. He remained unsigned into spring training in 2013. The draft picks a new club would have had to surrender to sign him were a factor in that wait.

Drew and Morales went through a similar wait. Both declined the 2013 qualifying offer of $14.1 million and entered the open market.

Both players signed in June 2014. By then the draft had already taken place. The pick compensation tied to each of them no longer applied. A club could add either player without forfeiting a draft selection.

Drew signed with the Boston Red Sox. Morales signed with the Minnesota Twins.

In all three cases, the cost sat with the club doing the signing. Any team that wanted Lohse, Drew or Morales before the draft would have given up draft selections to get him. Their former clubs stood to collect compensation only if each player signed somewhere else.

That cost fell on the buyer, but it still shaped each player's options. A club weighing a contract for one of them had to count the picks it would lose alongside the salary it would pay. For Lohse, that added cost was a factor in a wait that stretched into spring training.

The Drew and Morales signings show the other side of that calculation. Once the draft passed, the compensation attached to them ended, and the extra cost to a signing club went with it.

The cases also show the risk a player takes by saying no. Declining means giving up a guaranteed one-year salary for an uncertain market. Drew and Morales each passed on $14.1 million and then spent months without a contract.

The 2012 collective bargaining agreement replaced MLB's old Type A and Type B free agent classes with the qualifying offer. Compensation stopped hinging on where a player ranked and started hinging on a one-year salary offer he could accept or decline.

Under the earlier system, a player's class came from his place in player rankings. Compensation followed from that classification. The qualifying offer took rankings out of the equation.

In their place, the 2012 agreement put two decisions. The club makes one, and the player makes the other.

The club decides first whether to extend a one-year contract to its own impending free agent. A club that makes no offer has no claim to compensation if that player leaves. Under the new structure, compensation starts with an action the club takes, not with a label attached to the player.

The player then chooses between that guaranteed one-year salary and a search for a deal on the open market. His answer, not his ranking, determines whether compensation comes into play at all.

The offer is not tailored to the individual. In a given offseason, every club extending one offers the same amount. A league-wide salary formula sets that figure, not the player's own record. Two players with very different track records face the same number.

That uniform price turns the question of a player's value into a test both sides answer. A club weighing an offer has to decide whether the player is worth that salary for one season. A player weighing it has to decide whether the open market will pay him more than that.

That design puts a price on the club's choice. A team that extends the offer must be ready to pay the full one-year salary if the player accepts. If he declines, that salary commitment falls away.

The framework built in 2012 remained in place through the 2023-24 offseason.

#5473. Circle Begins CCTP V1 Wind-Down Amid Doc Mismatch

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Burn limits on Circle's legacy USDC bridge began falling on October 31, and the V1 contracts pause on December 1.

On the same migration page, a block of instructions written for AI coding assistants still says Noble, Sui and Aptos "still require V1." Circle's own release notes say two of those three chains moved to V2 weeks ago.

Circle's legacy cross-chain transfer protocol entered its final month today. From October 31, burn limits on CCTP V1 start falling toward zero, and on December 1 the V1 contracts pause. Any app still using them will stop moving USDC between chains.

Most coverage has focused on those two dates. But the guide developers are told to follow, Circle's V1-to-V2 migration page, contains a mistake in the section written for AI tools.

Embedded in the page is an "Agent Instructions" block, guidance meant for AI coding assistants that read the documentation for developers. It says: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1." For two of those three chains, Circle's other published records say the opposite.

The schedule is fixed. Circle announced in an August 27 blog post that "CCTP V1 (Legacy) deprecation begins October 31, 2026 and completes on December 1, 2026."

From today, V1 burn limits fall, and the migration guide says "message limits will tighten over time until no new burns can be initiated." On December 1 the V1 contracts pause, and any integration still pointing at them can no longer transfer USDC between chains.

Circle has been firm about this. "Migration from CCTP V1 (Legacy) to CCTP V2 is required, not just recommended," the company wrote, adding that V2 "uses separate contracts and APIs and is not backward compatible."

Funds already in transit are protected. The guide says "all pending redemptions will remain available" during the phase-out, and that Circle "will maintain minter allowances greater than the total of pending attestations."

The migration page has two audiences. Human readers see the main guide. AI coding assistants also parse a separate instruction block, which tells them how to answer developer questions.

In that block, the guidance is clear: "Noble, Sui, and Aptos still require V1."

The main text above it says something different. According to the human-facing guide, "CCTP V2 contracts are available on all CCTP V1 chains except for Noble and Sui," and "Sui will be supported by V2 before the deprecation begins." Aptos isn't listed as an exception there at all.

So one page gives two different answers about the same chains, and the out-of-date answer is the one written for AI tools.

Circle's 2026 CCTP release notes show how out of date the instruction is:

Circle's supported chains and domains page now lists both Sui and Aptos in its CCTP table, with Standard Transfer support. The page's V1-only section names one chain: Noble.

As of today, Aptos has had V2 for more than two months and Sui for more than three weeks. The instruction telling AI tools that both "still require V1" was overtaken by Circle's own updates before the shutdown began.

Noble is the one chain in that line where the instruction is still accurate, and it is leaving CCTP entirely.

In a September 10 announcement, Circle said "Noble will not receive CCTP V2" and set out its exit:

For Noble, V1 is the only route available, and it is being closed.

A wrong line in documentation would normally be a small issue, but the timing makes this one more serious.

Many developers now ask AI assistants to write or update integration code, and those assistants read documentation like this page. A developer asking how to bridge USDC to Sui or Aptos could be told, based on Circle's own instruction block, to use V1. That is the route whose burn limits started falling today and which pauses in a month.

The fix in the code is not small either. Moving to V2 means:

An integration built on V1 now would have to be rebuilt within weeks.

For teams working with Sui and Aptos, the published records point one way: build on V2, using the contract addresses for domains 8 and 9. Don't follow the V1 guidance from the agent-instruction block.

For Noble, the deadline is January 12, 2027. Before then, integrators need to remove Noble as a CCTP route, and holders need to move or redeem their USDC.

For everyone else, the burn-limit reductions have started. December 1 is the last day V1 integrations work, and any app still on V1 after that will stop moving USDC between chains.

#5472. Amazon’s Ring tries again with a $250 flying home security drone and a $1,000 patrol robot

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 5:30 amNovember 10, 2026 at 5:42 am

Amazon’s Ring unveiled a $249.99 flying indoor security drone and a $999.99 mobile patrol robot for businesses, bringing back two ideas that stalled in earlier incarnations.

The Ring Drone Cam and Ring Rover Cam, announced Tuesday, are the first products under the Ring Robotics name, which the company calls “a new category of autonomous, mobile security.” Both devices use a system Ring calls AI Pilot to map a home or business, suggest spots worth checking, and find their own way around obstacles such as furniture and shelving.

The drone stays docked with its camera off until it’s sent out on a schedule, on demand, or automatically when another Ring device is triggered. The Rover patrols stores and offices, using a periscope camera to see over counters and shelving.

The Rover is available for preorder in the U.S. and is scheduled to ship Dec. 16. The Drone Cam is slated for Jan. 27, 2027, but Ring is only taking email sign-ups for now. The fine print notes that the drone hasn’t yet received the required authorization from the Federal Communications Commission.

Scheduled flights and patrols, and reviewing the Rover’s recorded video, require a Ring Protect subscription plan. Ring didn’t say which plans qualify.

Ring says customers wanted to see spots a fixed camera can’t reach, and rooms where they wouldn’t want one mounted.

“The honest answer wasn’t more cameras; it meant reimagining what a security device could be,” said Jamie Siminoff, Ring’s founder and chief inventor, in a statement. “That kind of invention is hard, and it takes time.”

Ring unveiled a flying indoor camera called the Always Home Cam in 2020, also priced at $249.99. The company later opened an invitation list, but the device never went on general sale.

The original drone flew only along paths that owners mapped out with it in advance. Ring says the new one builds a floor plan as the owner carries it through the house, suggests spots to check, and plans its own routes.

The Rover Cam traces back to Astro for Business, a rolling security robot that Amazon launched in November 2023 at a starting price of $2,350. Amazon discontinued it less than a year later, refunding customers and shutting the robots off.

Astro for Business was a spinoff of Amazon’s Astro home robot, an Alexa-powered device on wheels that debuted in 2021 and can patrol the house on its own.

Ring says the new robot was inspired by Astro customers who said roving security was their favorite feature. The Ring team “leveraged the best of Astro” to build it, the company says. Ring is pitching the Rover as “not a home robot that also does security, but a purpose-built security robot.”

The original Astro for the home remains an invite-only product. Amazon has redeployed much of the Astro team to work on a new home robot, CNBC reported Sunday. In March, Amazon acquired Fauna Robotics, a New York humanoid robot startup, saying it would become part of a new Personal Robotics Group. Ring’s announcement doesn’t mention either effort.

The Rover also extends Ring’s push into commercial security, following a $5,000 surveillance trailer for parking lots that it unveiled in January. In security robots, it competes with companies such as Knightscope, which rents its robots through a subscription, and Cobalt AI. At $999.99, the Rover costs less than half what Astro for Business did.

On the security drone front, Indoor Robotics makes a ceiling-docking drone that patrols offices and warehouses, but flying security cameras for the home remain rare.

Siminoff, who launched Ring’s predecessor, Doorbot, in 2012 and sold Ring to Amazon in 2018, left the company in 2023 and returned last year to lead Ring and Amazon’s related home security businesses. Last month, Ring unveiled its first smart lock, a $249 deadbolt with no keyhole and a dial that recharges a dead battery by hand.

In just a few weeks, AWS re:Invent brings advanced and expert-level sessions on the services you build on every day, from serverless and containers to databases and developer tools. Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.

#5471. From Palestine to Gibraltar, 10 cases of home games played elsewhere

Free daily briefing on global business news.

National teams playing home games abroad usually face war, travel limits or failed stadium checks, and these 10 cases from football and cricket show why

A home game is a line on a fixture list before it is a place on a map. The team named first usually wears its first-choice kit and uses the home dressing room. Nothing in that arrangement requires the match to be played inside the team's own borders. When a country cannot host, the fixture moves abroad and keeps its home label.

That gap between label and location explains why national teams playing home games abroad have become a recurring feature of international sport.

The decision rarely rests with the team alone. In football, FIFA and continental confederations such as UEFA set rules on where competitive internationals may be staged. Those rules cover security, stadium inspections and licensing. In cricket, a home board needs visiting teams willing to tour. Without them, it must find another venue.

Three causes recur across these cases. The first is war or a security threat serious enough that teams, officials and fans cannot be protected. The second is restricted movement, which can stop players from reaching a venue or crossing borders to train together. The third is infrastructure. A stadium can fail an inspection or lack the license a competition demands, even in a country at peace.

The 10 cases that follow are a selection, not a complete list. Nine come from international football and one from cricket. They cover Europe, the Middle East, North Africa, the Caribbean and Central and South Asia. Some relocations followed a single event, such as the 2009 attack on the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore. Others grew out of long-running conflict or security restrictions, as in Libya and Iraq. Gibraltar's case had nothing to do with security.

A relocated home match still counts as a home fixture in the competition's records. What changes is the setting. The team plays on a pitch abroad, and the size of its crowd depends on which supporters can travel or live nearby. Several hosts in this selection are neighbors, such as Jordan for Palestine, Tunisia for Libya and Tajikistan for Afghanistan. Others sit farther away, such as Malaysia for Syria and Hungary for Israel.

Taken together, the cases show a fixture list responding to events outside sport: conflict, restricted movement and stadium standards.

Palestine's national football team has repeatedly staged home fixtures outside Palestine because of movement and security restrictions. Jordan has hosted some of those matches at the Amman International Stadium.

The team also has a home venue inside the West Bank. The Faisal Al-Husseini International Stadium in Al-Ram has hosted Palestine home matches as well.

That gives Palestine two kinds of home ground. One sits in Palestinian territory. The other is in Amman, the Jordanian capital, on the far side of an international border.

A fixture at Al-Ram is a home game in both senses. The town lies in the West Bank. A match there is played on Palestinian soil.

A fixture in Amman is a home game on the schedule only. Palestine is still the named host. The stadium, however, is in another country.

The venue for a Palestine home match is therefore not settled by geography alone. Over the years, the team's home fixtures have been played both in the West Bank and in Jordan.

Movement restrictions bear on who can reach a ground. A home international needs players, coaching staff, match officials and the visiting team to arrive and leave on schedule. Security restrictions add a second test: whether the host can protect everyone inside the stadium. When those conditions cannot be met in the West Bank, Amman provides a stadium across the border.

Ukraine could not play competitive home matches on its own soil after Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022. In Euro 2024 qualifying, its home game against England was played in Wrocław, Poland. Its home game against Italy was played in Leverkusen, Germany.

The obstacle was security, not facilities. Ukraine had stadiums built to international standards, including Kyiv's Olimpiyskiy Stadium, which hosted the Euro 2012 final. Air-raid alerts and missile strikes ruled out staging a fixture with visiting players, officials and fans inside the country.

Wrocław sits in southwestern Poland, near the German and Czech borders. It was one of the host cities when Poland and Ukraine jointly staged Euro 2012. Its stadium was built for that tournament and already met UEFA standards.

Leverkusen is a city in the western German state of North Rhine-Westphalia. It is home to the Bundesliga club Bayer Leverkusen. The match against Italy was played at the BayArena, the club's ground. Germany was also the host of Euro 2024, the tournament Ukraine was trying to reach.

Ukraine did reach those finals, though not through its qualifying group. It advanced through the playoffs and then played its tournament matches in Germany.

The displacement extended beyond the national team. Ukrainian clubs could not host European ties at home either. Shakhtar Donetsk had already left Donetsk after fighting began in eastern Ukraine in 2014. After the full-scale invasion, it staged Champions League home matches in Warsaw and later in Hamburg.

Domestic football took a different route. The Ukrainian Premier League restarted in August 2022. Matches were played behind closed doors and halted when air-raid sirens sounded. That kept a league running inside the country while the national team relied on borrowed venues abroad.

The invasion also changed the fixture list for the other side of the conflict. FIFA and UEFA suspended Russia's national teams and clubs from their competitions in February 2022. Russia was left without competitive international fixtures, home or away.

Haiti played its home matches in 2026 World Cup qualifying in Curaçao rather than in Haiti. Gang violence at home ruled out hosting, and the Ergilio Hato Stadium in Willemstad served as the team's stand-in home ground.

The move took the national team away from its usual base. Haiti has traditionally played home internationals at the Stade Sylvio Cator in Port-au-Prince, the capital. Armed gangs have taken control of large parts of Port-au-Prince in recent years. The violence has displaced residents, shut businesses and forced repeated closures of the city's international airport.

The Ergilio Hato Stadium is Curaçao's national stadium and the home ground of Curaçao's own national team. It is named after Ergilio Hato, a goalkeeper from the island.

Curaçao is a small island in the southern Caribbean, off the coast of Venezuela. It is a constituent country within the Kingdom of the Netherlands, and Willemstad is its capital. Like Haiti, Curaçao belongs to CONCACAF, the confederation that governs football in North America, Central America and the Caribbean. CONCACAF organizes World Cup qualifying for the region.

The arrangement left Haiti without a guaranteed home crowd. Supporters based in Haiti had to leave the country to watch matches billed as Haiti home games.

The 2026 tournament is the first World Cup to feature 48 teams, up from 32. The U.S., Canada and Mexico co-host it, and all three qualify automatically. CONCACAF received six direct places, including the three hosts' automatic spots. The region also received two places in an intercontinental playoff. That expansion opened more routes to the finals for teams such as Haiti.

Haiti's only World Cup finals appearance before the 2026 cycle came in 1974, in West Germany. At that tournament, Emmanuel Sanon scored against Italy, ending goalkeeper Dino Zoff's long run of international minutes without conceding. Sanon also scored against Argentina, giving him both of Haiti's goals at the finals.

Syria played its home leg of the 2018 World Cup Asian qualifying playoff against Australia in Malaysia. The match was staged at the Hang Jebat Stadium in Malacca and finished 1-1.

Syria's civil war, which began in 2011, left the country unable to host international football. Its national team had to find venues abroad for competitive home matches. It also played its other home matches in that final qualifying round outside Syria.

The playoff was a two-legged tie between the third-placed teams from the two groups in Asia's final qualifying round. Australia finished third in one group. Syria finished third in the other, which also included Iran and South Korea. Away goals would break a tie on aggregate. The winner moved on to an intercontinental playoff for a place at the tournament in Russia.

Syria clinched third place on the final matchday. Omar Al Somah scored a late equalizer in a 2-2 draw away to Iran. The country had never qualified for a World Cup. The playoff left its team two rounds from a first appearance.

Malacca is a historic port city on Malaysia's west coast, southeast of Kuala Lumpur. The Hang Jebat Stadium takes its name from a warrior in Malay legend. Hosting there meant the Syrian squad traveled to Southeast Asia for a fixture listed as its own.

Robbie Kruse put Australia ahead in Malacca. Omar Kharbin equalized for Syria with a late penalty. The result left the tie level but gave Australia an away goal heading into the second leg in Sydney.

Australia won that match 2-1 after extra time. Tim Cahill scored both Australian goals. Al Somah gave Syria an early lead and later hit the post with a free kick in extra time. A goal there would have put Syria through on away goals.

Australia went on to beat Honduras in the intercontinental playoff and qualified for the 2018 World Cup. Syria's campaign ended in Sydney.

Libya's national football team has played home matches in neighboring Tunisia. Years of conflict left Libya without venues approved to stage international fixtures.

Those games keep their Libyan label. Libya is still listed as the home side, even with the match played across the border.

The conflict traces back to the 2011 uprising that ended Muammar Gaddafi's rule. Rival armed groups and competing administrations later fought for control of the country.

Venue approval decides where a competitive international can be played. A stadium must be cleared before it can host one. Libya's grounds lacked that clearance during the years of conflict. The national team needed a host abroad.

Tunisia lies along Libya's western border. Its stadiums gave the team a home base in North Africa.

The disruption reached beyond single fixtures. Libya had been chosen to host the 2017 Africa Cup of Nations. The tournament was moved because of the security situation. Gabon staged it instead.

The same conditions that sent individual matches to Tunisia also cost Libya a full continental tournament.

Afghanistan's national football team has played home matches in Dushanbe, the capital of Tajikistan. Security conditions inside Afghanistan kept the country from hosting those games.

The obstacle was security, not the condition of a stadium. A pitch that meets the regulations is only part of what a competitive international requires. Visiting players, referees and spectators must also be able to travel to the venue and stay there safely.

Dushanbe sits across the border from Afghanistan. Tajikistan shares a frontier with northern Afghanistan, and much of it follows the Panj River, one of the headwaters of the Amu Darya.

The Afghanistan Football Federation runs the national team. It belongs to FIFA and to the Asian Football Confederation. Those two bodies set the rules on where the team's competitive matches may be staged.

A match in Dushanbe still counts as an Afghanistan home fixture in the competition's records.

Pakistan's national cricket team played its home international series in the United Arab Emirates for years after gunmen attacked the Sri Lanka team bus in Lahore in March 2009. Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah became its main home venues.

The attack took place on March 3, 2009. The Sri Lankan squad was traveling to the Gaddafi Stadium for the third day of a Test match against Pakistan. Several Sri Lankan players were wounded. Pakistani police officers escorting the convoy were among those killed.

International sides stopped touring Pakistan after the shooting. Visiting boards declined to send teams, which left Pakistan with no opponents willing to play on its soil.

The fallout reached beyond bilateral tours. The International Cricket Council removed Pakistan as a co-host of the 2011 Cricket World Cup. The tournament went ahead in India, Sri Lanka and Bangladesh.

The UAE already had grounds built for international cricket. The International Cricket Council has had its headquarters in Dubai since 2005. The Emirates are also home to large South Asian expatriate communities, including many Pakistanis.

Each of the three venues has its own history. Sharjah Cricket Stadium staged one-day international tournaments from the 1980s and has hosted more one-day internationals than any other ground. Sheikh Zayed Cricket Stadium in Abu Dhabi opened in 2004. The Dubai International Cricket Stadium, in Dubai Sports City, opened in 2009.

The UAE was not Pakistan's only stand-in host. In 2010, Pakistan staged a two-Test home series against Australia in England. Lord's and Headingley hosted the two Tests.

Domestic cricket moved to the Gulf too. The Pakistan Super League, the country's professional Twenty20 competition, launched in 2016 with its first season played in the UAE.

Cricket relocations differ from football ones in a practical way. A cricket tour often runs for several weeks and can include Tests, one-day internationals and Twenty20 internationals. That means the stand-in country hosts an entire visiting tour, not a single match night.

Gibraltar played home qualifiers at the Estádio Algarve in Portugal because its own ground, the Victoria Stadium, did not meet UEFA's requirements for some competitive internationals. The move had nothing to do with war or security. It came down to whether a venue passed the governing body's standards.

Gibraltar is a British Overseas Territory on the southern tip of the Iberian Peninsula. It joined UEFA as a full member in 2013. That gave its national team a place in European qualifying competitions. Gibraltar later became a FIFA member in 2016, which opened World Cup qualifying as well. Membership did not come with a stadium ready for every fixture those competitions involve.

UEFA sets infrastructure rules for the venues used in its competitions. Its Stadium Infrastructure Regulations grade grounds into categories. The rules cover areas such as seating, floodlighting, media facilities and the playing surface. A ground that falls short of the required level cannot stage the matches those rules apply to. That holds even if it hosts regular domestic football.

The Victoria Stadium is Gibraltar's main football ground. It sits beside Gibraltar International Airport, on a territory where flat land is scarce. It also stages the territory's domestic league matches.

Portugal provided the alternative. The Estádio Algarve stands between the cities of Faro and Loulé in the country's southern Algarve region. It was built as a host venue for Euro 2004, the European Championship that Portugal staged that year. UEFA accepted it for Gibraltar's qualifiers, and the team played its home fixtures there.

The arrangement meant Gibraltar's supporters had to leave the territory to watch a home match. Spain is the only country that shares a land border with Gibraltar. Portugal does not border it at all. The overland route to the Algarve therefore crosses Spain before reaching the Portuguese border.

For Gibraltar, a home qualifier meant a trip through one country to play in another.

Israel played its home UEFA Nations League matches in Hungary in autumn 2024. The fixtures moved because UEFA matches could not be played safely in Israel during the conflict.

UEFA organizes the Nations League and sets the conditions for its matches. A national association cannot choose any venue it likes for a competitive fixture. The governing body has to accept that a site is safe for players, officials and spectators. When a country cannot meet that test, the match is staged elsewhere.

Israel belongs to UEFA, the governing body for European football, rather than to Asia's confederation. Its national team therefore enters UEFA competitions, including the Nations League. Hungary is also a UEFA member.

Moving the fixtures to Hungary kept them inside UEFA's own membership. The matches stayed under the same competition rules, at a venue that still had to meet UEFA's standards for the Nations League.

The Nations League is UEFA's competition for national teams. It is played during international windows outside the major tournaments. Group results decide standings, as well as promotion and relegation between leagues. A home game in the competition is a competitive fixture, not a friendly. It cannot be dropped from the schedule without affecting the group table.

The matches in Hungary kept their status as Israel's home fixtures in the group. The venue moved, but the fixture's designation did not. Israel's squad traveled to another country to play matches it was formally hosting. Its opponents also traveled to Hungary instead of making the trip to Israel.

The cause sets Israel's case apart from relocations driven by stadium standards or licensing rules. The condition of Israel's grounds was not the reason for the move. The question was whether UEFA matches could be held safely in the country at all during the conflict. A stadium upgrade could not settle that question. The answer depended on security conditions in the country, not on construction work or an inspection.

Iraq played its home football internationals outside the country for years. FIFA had restricted Iraq from hosting competitive internationals because of security conditions.

Those fixtures moved to other countries. Qatar, Jordan and Iran were among the places where Iraq lined up as the home side.

The restriction came from FIFA, football's world governing body, rather than from Iraq's own federation. It applied to competitive internationals, the matches that count toward qualification and tournament standings.

The grounds for the restriction were security conditions inside Iraq. That made the issue one of safety, not a decision Iraqi football officials could reverse on their own.

The hosts differed in their relationship to Iraq. Jordan and Iran share land borders with Iraq. Qatar has no border with Iraq and lies farther down the Persian Gulf.

The restrictions did not end in a single ruling. FIFA lifted them in stages.

#5470. How the UEFA Nations League works: promotion, relegation and Euro routes

Free daily briefing on global business news.

UEFA Nations League promotion and relegation decide where Europe's national teams play, and the results also open routes to the Euros and World Cup

The UEFA Nations League gives Europe's national teams a tiered competition in which results carry consequences. A strong campaign can lift a team into a higher league, and a weak one can drop it down. Results can also open a route to major tournaments.

UEFA's Executive Committee approved the competition in 2014, and the first edition was played in 2018-19. Teams are sorted into four tiers, League A through League D, according to UEFA rankings. League A holds the strongest national teams and League D the weakest. In the 2024-25 edition, Leagues A, B and C each had 16 teams, split into groups of four.

UEFA Nations League promotion and relegation follow from that tiered structure. A team that wins its group in League B or League C moves up a tier for the next edition. A team that finishes fourth in a League A or League B group drops down one tier. Third-placed teams in those two leagues face two-legged play-offs against runners-up from the tier below. A place in the higher league is at stake.

League A carries its own prize. Since the 2024-25 edition, the top two teams in each League A group have advanced to two-legged quarter-finals. The four winners then meet at a finals tournament in a single host country. Portugal, France and Spain have all lifted the trophy, and Portugal has won it twice.

The results also reach beyond the Nations League itself. For Euro 2024, play-offs gave Nations League group winners that missed out in the main qualifying groups a second route to the European Championship. Georgia, Ukraine and Poland all reached Euro 2024 that way. For the 2026 World Cup, four Nations League group winners that finished outside the top two of their qualifying groups received places in UEFA's play-offs.

The 10 slides below take each part of the format in turn. They cover why UEFA created the competition, how the leagues are seeded and how groups and knockout rounds work. They then explain how teams move between tiers and how the competition links to Euro and World Cup qualifying. The final slide lists every winner from 2019 to 2025.

UEFA created the Nations League to replace many low-stakes international friendlies with competitive matches between national teams of similar strength. UEFA's Executive Committee approved the competition in 2014, and the first edition was played in the 2018-19 season.

Before the competition began, friendlies filled many of the dates reserved for national-team football outside tournament qualifying. A friendly result earns no points, no trophy and no qualification place. Nothing carries over beyond the match itself.

That absence of consequence shaped how the games were used. Coaches could treat them as a chance to try fringe players or new tactics. Opponents could be picked for convenience rather than competitive balance. That sometimes left a strong side facing a much weaker one.

The Nations League takes over many of those calendar slots and attaches stakes to them. Each match feeds into a group table. Final positions carry consequences for the next edition of the competition. In some cases they also affect qualification for major tournaments.

Matching teams of similar strength is the other half of the design. UEFA does not throw every European national team into a single pool. It sorts them into tiers using its own rankings. A team therefore plays its group matches against opponents near its own level.

That structure changes what an international break offers at both ends of the scale. A smaller football nation gets competitive games it has a realistic chance of winning. A leading side gets regular meetings with other leading sides, with something riding on the result.

The Nations League did not end friendlies altogether. National teams still arrange them, particularly as warm-up matches before major tournaments.

It also did not replace the qualifying campaigns for the European Championship and the World Cup. Those campaigns continue, and the Nations League runs alongside them as a separate competition.

UEFA places each national team in the Nations League into one of four tiers — League A, League B, League C or League D — based on its UEFA ranking. League A contains the strongest sides, and League D contains the weakest.

The letters run from the top down. A team's letter reflects its standing among Europe's national sides at the start of an edition.

Ranking-based tiers put teams of similar strength in the same league. That follows UEFA's aim of matching national sides against opponents close to their own level.

The top three tiers were the same size in the 2024-25 edition. Leagues A, B and C each had 16 teams that season. That put 48 national sides in those three tiers combined.

League placement tells fans what level of opposition a side will meet. A team in League A plays other top-ranked nations. A team in League C or League D plays nations closer to its own standing, not the strongest sides on the continent.

The assignment is not permanent. Results in one edition decide which league a team enters for the next. The rankings set the starting order, and the matches reshape it over time.

Every team in Leagues A, B and C begins the Nations League in a group of four. Each side plays its three group opponents twice, once at home and once away, for six group matches in all.

The double round means no pairing is settled by one game at one team's ground. Each team hosts every opponent once and visits every opponent once. That gives every side an even split of three home matches and three away matches. Home advantage is therefore shared equally across the group.

A group of four contains six distinct pairings. With each pairing played twice, every group stages 12 matches.

Those 12 matches fit into six matchdays. On each matchday, all four teams in a group are in action across two games. No team sits out a round while its rivals play.

League A shows how those numbers scale. In the 2024-25 edition, League A was divided into four groups. Each League A team met three other League A sides home and away. Together, the four League A groups staged 48 matches.

Leagues B and C used the same layout in 2024-25, with four groups each. That made 12 groups across the top three leagues. Those 12 groups accounted for 144 group matches between them.

Because each league is a single tier, all three of a team's group opponents come from the same level of the competition. A League A side does not meet a League C side in the group stage.

Every team in a group finishes with the same number of games played. No side ends the group stage with a game in hand. The final standings compare teams on equal terms.

The final group table decides what happens next. A team's finishing position can send it forward, up or down, and the consequences differ by league.

League A teams compete for the UEFA Nations League title through a knockout bracket. Since the 2024-25 edition, the top two finishers in each League A group advance to two-legged quarter-finals. The four winners move on to a finals tournament hosted by one country.

League A is the top tier of the competition, and only its teams can win the title. Its four groups each send their top two forward, producing eight quarter-finalists. Those eight teams meet in four ties.

Each quarter-final is played over two legs. Every team plays once at home and once away. The aggregate score across both matches decides who advances. That gives each side a home fixture before the competition moves to one host nation.

The four quarter-final winners then travel to the Nations League Finals. This stage is a short tournament held in one country. It includes two semi-finals and a final, and the winner of the final takes the trophy.

The current bracket replaced a simpler route. Before 2024-25, only the four League A group winners qualified for the finals. There were no quarter-finals. Finishing second in a League A group therefore ended a team's chance of winning the title.

The change doubled the number of teams with a path to the trophy, from four to eight. A runner-up can now reach the finals without winning its group. A group winner no longer goes straight through. It has to win a two-legged tie first.

The format also lengthens the campaign for the strongest sides. On top of its group fixtures, a side that reaches the final plays four more matches: two quarter-final legs, a semi-final and the final itself.

Group position in League A therefore carries two kinds of stakes. The top two in each group chase the trophy through the knockout rounds. The bottom two play for their place in the top tier, through direct relegation or a play-off.

Group winners in League B and League C are promoted. Each one moves up a single tier for the next edition of the UEFA Nations League.

The step is always one league. A League B group winner joins League A, the top tier. A League C group winner joins League B.

No team can skip a tier. A side starting in League C needs to win its group in two consecutive editions to reach League A. The first group win lifts it to League B. The second lifts it to the top tier.

Only first place brings automatic promotion. A runner-up in either league does not go up directly, and neither does a third-placed team.

League B and League C each contained four groups in the 2024-25 edition. That meant four teams earned direct promotion from League B and four from League C, eight in all.

The reward is a higher level of opposition. A side promoted from League B spends its next campaign in League A, against the highest-ranked national teams in the competition. A side promoted from League C moves into the tier directly below League A.

Promotion to League A also changes what a team can win. Only League A teams can reach the quarter-finals and the finals tournament. A side that climbs out of League B becomes eligible for the trophy in its first season in the top tier.

The system means a team's league is not set by its ranking alone. Group results in one edition decide where it plays in the next.

The team that finishes fourth in each League A group drops straight to League B for the next edition. The same rule applies one level down: fourth place in a League B group means automatic relegation to League C.

Fourth place is the bottom of the group. In the 2024-25 edition, every group in Leagues A and B had four teams. Each side played the other three home and away, for six matches. A team that finishes last after those matches does not enter the promotion and relegation play-offs. Its move to the lower tier is settled once the group stage ends.

League A had four groups in 2024-25. That meant four League A teams went down directly. League B also had four groups, which sent four more teams from League B to League C. Across the top two tiers, direct relegation covered eight teams in that edition.

Relegation from League A carries a specific cost. League A holds the strongest national teams under UEFA's ranking-based placement. It is also the only tier that plays for the Nations League title. A team that drops to League B has no route to the quarter-finals or the finals tournament in the following edition. It must first win promotion back before it can contest the trophy again.

Relegation from League B to League C is a drop to the third of four tiers. The relegated team then plays opponents from a lower tier in its next campaign.

Relegation does not have to last long. A relegated team that wins its group in the lower league is promoted for the next edition. That means a side can return to its old tier after a single campaign.

Direct relegation applies only to fourth place. Third-placed teams in Leagues A and B are not relegated automatically. They play two-legged play-offs against runners-up from the tier below. The winner of each tie takes the place in the higher league.

The Nations League settles some movement between its top three tiers through play-offs. Third-placed teams in League A face League B runners-up, and third-placed teams in League B face League C runners-up. Each tie runs over two legs, with a place in the higher league at stake.

These ties sit between the automatic outcomes. Group winners in League B and League C move up without extra matches. Fourth-placed teams in League A and League B go straight down. The teams in between get either a last chance to stay up or an extra route to climb.

For a League A side, finishing third means it has to defend its place. If it wins the tie, it stays in League A for the next edition. If it loses, the League B runner-up takes its spot, and the League A team drops a level.

The same structure applies one tier lower. A League B team that finishes third must beat a League C runner-up to remain in League B. If the League C side wins instead, it is promoted, and the League B team moves down.

League B is the only tier involved in both sets of ties. Its runners-up play upward against League A opposition. Its third-placed teams play downward against League C opposition. As a result, no finishing position in a League B group keeps a team in League B automatically. The winner moves up, the fourth-placed side drops, and the two teams in between go into play-offs.

League A is arranged differently at the top. In the current format, its first- and second-placed teams advance to the quarter-finals. Their place in the top tier is not in question. Only the bottom two in each League A group face any risk of dropping.

A League C runner-up has two ways to reach League B. It can win its group outright, or it can finish second and then beat a League B side over two legs.

The two-legged format gives each team one home match and one away match. The outcome depends on the combined result across both games, not on a single match.

Nations League results give national teams a second path to the European Championship. A team that misses out through the main qualifying groups can still reach the tournament through play-offs filled on the basis of Nations League performance.

Group winners get first claim on those play-off places. When a group winner has already qualified through its group, its place passes to another team based on Nations League results.

The main qualifying groups remain the primary way into the European Championship. The play-offs come into play only for teams that miss out there. A team's Nations League campaign decides whether it gets that second chance.

For Euro 2024, which Germany hosted, the 2022-23 Nations League set the play-off field. Twelve teams entered three separate paths. Each path had one-off semi-finals and a final, and each path winner took one of the tournament's 24 places.

Georgia beat Greece on penalties in its path final in Tbilisi after a 0-0 draw. That result sent Georgia to its first major tournament. Both teams had reached the play-offs as League C group winners.

Ukraine won another path final, beating Iceland 2-1 in Wroclaw, Poland. Ukraine played that home tie in Poland because of Russia's invasion.

Poland beat Wales on penalties in Cardiff after a 0-0 draw to take the third place. Each of the three winners reached Euro 2024 after falling short in the main qualifying competition.

Two of the three deciding matches — Georgia against Greece and Poland against Wales — went to penalty shootouts. In both, a full European Championship place rested on a single shootout.

The route also changes what a poor qualifying campaign means for a team. Finishing outside the automatic places in a qualifying group does not end a team's Euro bid if its Nations League results earned a play-off spot. The two competitions run as separate tracks. A strong result in one can make up for a weak result in the other.

Nations League results carried over into qualifying for the 2026 World Cup. Four Nations League group winners that did not finish in the top two of their World Cup qualifying groups received places in UEFA's play-offs.

The rule gave those teams a fallback after their main qualifying campaigns fell short. A finish below second place in a qualifying group would otherwise have ended their chances. A Nations League group title kept them in contention instead.

The route depended on how a team's qualifying group ended. Teams that finished in the top two of their qualifying groups did not use it. A Nations League group title mattered most to teams whose qualifying campaigns went poorly.

The 2026 World Cup is co-hosted by the U.S., Canada and Mexico. It is the first edition with 48 teams, up from 32 at the 2022 tournament in Qatar. UEFA's share of that field is 16 places.

The link gave Nations League matches weight beyond the competition's own standings. A single group game could shape a team's chances of reaching a World Cup. That stake sat alongside the promotion and relegation consequences of the same result.

A play-off place does not guarantee a spot at the finals. Teams that enter through the Nations League must still come through the play-offs to qualify.

The World Cup rule mirrors the route UEFA already offered for European Championship qualifying. In both cases, Nations League form serves as a safety net when main qualifying falls short.

Portugal has won the UEFA Nations League twice, in 2019 and 2025. France and Spain have each won it once, and Spain has played in more finals than any other country.

Portugal took the first title in 2019 with a 1-0 win over the Netherlands in Porto. The first champion won the trophy in one of its own cities.

France claimed the 2021 title. It beat Spain 2-1 in a final played in the Italian city of Milan.

Spain won in 2023 after its final against Croatia in Rotterdam went to penalties. That title came two years after Spain lost the 2021 final to France.

Portugal added its second title in 2025. The final against Spain in Munich finished 2-2, and Portugal won the shootout. No other country has won the Nations League more than once.

Spain has played in three of the four finals, in 2021, 2023 and 2025. It won one and lost two, to France and then Portugal. That makes Spain the only country to lose more than one Nations League final.

The Netherlands and Croatia have each reached one final and lost it. The Netherlands fell to Portugal in 2019. Croatia lost to Spain in 2023.

Penalties settled two of the four finals: Spain against Croatia in 2023 and Portugal against Spain in 2025. The other two were decided by a single goal. Portugal won 1-0 in 2019, and France won 2-1 in 2021.

Each final so far has been played in a different country. The hosts run from Portugal in 2019 to Italy in 2021, the Netherlands in 2023 and Germany in 2025. Portugal is the only host nation to win the final on home soil.

Every champion has come from League A. It is the only tier whose teams can reach the finals tournament.

#5469. PitchBook to give early-stage startups free access, using their data to feed a new tool for VCs

by Todd Bishop on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:23 amNovember 10, 2026 at 7:25 am

PitchBook announced a new program to give early-stage startups free use of its private-market data, if they share their financials and other company details.

The Seattle-based company says the new program, dubbed PitchBook for Startups, will feed PitchBook Origin, a new deal-sourcing product that helps venture capitalists and other investors find startups before they raise their first institutional round.

PitchBook announced both offerings Tuesday morning at Web Summit in Lisbon. Owned by Morningstar since 2016, the company has more than 3,000 employees and sells subscriptions to venture firms, private equity investors and dealmakers.

The launches come as first-time startup financings hit a record. There were an estimated 8,625 such deals in the U.S. through the third quarter, already more than the 8,507 in all of 2021, according to the PitchBook-NVCA Venture Monitor. PitchBook attributes part of the surge to AI, which it says is making it easier to start companies.

The startup program is open to pre-seed and bootstrapped companies that haven’t taken money from a venture firm or other institutional investor, or raised a priced round, the type of funding round that sets a valuation.

Founders can use PitchBook to find investors who are active in their sector and stage, and to compare their valuation and growth against similar companies.

To keep their free access, startups must update their company information every quarter. PitchBook says that information can include financials, team growth and product milestones. Only “select portions” of that data will go into Origin, the company said, without saying which.

Origin covers about 25 million companies, including stealth, pre-funding and bootstrapped companies. About 15 million of them are new to PitchBook. It scores companies on how well they match an investor’s criteria and sends alerts when they show new activity.

“What’s been missing is visibility into the stage before a company raises, when the most important signals are the hardest to see,” said Paul Santarelli, PitchBook’s chief solutions officer, in a statement announcing the products.

PitchBook didn’t disclose pricing for Origin, and the product’s web page currently asks investors to join a waitlist.

Go hands-on with new launches the same week they’re announced, and hear directly from the engineers who built them. Experience the depth you won’t find anywhere else.
