#5467. This Ford sculptor has carved cars out of clay for 40 years. AI and VR just cut his work time in half

John “Rex” Allen is 68, wears cowboy boots, a black baseball cap, and he’s spent four decades building life-size cars out of clay. These days he builds inside a virtual-reality headset, too.

He does his work upstairs at Ford Motor Company’s gleaming new headquarters in Dearborn, Michigan, where the bird sounds in the yard aren’t even real. Just over four miles away, the 109-year-old Rouge Plant looks much the way it did in the 1920s, except with 3D-printed parts patching the factory together and a “Green Roof” overhead that is one of the world’s largest.

The new Ford World HQ opened in November 2025 as a 21st-century expression of the Ford Rouge logic, according to Ford Land CEO Jim Dobleske. World HQ stacks modern teams vertically the way Henry Ford stacked steel and assembly at the Rouge. It used to take 30 minutes to move a car from one end of the old design center to the other; now it takes “just over three minutes.” The birdsong in the courtyard is piped in, predator calls included, to keep Michigan’s ever-present geese away from workers wolfing down their lunches. “Those are not real birds,” Dobleske said, “that’s all fake.”

Fortune visited Ford in 1947 to document the “rebirth” of the company, when founder Henry Ford died and his grandson, Henry Ford II, was leading the postwar modernization of the iconic American manufacturer. Nearly eight decades later, Detroit as a whole is 13 years on from its historic bankruptcy process, but General Motors was the only member of the “Big Three” auto firms to post a net profit in 2025.

All three OEMs, or original equipment manufacturers, announced major pullbacks in their electric-vehicle strategies in 2025 as the federal government scrapped subsidies, prompting Ford CEO Jim Farley to (accurately) predict that the EV market would be cut in half as a result. In December, Ford announced about $19.5 billion in charges and pivoted to another rebirth: a race against the calendar.

Upstairs at Ford World HQ, Allen is looking at his clay cars, his monitors, his plastic models and his virtual reality glasses.

The Ford modeling studio is massive, with ceilings 25 to 30 feet high and a wide-open, blank space that feels like an empty Hollywood studio, awaiting a Gilmore Girls set or a replica of the Titanic.

Allen, with his thin white mustache complementing his mane of white hair, is doing what he’s always done: building cars out of clay.

Like most Michiganders who still work in auto manufacturing, Allen has an unimpressed air about his remarkable, unusual career. Asked how he joined the ranks of elite auto sculptors, he explains that he felt forced into it by fear of automation. “I used to be a machinist, and then it started becoming robotic, so I got out of that business real quick.” He reasoned that he’d always been a “bit of an artist,” and in high school loved comic books and cars and ran a side hustle airbrushing the “Rat Fink” mascot and other Kustom Kulture motifs onto T-shirts for other kids. Sort of a Mickey Mouse by way of R. Crumb, Rat Fink was a neon-green rodent mascot that exemplified the proto-punk vibes of Southern California car culture of the 1960s, but Allen said his tastes also ran a bit less gonzo — he used to carve Disney characters out of wood and clay for extra credit in art class, along with watercolors and oil paintings for extra credit in art class. “I made good money in high school,” Allen shrugs. “I loved doing that stuff.”

He didn’t set out to become a clay-man, either. “Somebody told me they created cars out of clay,” he explains, “which I had no idea of, so he introduced me to a guy that owned a business. And I mean, I fell right into it.” Allen recalled that he “tried it once” and the results spoke for themselves. He was 26 and soon found himself working 100 hours a week, pulling down roughly $100,000 a year.

Allen wasn’t in-house at Ford, then. At that time, Detroit had a dense web of small model shops that handled overflow work for the Big 3 — Ford, General Motors and Chrysler (now Stellantis), along with their suppliers — and Allen worked at a half-dozen of them. Work was steady. “You could grab a job any day of the week in one of these places,” he said, recalling that he worked on the original concept for the Dodge Viper at a Chrysler satellite studio. He’s now been at Ford for 24 years.

So, why clay? Allen and his colleagues, Nic Navarro, Shawn Fairall and Michael Smith, explained that it’s been that way for nearly a century. “Having the physical property in front of you to have the conversation with multiple people has always been a key part of the process,” Fairall said. “There’s always kind of this general misconception that computers have taken over car design,” Fairall said. “Clay has never really gone away.”

Smith, who leads research and development for Ford’s design team, always describes it to interns the same way. “We don’t sell pretty pictures of cars,” he said. “We sell vehicles.” He said a director might look at the clay and say, “you need to pull this back three more inches.”

It used to take about two weeks for one modeler to sculpt one full-size model, Allen said, and every change meant more weeks of work to do by hand. About six years ago, that changed with virtual reality and 3D printing. Now Allen can knock out a design’s theme in five days.

Allen said he’s seen a lot of upgrades in 40-odd years. First came “sweeps,” templates that modelers could drag along a car’s side. “That was a wow factor there for a while,” Allen said. Then came machines that could map the body, cut pieces out of it, and eventually shape an entire side. Now the team can rough out a car in clay, scan it in about 20 minutes, put on a headset to refine the shape digitally, and have a mill carve out the new surface over a few shifts, then continue working the surface by hand for the finishing touches. They call it hybrid sculpting. “This one is leaps and bounds,” Allen said, “further than anything we’ve ever done.”

“Because of technology, we’ve reduced the people over the years, so there’s less and less of us,” Allen said, adding, “we still have the same amount of work.” He said he thought this “virtual reality way of working would help keep us employed, basically, and it seems like it has, because we’re able to flip more designs now because of it.”

Those saved weeks matter because of what Ford is trying to pull off.

So what is the shape of the new Ford being born? The answer is in four parts. Ford sold about 650,000 fewer vehicles in the U.S. than GM last year, yet brought in slightly more revenue: $187.3 billion to $185 billion. The difference is mainly Ford Pro, the commercial arm that sells trucks and vans to businesses and governments earned $6.8 billion before interest and taxes in 2025 at a 10.3% margin. That’s more than double the earnings of Ford Blue, the gas and hybrid business, which made $3 billion, while the EV unit called Model e, lost $4.8 billion.

Kumar Galhotra, Ford’s chief operating officer, explained to Fortune how Ford’s next plan for Model e started with a skunkworks operation in California. “We tore down multiple Chinese OEM vehicles,” he said. “It was clear that because of the labor advantage and certain subsidies and battery areas, that their batteries are cheaper than ours.” So the team stopped trying to win on battery cost and designed around a smaller battery instead, with cleverer aerodynamics, fewer frictional losses and more efficient motors. “In the end, we’re pretty much equal in total system cost,” he said of Ford’s projection against China’s BYD, calling it “first principles thinking.”

The first vehicle on Ford’s new Universal EV platform is the Fathom, a $28,350 midsize electric pickup due in 2027. Ford says it will be able to send more than 10 kilowatts into a house during a blackout without the expensive wall-mounted inverter the F-150 Lightning needed. Asked how Ford makes money on that, a spokesperson said: “We see it as a compelling reason to buy Fathom.”

The rebirth includes a brand new business, Ford Energy, built to get a return on the billions Ford has sunk into batteries. By around March of 2025, veteran executive Lisa Drake could see that her battery plants just “weren’t full,” but Ford had already licensed lithium-iron-phosphate cells from China’s CATL and was building batteries in Marshall, Michigan. The same chemistry turned out to be close to ideal for energy storage for utilities and power developers racing to meet demand from data centers and an aging grid. “We actually were very fortunate,” Drake told Fortune. “I had a license for the best tech on the planet and the right tech for storage.”

In December, the board gave her $2 billion to start Ford Energy and she is retooling a Kentucky plant that used to make F-150 Lightning batteries, reusing about 30% to 40% of the equipment, with production set to begin in late 2027. The target customers are utilities, renewable energy developers and even data centers and hyperscalers, which don’t buy batteries directly but need power.

It’s part of Ford’s giant race against the calendar — Galhotra said Ford will end up “refreshing about 80% of our North American portfolio” between 2027 and 2029. And that’s where Rex Allen comes in. Every week saved in the clay studio will get to that refresh quicker.

Allen isn’t the only unlikely face of innovation at Ford. Over the river in Dearborn, another wears a giant Luigi-shaped mustache. His name is Greg Foresi.

The Ford Rouge Plant shows its age in a good way — a living museum, the first fully integrated auto factory in the world, still turning out cars in minutes through a century-old assembly line. And walking around, like a friendly engineer beat cop, is Foresi, the 3D-printing guy.

Foresi, who wears the horn-rimmed glasses of a Buddy Holly or a young Elvis Costello, got his signature look when he shaved off his eight-inch beard to play Luigi to a friend’s Mario one Halloween. When “mustache guy” shows up, he takes random requests from nearly everyone on the factory floor. That’s because he manages the 3D-printing lab, where roughly a dozen machines whirr away, steadily adding to nearly 300 tools and components in Foresi’s database, including about 50 individual socket covers.

“I’m out on the floor all day talking to people, trialing tools, evaluating equipment,” said the 35-year-old Foresi. Sometimes he gets five requests in one day, and sometimes nothing for five days. Foresi and his team point me toward a factory-floor wheel that isn’t black like the other ones, but a bright royal blue. This is a specialized part that filled a gap in availability during a supply-chain disruption. When Foresi saw the shortage coming, he printed his own.

Foresi explained that they didn’t have time to test the part. The choice was either trying the blue wheel and potentially creating a line stoppage — or not trying and definitely creating a stoppage. Some versions of the wheel failed, but Foresi said iterative improvements were made. “We avoided the problem entirely,” he said. Galhotra explained that Ford makes a new F-150 every 54 seconds at the plant, making Foresi’s blue wheel a hugely important component, but also not inherently scalable.

“One of the most radical things about 3D printing is that it decentralizes your logistics,” Foresi said. Galhotra put the limits plainly, saying that right now it’s “good for patches here and there,” like when a part is back-ordered or only can be flown in from somewhere else. Foresi agrees: “It’s not remotely close to replacing our conventional supply chain,” he said, adding that he gets “crazy requests” he has to turn down constantly. Some people think 3D printing is a joke, and other people “think that you can just 3D-print anything.”

Foresi had his own doubts at first. After stints at a supplier and a Ford stamping plant in Kansas City, he landed at the Dearborn truck plant as the only mechanical engineer in the final assembly department — ”a pretty intense job,” he said. “I’ve seen everything in the plant break and fixed everything,” Foresi said, recalling a line of people always waiting outside his cubicle. So when his talent was recognized as a fit for 3D printing (his “boss’ boss asked,” he said), his first instinct, like Allen’s, was fear for his job. His first instinct was that the job wouldn’t last, that 3D printing would lose favor and he’d be moved to a new role.

“I was worried that it was just a fad with the company and that it would lose energy and I would get laid off or something,” Foresi said. “They were like, ‘Too bad, you’re doing it anyway.’” Foresi hastened to add that he never felt pushed into taking the job or truly feared that he would be laid off; but he did think he might get reassigned. “After two or three months it became clear both to management and myself that printing was becoming so useful that a full-time position was needed.”

Mike Aragon and Alicia Boler Davis are both newcomers to Ford’s C-suite. The two Amazon veterans said have grown close, Aragon said, as their teams depend on each other and they bond over similar big-tech career transitions. Aragon recalls showing up for a leadership meeting five minutes late and CEO Jim Farley turning to him and saying, “Hey Mike, I want you to take on this AI initiative.” Boler Davis, a Detroiter who spent nearly 25 years working at GM before seven years out of manufacturing, said her return was like “drinking out of a firehose” and that she’s still “relearning the language, learning the culture.”

Boler Davis described the services and efficiencies that come from her use of smart data connected to a nationwide fleet and said she’s working toward a Ford Pro that can predict when a car will need a repair, or provide AI-enhanced advice to customers. As president of Ford Integrated Services, Aragon leads the teams that develop and scale digital products. “This is another reinvention on top of the reinvention that we already had to do,” he told Fortune.

At the Ford Accelerate event in Detroit in late September, Farley described to Fortune during a media briefing how Ford Pro actually uses AI to help dealership technicians, citing the example of an engine removal from a Ford Super Duty truck. “It’s like a two-day job” to take apart a Super Duty, he said, and AI is invaluable in walking customers through the process. “We are using AI for them to say, ‘Okay, do this, do that,’” he said. “They’re good mechanics, they just don’t know. They’ve never done it before.”

Galhotra was more measured about how far Ford has to go. There’s the AI that software companies talk about, on the one hand, and then “AI that’s going to change factories of how we build physical things, and in that second category, I haven’t seen really good execution yet. And even ourselves, we’re at the beginning of that journey.”

Boler Davis said some of Ford Pro’s fleet customers have pushed back. “We have some customers that, you know, don’t want you monitoring the vehicle or connected or don’t want to use the AI,” she said. Stressing that the cost of downtime can be hundreds, even thousands of dollars per vehicle on a given day, she said Ford Pro wants to empower fleet managers to help unlock the potential for their business. The tool isn’t to “get rid of the fleet manager,” she said, but to “make their job easier.”

Part of Ford’s pull for Aragon is personal. He said he remembers being driven to school in his grandfather’s 1963 F-100 truck. “I just remember the smell, which is like the smell of the nylon, and the dust — and then the Camels [cigarettes].” He said he’s planning to rebuild a model from the early ‘70s, which he’s planning to drive to work every day.

He’s not the only one at Ford with a project in the garage. Fairall restores old Volkswagens — he’s finished an ‘84 Westfalia Bus and is working on a ‘65 Split Window Bus. Allen is building his own car on the side, and he’s 3D-printing its front end. Asked whose intellectual property that makes it, Allen immediately responds, “It’s my car. “

Allen once feared the future enough to steer his son away from clay, though. Years ago, he brought his son, Derek, into a satellite studio and paid Derek to work six hours a day for him. “He started heading down this path,” Allen said, “he was getting pretty good at it. But I wanted him to be much more than just a modeler because I was worried about where modeling was going.” He steered him into engineering instead. “I always thought virtual reality would be there, but not in my lifetime,” he said. “I didn’t think I’d be part of it exactly.”

Allen says he thought he was ready to retire eight years ago, but now he’s excited to train the next generation of modelers in both virtual reality and clay. “I’m very excited about this whole chapter in my life,” he said. “I hop out of bed in the morning so I can come to work.”

Nick Lichtenberg is business editor and was formerly Fortune's executive editor of global news.

#5466. Allen Family Philanthropies gives $10M to hundreds of small arts groups across Washington state

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 10, 2026 at 7:30 amNovember 9, 2026 at 2:56 pm

Allen Family Philanthropies and Seattle nonprofit ArtsFund awarded $10 million to 745 small arts and culture organizations across Washington state, and renewed the grant program for another $10 million next year.

The latest Community Accelerator Grant awards range from $2,500 to $25,000 and reach organizations in 37 of the state’s 39 counties. The 2027 renewal brings the program’s total to $50 million over five years.

For 2026, the program focused on groups with annual budgets under $1 million, which raised the average award by about 25%, from $10,753 last year to $13,423.

The change followed a sector analysis by Allen Family Philanthropies and SMU DataArts. It found that smaller arts groups lost an average of one staff position between 2023 and 2024, while organizations with budgets over $1 million added an average of five.

“The incredible reach of this program across our state, along with the significant findings from our report, show just how much this type of flexible support is needed to bolster Washington’s rich and diverse arts and culture sector,” said Lara Littlefield, executive director of Allen Family Philanthropies.

Of this year’s grantees, 496 are in Northwest Washington, 132 in Southwest, 67 in Eastern and 50 in Central Washington. Recipients include 12 of the state’s 29 federally recognized tribes, and more than 22% are in rural counties.

A handful of the organizations blend art and technology, including Tacoma’s Fablab Nonprofit ($25,000), Seattle-based Simulated Immersive Experimental Realities ($15,000) and Bellingham Makerspace ($2,500).

The Old Hotel Art Gallery in Othello, in Adams County, has received a $25,000 grant each year since 2024. The gallery used the money to pay staff a living wage, to keep operating until its annual fundraiser, and to renovate its historic building, which now brings in rental income.

Gallery director Samantha Copas said the 2025 award “truly kept our doors open.”

Allen Family Philanthropies, formerly known as the Paul G. Allen Family Foundation, was founded in 1988 by the late Microsoft co-founder and his sister, Jody Allen. Arts and culture is one of its core program areas, along with youth and the environment. Last year the foundation committed nearly $7 million to eight Seattle Center nonprofits, including KEXP and the Museum of Pop Culture, to expand youth access to the arts.

ArtsFund will hold a virtual webinar in the spring for organizations interested in applying for 2027 grants. Details will be posted here.

#5465. The NFL injury report explained: what questionable, doubtful and out mean

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The NFL injury report explained, from questionable, doubtful and out designations to practice participation, the Friday report and game-day inactives, and why the labels matter

The NFL injury report is a league-mandated public disclosure. Every team must file one for each regular-season game. The result is that everyone sees the same official information at the same time. It shows which players are hurt, what is wrong with them and whether they are expected to take the field.

Opposing coaches read it while preparing for a game. Fantasy football managers read it to set lineups. Bettors read it before placing wagers. Reporters read it to explain why a starter is missing. Each group works from the identical official list.

The report has a simple structure. Each entry names a player, the body part or illness involved and how much he took part in practice that day. Teams submit the report to the league, and the league makes it public. Later in the week, the report adds a game status for players whose availability is in question.

The game statuses each carry a specific meaning, and they are not interchangeable. Questionable signals uncertainty. Doubtful signals that a player is unlikely to play. Out means the player will not play in that game. A fourth label, probable, once sat at the top of the scale, but the league dropped it starting with the 2016 season.

The labels do not tell the whole story on their own. Practice participation — full, limited or did not participate — adds context that a game status alone does not provide. Timing matters too. For a typical Sunday game, teams release reports on Wednesday, Thursday and Friday. Only the Friday report carries game designations. The final answer arrives on game day, when teams submit their inactive lists about 90 minutes before kickoff.

Injured reserve sits outside this weekly system. It is a roster move, not a game status, and it works under its own set of rules.

The 10 slides below walk through each piece of the system. They cover who files the report, what each label means and how the weekly schedule unfolds. They also explain where injured reserve fits and why the league requires accurate information. Read together, they explain how a single injury listing moves from a Wednesday practice note to a game-day decision.

The NFL injury report is a required public disclosure that every team must file for each of its regular-season games. It names the players who are hurt or ill, identifies the body part or illness involved and records how much each player took part in practice.

The requirement covers every club in the league. No team is exempt. The obligation attaches to each game on the regular-season schedule rather than to the season as a whole. A team therefore produces a new report for every matchup it plays.

Both clubs in a game carry the same duty. Each matchup therefore produces two reports, one from each side, covering the players on each roster who are dealing with a problem that week.

Each entry links a named player to a specific problem. An injury is listed by the part of the body affected, such as a knee, an ankle or a hamstring. A player who is sick rather than hurt is listed with an illness instead.

Listing by body part keeps each entry brief. It also means an entry does not reveal a diagnosis or its severity. A knee listing alone does not show whether the problem is minor or serious.

The second core element is practice participation. Alongside the injury itself, the report shows how fully each listed player practiced. That pairing gives readers two separate pieces of information about a player's condition in the same entry.

Teams do not publish the report through their own channels. Each club submits it to the league, and the league then makes it public. The information reaches fans, media and opposing teams through a single official route.

The report is a statement about players, not about the whole roster. A player who is healthy and practicing normally does not need to appear on it at all. Appearing on the report does not mean a player will miss time.

Practice participation is the part of the NFL injury report that records how much work each listed player did on a given day. Teams describe it with one of three labels: full participation, limited participation or did not participate.

These labels describe what happened at practice. They do not say whether a player will suit up for the game. Game-status designations sit in a separate part of the report and serve a different purpose.

Full participation means the player took full part in practice. It is the strongest signal of health this section offers. A player can still appear on the report with a full listing because the injury itself remains on file.

Limited participation means the player practiced, but not fully. The label covers a wide range of workloads. It does not show which drills a player sat out or how much of the session he missed. Two players with the same limited listing may have done very different amounts of work.

Did not participate means the player stayed out of practice that day. The label on its own does not explain why. The body part or illness listed beside the player's name usually supplies that context.

Some absences have nothing to do with health. Teams can mark an entry as not injury related. A rest day or a personal matter falls into this group. A did-not-participate entry marked this way says little about a player's physical condition.

Teams do not always hold a real practice. When no real practice takes place, the report lists estimated participation instead. In that case, the team reports the level of work it expects each player would have managed in a normal session.

An estimate is a judgment, not a record of work done. A limited listing on an estimated report reflects the team's assessment rather than a session that actually happened. That distinction matters when a reader compares one day's entry with another's.

Questionable is the NFL injury report's label for a player whose availability for the upcoming game is uncertain. It does not predict that the player will sit or play. It signals only that the team has not ruled him in or out when the report is filed.

Older versions of the report attached a percentage to each game-status label. The league no longer does that. Questionable now carries no official numerical chance of playing. Any figure attached to it today is an outside estimate, not league policy.

Without a number, questionable covers a wide range of situations. A player managing a minor problem and a player facing a real chance of missing the game can carry the same label. The designation itself does not distinguish between them.

Players working through the league's concussion protocol can carry the questionable tag late in the week. A player in the protocol cannot return until both the team physician and an independent neurological consultant clear him. That clearance can come after the team files its final weekly report.

Practice participation helps narrow the picture. A questionable player who closed the week with full participation presents a different case from one who did not practice on any day. A player who moved from did not participate to limited also shows a different trend from one who stayed limited all week.

The designation reflects the team's view when the last report of the week is filed. A player's condition can still change before kickoff. Teams can downgrade a questionable player to out after that report. A downgrade means he will not play.

The inactive list settles the matter on game day. A questionable player left off that list is available to suit up. One who appears on it will not play, whatever the earlier report said.

For fantasy managers and bettors, questionable marks an open question rather than a final verdict. The practice record, any late downgrade and the inactive list together carry more information than the label alone.

Doubtful means a player is unlikely to play in the upcoming game. On the NFL's game-status scale, it sits between questionable, which signals genuine uncertainty, and out, which means the player will not suit up.

The label shows which way a team is leaning. A questionable player could go either way. A doubtful player carries a clear lean toward missing the game, but the team has not ruled him out.

Doubtful is not a final decision. The team keeps the option of playing him. He stays on the roster and can still be named active on game day. The definitive answer comes with the inactive list the team submits shortly before kickoff.

A team can also settle the question earlier. If it decides before game day that the player will not play, it can downgrade him from doubtful to out. That change tells everyone the absence is confirmed.

Doubtful appears only on the week's final injury report, the one that carries game designations. Earlier reports in the week list a player's injury and practice work but no game status. A player can therefore be on the report all week and pick up the doubtful tag only at the end.

Doubtful is a game-status designation, not a practice label. Reading it next to the player's practice entries gives a fuller picture. A doubtful player who sat out every session that week presents a different case from one who was limited late in the week. A late-week limited session shows the player was back on the field in some capacity.

The designation applies to one specific game. A player listed as doubtful this week starts fresh on the next week's report, where he may carry a different label or none at all.

Like the other game designations, doubtful can be attached to an illness as well as an injury.

For anyone planning around the game, the label works as an early signal of a likely absence. A doubtful listing is the team's public notice that it does not expect the player on the field.

An out designation means the player will not play in that game. It is the most definitive game-status label on the NFL injury report. It leaves no room for a late decision.

Questionable and doubtful both describe a degree of uncertainty. Out removes it. Once a team lists a player as out, his availability for that game is settled.

The label covers one game at a time. On its own, it does not say how serious an injury is or how long recovery will take. A player can be ruled out with a minor strain one week and practice fully the next. Another player can carry the same label for several straight games while a longer injury heals.

Each new game brings a new report. The status does not carry over automatically. A player listed out this week has his availability assessed again for the next game.

The entry also shows why the player is out. The report names the body part or illness involved, such as a knee, a hamstring or a concussion. Readers see the status and its cause on the same line.

Practice participation sits alongside the designation. The report records whether a player practiced fully, in a limited way or not at all during the week. Those entries describe how the week went. The out designation records the outcome for the game.

Out does not change a player's roster status. He stays on the team's roster even though he will not play. That separates the label from roster transactions, which move a player into a different category altogether.

The certainty matters on both sidelines. A team that rules a player out can build its game plan around his absence before kickoff. The league publishes the report. The opponent therefore works from the same information.

The label is read closely outside the stadium as well. An NFL player who does not appear in a game earns no fantasy points. Fantasy managers treat an out designation as a signal to change their lineups. Bettors read it the same way — as a confirmed absence rather than a possibility.

The NFL stopped using the probable designation starting with the 2016 season. Probable had told readers that a player was likely to play. Its removal left the injury report with three game-status labels instead of four.

Before the change, the report used a four-step scale. Probable sat at the top, followed by questionable, doubtful and out. Each label signaled a different level of confidence that a player would be available on game day.

With probable gone, the scale has three steps: questionable, doubtful and out. Questionable is now the least severe label a team can assign.

Players who once would have carried a probable tag did not disappear from the report. A player who is expected to play but still has an injury is usually listed with his practice status and no game designation. His name, the injury and his participation level still appear. The game-status column next to him stays blank.

That blank space carries meaning. A player on the report without a designation is generally someone the team expects to have available. A player with questionable next to his name is someone whose availability is still uncertain.

The change shifts more of the reading work onto the practice entries. Under the old system, one word summed up the team's outlook for a lightly injured player. Now readers build that outlook from the participation notes logged across the practice week.

Older news coverage, archived reports and past fantasy football advice can still mention probable players. Those references describe a system that ended before the 2016 season began. They do not reflect how current injury reports are written.

Anyone comparing injury reports across seasons should keep the switch in mind. A probable listing in 2015 and an entry with no game designation in 2017 could point to the same expectation that a player would suit up. The two entries record it under different reporting rules.

For a typical Sunday game, NFL teams file three injury reports during the week: one on Wednesday, one on Thursday and one on Friday. The Friday report is the one that carries game-status designations such as questionable, doubtful and out.

The Wednesday and Thursday reports serve a different purpose. They record which players are hurt or ill, the body part or illness involved, and how much each player took part in that day's practice. They do not assign a game status. A player listed on Wednesday is not being ruled in or out for Sunday at that point. Teams submit each of these daily reports to the league, which then makes it public.

Each report captures a single day. Read together, the three releases form a sequence. A player whose practice participation rises from Wednesday to Friday shows a different trend from one whose participation stays flat or drops. A name that appears on Thursday but not on Wednesday points to an injury or illness that surfaced midweek.

Friday changes the nature of the document. Alongside the practice information, teams attach a game designation to players whose availability is in doubt. That makes the Friday release the main public statement of a team's expectations before the weekend.

The Friday report is still not the last word. Game status can shift between Friday and kickoff. A team can still update a player's status after the Friday release, such as downgrading him to out. The final list of players who will not suit up comes later, on game day itself.

Not every game falls on a Sunday. Teams that play on a Monday, a Thursday or another day follow a shifted version of the same cycle. The specific release days move with the date of the game. The Wednesday-to-Friday pattern does not carry over unchanged.

For a non-Sunday matchup, the timing of that week's reports differs from the standard Sunday pattern.

Every NFL team must submit its list of inactive players about 90 minutes before kickoff. That list is the final, official word on who will not suit up. It can also differ from the game designations a team gave on its Friday report.

The inactive list answers a narrower question than the weekly injury report. The injury report describes health and practice work across a week. The inactive list simply names the players on the active roster who will not dress for that specific game.

Those two documents do not always line up. A player listed as questionable on Friday has no settled status until inactives arrive. He either appears on the list or he does not. That ends the uncertainty for that game.

Change can run in either direction. A player who seemed likely to play can suffer a setback over the weekend or in pregame warmups and end up inactive. A player carrying a game designation can also be cleared and take the field.

Not every inactive player is hurt. Teams cannot dress their entire active roster, so some healthy players sit out each week. Coaches decide who stays in uniform based on depth at each position and the needs of that matchup. A name on the inactive list does not, by itself, signal an injury.

The timing matters to anyone tracking player availability. Fantasy football managers and sports bettors watch for the list closely. It is the last official update before the game begins. For a player listed as questionable, it is often the first definitive one.

A player's status can remain open until that deadline. As a result, a Friday questionable tag can leave fans waiting into game day for an answer. The requirement applies to every game, whether it kicks off on a Sunday afternoon, a weeknight or in prime time.

The inactive list is also separate from roster transactions. A player on it remains on the team's active roster. He can be available the following week without the team making any move. That distinction separates a one-game inactive from longer-term absences handled through formal roster changes.

Injured reserve is a roster transaction, not a game-status label. A player marked out on the weekly injury report is ruled out of one game. A player placed on injured reserve must sit out a minimum number of games before he is eligible to return.

The two terms describe different things. Out is a designation tied to a single upcoming game. It tells the public that the player will not take the field that week. It says nothing about the weeks after that. The following week, the player goes through the reporting cycle again, and his status is set fresh.

Injured reserve runs on a different timeline. Moving a player there changes his roster status rather than his availability for one game. Once the move is made, the player cannot come back simply because he has healed. He has to wait out the required minimum first.

That minimum has not stayed the same. The NFL has changed the number of games an injured reserve player must miss over the years. To work out how long a specific player will be sidelined, check the rule in force for that season.

The two terms also surface in different places. Out appears on the weekly injury report, next to the player's practice participation. A move to injured reserve is announced as a roster transaction. A player on injured reserve is already ineligible to play. He does not need a weekly game designation to confirm it.

The terms carry different expectations as well. An out designation leaves open a quick return, sometimes as soon as the next game. Injured reserve signals that the team expects the player to be unavailable for at least the minimum stretch. A team can also list a player as out for several straight weeks without ever moving him to injured reserve.

For anyone following a team, each term answers its own question. Out answers whether a player will appear this weekend. Injured reserve answers a longer question: the earliest point at which he is allowed to return to the field.

The NFL requires teams to report player injuries accurately, and the league can discipline a club that fails to do so. That requirement turns the weekly injury report from a courtesy into an obligation.

Accuracy applies to every element a club files. A game status has to reflect the team's honest read of a player's availability. A practice entry has to reflect the work the player actually did, not a softer or harsher version of it. The obligation holds for each report a team releases during the week, not only the one that carries game designations.

Misreporting can run in either direction. A club might hide an injury to keep an opponent guessing about a key starter. It might also list a healthy player with an injury to create doubt that does not exist. Both versions mislead the opposing staff and anyone else relying on the report.

Competitive fairness is the main reason the rule matters. Both teams in a game prepare with the same official information about each other. A club that shades its report gains an edge its opponent cannot see or correct before kickoff.

Public trust is the second reason. The report reaches a far wider audience than the two coaching staffs. For readers outside the building, the report is the league's official record of who is hurt. Their confidence in the report depends on the league holding clubs to it.

The rules also give teams an honest outlet for absences that have nothing to do with injury. A player can be listed as not injury related. A club therefore has no reason to invent an ailment to explain a missed practice.

Enforcement rests with the league itself. The NFL receives each club's report, publishes it and can act when a filing falls short. Penalties can include fines against the club.

#5464. Nvidia’s new chairman Harvey Jones is a ‘charming elder statesman’ set to lead the search for the next CEO. But did he enable the current crisis?

In the wake of former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s stunning departure from the company, employees received an email from someone most of them had probably never heard of before, even though he’d been affiliated with the company and its board for decades. His name is Harvey Jones, and he was writing to tell them that he’d just been appointed the company’s first-ever Chair of the Board, and that Nvidia CFO Colette Kress would serve as interim CEO.

“I’m writing to share an important update,” Jones’ note began, according to leaked screenshots of the email. He then tried to reassure employees no doubt left shaken by the past weeks’ revelations and the sudden departure of Jensen Huang, a man who co-founded the company and, until today, had been synonymous with its success. “The Board takes seriously our duty as steward of this great company,” Jones said.

That sense of calm and confidence is something Jones is known for, according to two longtime friends and former coworkers. Although Jones, 73, may not be a household name, he has worked in the technology industry, and in semiconductors, for over 30 years, according to his biography on the Nvidia website. He founded two companies, served as CEO of another, and since 2004 has been managing partner of investment firm Square Wave Ventures. He’s been on Nvidia’s board since 1993, the year Huang founded the company.

Jones comes from a successful Connecticut family—his full name is Harvey Jones III—with an “old school, conservative” way about him, Penny Herscher, who has known Jones since 1984 and used to work for him, tells Fortune. His father was a U.S. Army Colonel and church-goer, who then became a vice president at the Walt Disney World Company. Jones himself is a billionaire, which Forbes says is “almost entirely due to his Nvidia director’s compensation” and the fact that he owns 0.03% of the company.

“Harvey has a deep sense of history,” Chris Rowen, who cofounded the semiconductor processor company Tensilica with Jones in 1997, tells Fortune. He has a house on Nantucket and enjoys sailing classic yachts and fine art. “He has a smooth polish,” Rowen said. But Rowen also said that, despite outward appearances, there’s nothing effete about Jones. “He is such a gentleman, so articulate, and so well-sanded on the outside that you might worry there isn’t a deep fierceness and technical insight inside, but beneath that smooth exterior is a really bright, insightful, aggressive guy.”

At a time of great turbulence, Jones can offer Nvidia a “steady pair of hands” to “sort out” its next chapter, Herscher said. She described him as a “charming elder statesman” who at this point in his career is likely “very hard to ruffle.”

Jones and Rowen played distinct roles during their time at Tensilica. As the CEO, Rowen was an enthusiastic technical and operational leader overseeing the team. As chairman, Jones offered a reassuring presence. “His experience was such that he exuded this confidence and experience,” Rowen said. “If he thought we were on the right track, people were instantly comforted. He really communicated a sense of the larger picture and gave people a great deal of confidence that the wider world needed and approved of what we were doing.”

“He’s very strategic,” Herscher said. “I’m sure he’s right now figuring out the right strategy and steps going forward. He’s always looking around corners.”

Jones’ experience and board tenure also begs the question of how he failed to identify the enormous reputational risk of Huang’s affairs, three of which are known as of this writing. Huang also notoriously had many reports, up to 60 at one point, and no clear successor or succession planning.

“Jones may be the right person to steady the ship, but his longevity is both his greatest qualification and the strongest reason to scrutinize his leadership,” Jonathan Tower, managing partner at the VC firm Catapult tells Fortune. “The board cannot simply present itself as the solution without examining its role in creating the problem.”

Case in point: Huang’s affair with Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of health care, was known inside the company, and appears to violate its code of conduct, The New York Times reported. The code of conduct instructs all employees to “avoid situations where our actions create conflict” including “personal relationships.” The board promises to promptly investigate all reports of misconduct. What happened?

“Major companies often brief their key leadership about potential risks including the theft of intellectual property, legal and regulatory risks, and reputational risks,” Nick Reese, a former Department of Homeland Security employee and assistant professor at NYU SPS’ Center for Global Affairs, tells Fortune. “It is unimaginable to think that Nvidia, a company building geostrategically impactful technology, was not aware of these threats and would not have briefed its principles about them.”

Jones will likely lead the process to select Nvidia’s next CEO, Herscher said, though she had not spoken to him about it directly, and Nvidia did not respond to Fortune’s request for comment. But that’s typically how the process would work in a situation like this, Herscher said, drawing on her knowledge from sitting on three public boards, and being the co-founder of The Chairs Circle, which runs educational programs for board chairs.  The fact that Jones also sits on Nvidia’s Nominating and Corporate Governance Committee makes it even more likely that he will lead this process, she said, as usually that committee is involved in the process.

The search will likely take at least a few months, Herscher said. The board will likely hire a recruiter to identify candidates—something Bloomberg reported this week that Nvidia has already done. That firm will likely do the first outreach, Herscher said, and then Jones will speak to the most promising candidates, along with the rest of the internal search committee.

All signs point to Jones being an effective recruiter, with a wide net of contacts in the industry, Herscher said.

Longtime technology executive Chi-Foo Chan described Jones as “a very persuasive guy” in a 2019 oral history interview with the Computer History Museum, referring to the conversations the two had when Jones convinced Chan to join Synopsys, the electronics company Jones led from 1987 to 1998.

Nvidia shareholders are hoping those skills can wrangle a big fish to come in as Nvidia’s next CEO. Potential successors may include Rene Hass, who is currently the CEO of the chipmaker Arm.  President Trump, who allegedly did not act on reports of Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy, suggested former Apple CEO Tim Cook might be a good pick.

Whoever it is, they’ll need the right operational and product development chops to keep the GPUs flowing.

#5463. How MLB free agency works: 10 rules from opt-outs to compensation picks

Free daily briefing on global business news.

MLB free agency runs on service time, qualifying offers, opt-outs and draft pick rules, and these 10 explainers show how each piece shapes where players sign

Free agency in Major League Baseball is rarely a simple auction. Before a player signs with the highest bidder, a set of calendars, salary formulas and draft penalties comes into play. Those rules decide when he can talk to other clubs and what his signing will cost. They can change what a player is paid and which teams bid on him. They also help explain why one star signs in November while another is still unsigned when spring training camps open in February.

Nearly all of those procedures come from the collective bargaining agreement between Major League Baseball and the MLB Players Association. The current agreement was reached in March 2022, ending a 99-day lockout. It is scheduled to expire on Dec. 1, 2026. That date matters for anyone reading about the rules. The next round of bargaining could rewrite parts of the system described here.

The system follows a clear sequence. A player first has to earn enough service time to qualify. His club then gets a short head start to negotiate with him. After that, league rules and contract terms shape the bidding. A qualifying offer can attach a draft-pick cost to a player. A non-tender can push a younger player onto the market early. The competitive balance tax can lead a payroll-conscious club to walk away. An opt-out clause can return a star to the market before his contract was due to end.

This slideshow covers 10 of those mechanisms. It is a selection of key pieces, not a complete catalog of every provision in the agreement. Each slide explains one rule on its own terms, from the six-year service-time threshold to the compensation picks a club collects when a top player leaves. The final slide covers the posting system, which lets Japanese clubs make players available to major league teams before they reach free agency at home.

Taken together, the slides offer a working guide to MLB free agency rules for fans who follow the offseason closely and for readers who are new to it. Terms such as qualifying offer, non-tender, club option and competitive balance tax appear in transaction reports every winter. Each has a specific meaning. Each can also change where a player ends up and how much he earns.

A major league player becomes eligible for free agency once he has six full years of service time and his contract has expired. One year of service equals 172 days on the active roster or the injured list.

The regular season lasts longer than 172 days. A player can therefore earn a full year of service without spending every day in the majors. He cannot bank more than one year of service in a single season, however long the schedule runs.

Clubs and agents write service time as years and days. A player listed at 5.171 has five years and 171 days. One more day would give him six years. Without it, he stays under his club's control for another season.

The path to six years has three stages. Early in his career, a player's salary is set by his club at or near the league minimum. He then becomes eligible for salary arbitration, which covers the seasons before he reaches six years. Free agency comes last, when all 30 clubs can bid for him.

The six-year standard grew out of a long fight over the reserve clause. That clause once bound a player to his club from one year to the next. After the 1969 season, outfielder Curt Flood refused a trade from the St. Louis Cardinals to the Philadelphia Phillies. He sued to challenge the clause. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled against him in 1972 in Flood v. Kuhn.

The clause gave way through arbitration rather than the courts. In December 1975, arbitrator Peter Seitz ruled that pitchers Andy Messersmith and Dave McNally were free to negotiate with other clubs. Owners and the players union then wrote free agency into their 1976 labor agreement.

Service time also shapes when clubs promote their best prospects. Keeping a top young player in the minors for the first weeks of a season can delay his free agency by a full year. The 2022 collective bargaining agreement addressed that practice in part with the Prospect Promotion Incentive. Under it, a club can earn an extra draft pick when an eligible top prospect accrues a full year of rookie service. The player must then win Rookie of the Year or finish in the top three of MVP or Cy Young voting before he reaches arbitration.

For five days after the World Series ends, a team holds exclusive negotiating rights with its own free agents. Once that window closes, all 30 clubs can make offers. The open market then runs through the Winter Meetings in December and often well beyond them.

Inside the window, a player can re-sign with his current club before anyone else bids. His club must also decide by the end of those five days whether to extend him a qualifying offer. Rival clubs may not discuss contract terms with him during this stretch.

MLB's anti-tampering rules bar a team from negotiating with another club's player before the market opens. The league can discipline clubs that break those rules.

After the window closes, agents collect offers and clubs compare their options. A reported agreement is not final until the player passes a physical exam and the club announces the deal.

Shortstop Carlos Correa's winter of 2022-23 shows how much rides on that last step. In December 2022, he agreed to a 13-year, $350 million deal with the San Francisco Giants. The Giants raised concerns during his medical review, which focused on a lower right leg injury dating to 2014. The deal fell apart. He then agreed to a 12-year, $315 million deal with the New York Mets. That agreement also stalled over the medical review. In January 2023, he signed a six-year, $200 million contract with the Minnesota Twins.

The offseason calendar has other fixed dates. In November, clubs set their 40-man rosters. That roster decides which minor leaguers are protected from the Rule 5 draft. Clubs also face a November deadline to tender contracts to players still under team control. Players who are not tendered contracts become free agents.

The Rule 5 draft takes place at the Winter Meetings. Clubs also use those meetings for much of their face-to-face business with agents.

The market does not shut down after December. Manny Machado agreed to a 10-year, $300 million deal with the San Diego Padres in February 2019. Bryce Harper's 13-year, $330 million agreement with the Philadelphia Phillies came at the end of that same month. A player's timing tends to reflect what clubs want to spend, what rival bidders can offer and whether a draft-pick penalty is attached to his name.

The rules set the order of events, but they set no signing deadline. A free agent can stay unsigned past Opening Day while he waits for a better offer.

A qualifying offer is a one-year contract that a club can extend to its own departing free agent. The salary equals the average of the 125 highest player salaries in the majors. It was $20.325 million for the 2023 offseason and $21.05 million for both the 2024 and 2025 offseasons.

The figure is recalculated every year because it follows the top of the salary market. Every player who receives an offer that winter is offered the same amount. A club cannot adjust it for age, position or performance. The same salary can sit well above one player's market value and well below another's.

The timing is fixed. A club must extend the offer within five days after the World Series ends. The player then has 10 days to accept or reject it. If he accepts, he returns for one season at that salary. If he rejects it, he enters the open market with draft compensation attached to his name.

Eligibility has limits. The player must have spent the entire season with the club that makes the offer. A player traded at the deadline therefore cannot receive one from his new team. A player can also receive a qualifying offer only once in his career. Any later trip through free agency comes without the tag.

The system dates to the 2012 collective bargaining agreement. It replaced the older Type A and Type B rankings, which used statistical formulas to sort free agents and set compensation. Under the current rule, the club chooses which players to tag.

Clubs weigh two risks. If the player accepts, the club owes a large one-year salary. That commitment can strain a tight payroll. If the club does not make the offer, it gives up any claim to compensation when the player leaves. Teams with room to spend often tag players they expect to depart. Teams with thin budgets tend to hold back when an acceptance looks plausible.

Players face the reverse calculation. Accepting guarantees a high salary for one season. It also returns him to free agency the next winter, when no tag is possible. Rejecting opens the door to multiyear offers. It also adds a draft-pick cost that any signing club must absorb.

Most players who receive the offer decline it. No player accepted until November 2015, when Matt Wieters, Colby Rasmus and Brett Anderson each took that winter's $15.8 million offer. Players who accept have tended to be those facing questions about their age, injury history or demand on the open market.

A club that loses a free agent after making him a qualifying offer receives an extra pick in the next amateur draft if he signs with another team. The new club pays nothing to the old one directly. The reward comes only as a draft selection.

Compensation applies only when the player rejects that offer, the one-year contract his club can extend after the season. Two outcomes produce no pick at all. If the player re-signs with his former club, nothing is owed. If he accepts the offer, he stays under contract, and again there is no compensation.

Two factors decide where the extra pick lands. One is the size of the player's new contract. The other is the financial status of the club that lost him. The $50 million dividing line arrived with the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, and it remained in place under the 2022 agreement.

Under that framework, a club that receives revenue sharing gets a pick right after the first round if the departing player signs for $50 million or more. If he signs for less, its pick comes after Competitive Balance Round B. A club that paid the competitive balance tax in the previous season receives a pick only after the fourth round. Clubs in neither group receive a pick after Competitive Balance Round B.

The placement matters because of how the draft pays out. The draft now runs 20 rounds. Every selection in the first 10 rounds carries an assigned slot value. Those values add up to a club's bonus pool, the total it can spend to sign its picks. An earlier pick means a larger slot value, a bigger pool and an earlier choice among the available prospects.

The 2022 agreement added a lottery that sets the first six selections among clubs that missed the playoffs. Compensation picks sit outside that lottery. They are slotted into fixed positions after the rounds described above.

The system has changed shape before. When the qualifying offer began under the 2012 agreement, compensation picks were placed after the first round, with no payroll-based tiers. The tiered structure that followed ties a club's reward partly to its finances. Revenue-sharing recipients receive the most valuable placements. Tax-paying clubs receive the least valuable ones.

The compensation pick is a newly created selection. It is not taken from the team that signs the player. That club faces its own separate penalty. The two sides of the transaction run on different rules.

Compensation picks also cannot be traded. Only Competitive Balance Round picks can change hands in MLB. A club that earns compensation keeps the pick and makes the selection itself.

A club that signs a free agent who turned down a qualifying offer gives up draft picks and, in most cases, international bonus pool money. The size of that cost depends on the signing club's payroll status. Clubs that pay the competitive balance tax lose the most.

The tiered penalty dates to the 2016 collective bargaining agreement, which took effect for the 2016-17 offseason. The 2022 agreement largely kept it in place. A club that receives revenue sharing forfeits its third-highest pick in the next draft. A club that neither receives revenue sharing nor pays the tax forfeits its second-highest pick. It also loses $500,000 of international bonus pool money. A club that paid the tax in the prior season forfeits its second- and fifth-highest picks, along with $1 million of pool money.

The earlier rules worked differently. Under the 2012 agreement, which governed the 2012-13 through 2015-16 offseasons, a club that signed a tagged free agent generally lost its first-round pick. If that pick fell in the top 10, the club lost its second-round pick instead. That approach put a club's highest available selection at stake, regardless of its payroll.

The tiered system did not remove friction from the market. A club may value a tagged player less once it counts the lost selection. Pitcher Dallas Keuchel and closer Craig Kimbrel both rejected qualifying offers after the 2018 season. Neither signed during the winter or spring. Both agreed to deals on June 7, 2019, after that year's draft had begun. By then, a signing club no longer had to surrender picks for them. Keuchel joined the Atlanta Braves, and Kimbrel joined the Chicago Cubs.

The international bonus pool is the second half of the cost. Each club receives a pool of money for signing amateur players who are not subject to the draft. Those players come from outside the U.S., Canada and Puerto Rico. Losing part of that pool narrows a club's options in the next international signing period.

Clubs can offset the loss only in limited ways. Most draft picks cannot be traded under MLB rules. Picks in the Competitive Balance Rounds are the exception. International bonus pool space can also change hands in trades. A club that forfeited pool money can acquire more from another team to restore its spending room.

An opt-out clause lets a player walk away from the remaining years of his contract after a set season and return to free agency. The player alone makes the choice, typically shortly after the World Series ends.

Each clause is negotiated deal by deal. Some large contracts include one, and others do not. A player who declines to use it keeps playing under the original terms.

For a player, the clause offers a second shot at the market. He may outperform his salary, or prices around the league may climb after he signs. In either case he can leave guaranteed money behind in search of a larger deal. If he gets hurt or struggles, he stays and collects what he was promised.

That imbalance makes the clause a cost for the club. The team carries the risk of a declining player. It also risks losing one who plays well. A club may agree to the clause in exchange for a lower total commitment or other concessions in the deal.

Carlos Correa's contract with the Minnesota Twins shows the clause at work in a short deal. In March 2022 he signed for three years and $105.3 million, with opt-outs after the first and second seasons. He exercised the first one after the 2022 season and returned to the market.

Alex Rodriguez used one on a much larger contract. His 10-year, $252 million deal, first signed with the Texas Rangers, allowed him to opt out after the 2007 season. He did, and then re-signed with the New York Yankees for 10 years and $275 million.

A player who opts out enters free agency on the same footing as other players. If he meets the eligibility conditions, his former club can extend a qualifying offer and attach draft compensation to his signing.

Clubs can act before the deadline arrives. A team can offer extra years or more money to persuade a player to give up the clause. It can also plan its payroll around his likely departure.

The clause changes how a contract's length should be read. A five-year deal with an opt-out after the third season may work like a three-year deal if the player performs well. Contracts and transaction reports sometimes describe a similar right as a player option, and the two labels overlap in practice. The key details are who holds the decision and which years it covers.

An option is an extra contract year that one side, or both, can choose to keep or decline. The player holds a player option, the team holds a club option, and a mutual option requires agreement from both. Club and mutual options usually carry a buyout that is paid if the year is declined.

These decisions come shortly after the World Series, in the same early-offseason stretch when clubs handle the rest of their roster business. A declined option, from either side, sends the player into the market without a contract.

A player option puts the choice in the player's hands. If he believes he can earn more on the open market, he declines it and becomes a free agent. If he would rather keep the guaranteed salary, he exercises it and stays. A player coming off an injury or a weak season has a clear financial reason to keep the money.

A club option reverses that control. The team can pick up the year at the stated salary, or it can decline the year and pay the buyout. Clubs often decline when the salary is higher than the value they expect from the player. Picking up the option does not commit the team to keeping him. Clubs sometimes exercise an option and then trade the player. Club options also appear often in early-career extensions. There, they give a team control over what would have been a player's first free agent seasons.

A mutual option requires both sides to want the same thing at the same time. A player who has performed well tends to prefer the market. A club whose player has struggled tends to prefer the buyout. As a result, these options are rarely exercised, and the buyout often becomes the payment that matters.

The buyout is a fixed sum written into the contract. It counts as guaranteed money, so a club that declines an option still pays something. It also counts toward the contract's guaranteed value.

Vesting options add a performance trigger. The extra year becomes guaranteed automatically if the player reaches a target in the prior season, such as a set number of innings pitched or plate appearances. That structure shields a club from paying for an injured player's final year while still paying a healthy one.

Options also affect how headline figures read. A deal reported as seven years may include a club option on the final season, which means only six are guaranteed. The contract terms show how many years a team actually owes.

The competitive balance tax charges clubs whose payrolls pass a set threshold. Under the 2022 collective bargaining agreement, that threshold was $230 million for 2022 and $241 million for 2025. Clubs pay tax on every dollar above it.

The rate climbs with repetition. A club over the threshold for the first time pays 20 percent on the excess. A second consecutive year raises the rate to 30 percent. A third or later year raises it to 50 percent. Clubs that exceed the threshold by wider margins also pay surcharges on top of those base rates.

The higher rates do not last forever. A club that finishes a season under the threshold returns to the first-time rate the next time it goes over. The New York Yankees stayed under the 2018 threshold, which reset their rate after years as a repeat payer.

The tax payroll is built from average annual value, not the cash a player receives in a given season. A club takes the total guaranteed money in a contract, including any signing bonus, and divides it by the number of years. That figure counts against the threshold in every season of the deal. A front office can calculate a signing's tax effect before it agrees to terms.

Deferred money changes that calculation. In December 2023, Shohei Ohtani agreed to a 10-year, $700 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers. He is scheduled to receive $2 million a year during the contract. The remaining $680 million is deferred and paid from 2034 through 2043. Deferred dollars are discounted to present value for tax purposes. The deal counts about $46 million a year against the Dodgers' tax payroll.

The penalties reach beyond cash. A club whose payroll sits $40 million or more above the first threshold has its highest draft pick moved back 10 places in the next amateur draft. If that pick falls among the first six selections, the club's second-highest pick moves back instead.

The threshold also shapes the market below the stars. A club just under it may pass on a mid-tier free agent whose salary would push its payroll over. A club with room beneath the line can absorb the same contract without a tax bill.

Salary arbitration sets pay for players with three to six years of major league service time. A non-tender sends a player to free agency before he reaches the six-year mark. Both processes shape which players are available each winter.

A player in the arbitration window cannot sign with any club he chooses. His team still controls his rights. He can, however, ask a neutral panel to set his salary when he and the club disagree.

The format is known as final-offer arbitration. The player and the club each submit one salary figure, typically in January. If they do not settle, a panel of three arbitrators chooses one of the two numbers at a hearing. The panel cannot split the difference or pick a figure in between.

That all-or-nothing design raises the cost of an unrealistic filing. A club that files too low risks losing the hearing outright. A player who files too high faces the same risk. Most cases settle before anyone enters a hearing room. Hearings that do go forward are held in February. The panel weighs factors such as the player's performance and the salaries of comparable players.

Some players reach arbitration a year early under a rule known as Super Two. The group includes players with at least two years of service but fewer than three. To qualify, a player must rank in the top 22 percent of that group in service time. He must also have accrued at least 86 days of service in the previous season. A Super Two player gets four arbitration years instead of three. His salary begins to climb a year sooner as a result.

The tender deadline in November is where arbitration and free agency meet. By that date, a club must offer a contract to every arbitration-eligible or otherwise reserved player it wants to keep. A player who does not receive one is non-tendered. He becomes a free agent immediately, with no qualifying offer or draft compensation attached.

Clubs non-tender players for practical reasons. A projected arbitration salary may exceed what the club thinks the player is worth. A player may be recovering from an injury. A club may need to clear a spot on its 40-man roster. A non-tendered player can sign with any team, including the one that let him go.

The non-tender list adds a group of established major leaguers to the market weeks before the Winter Meetings. Unlike veterans who reached six years of service, many of these players are still in their arbitration years when they hit the open market.

A separate group arrives through minor league free agency. These players have spent a set number of seasons in the minors without being added to a 40-man roster. Most sign minor league contracts with new organizations. Some of those deals include invitations to major league spring training.

The posting system lets a Nippon Professional Baseball club make one of its players available to MLB teams before he reaches international free agency. If a major league team signs him, that team pays a release fee to his Japanese club.

The decision to post belongs to the NPB club, not the player. Once a player is posted, he has a 45-day window to negotiate with major league teams. Every MLB club can make an offer. If no deal is reached before the window closes, he returns to his Japanese team for the coming season.

The release fee is tied to the size of the contract and rises on a sliding scale. It equals 20 percent of the first $25 million, 17.5 percent of the next $25 million and 15 percent of any amount above $50 million. The signing team pays the fee on top of the contract. It does not come out of the player's salary.

Posting offers an earlier route than waiting out a career in Japan. NPB players can become international free agents on their own after a set number of years of service with their clubs. A Japanese club that expects to lose a star may post him a year or two early. That way it collects a fee instead of watching him leave without one.

Pitcher Yoshinobu Yamamoto took this route. The Orix Buffaloes posted him, and he agreed to a 12-year, $325 million contract with the Los Angeles Dodgers in December 2023. The fee went to Orix and was not part of the contract total.

Age and experience change the rules. A foreign professional must be at least 25 and have six seasons in a recognized foreign league to sign a standard free agent deal. A younger or less experienced player counts as an international amateur. His signing bonus is limited by each club's international bonus pool.

The Hokkaido Nippon-Ham Fighters posted Shohei Ohtani in 2017. He was younger than 25, so he came to the majors under those amateur limits when he signed with the Los Angeles Angels. He then completed six years of major league service. After the 2023 season, he entered free agency as an established player with no bonus pool restrictions.
